chunks.h: Chapter 1: Text is not numbers yet
chunks.t: Ask a language model to add 1234 and 5678 and it will often get the answer wrong, in a way that looks less like a reasoning failure and more like a transcription error. The cause sits upstream of every weight in the network. A model never sees the string you typed. It sees a sequence of integer token IDs. Each ID indexes a row in an embedding matrix whose shape is vocabulary size by model width, and at the other end an output projection maps the final hidden vector back to a score for every vocabulary entry. Those weights are often stored in fp16, two bytes per parameter. Before any matrix multiply happens, a tokenizer converts text into those IDs.

chunks.h: Chapter 1: Text is not numbers yet
chunks.t: Byte-level tokenizers first encode the text as UTF-8 bytes; character-level BPE, as in Sennrich et al., operates on Unicode characters. UTF-8 is a variable-width encoding. ASCII characters take one byte, many accented and Cyrillic characters take two, and emoji can take four. The tokenizer turns that byte stream into pieces that trade sequence length against vocabulary size, and the model inherits every choice in that trade.

chunks.h: Byte-pair encoding began as a compressor
chunks.t: That scheme is byte-pair encoding, and it was not invented for language models. Philip Gage published it in the C Users Journal in 1994 as "A New Algorithm for Data Compression." The idea is almost embarrassingly simple. Take a stream of symbols. Count every adjacent pair. Find the pair that occurs most often. Replace every instance of that pair with a new symbol that did not previously exist. Repeat. Each round replaces every occurrence of that pair with the new symbol, shrinking the stream by one symbol per occurrence, and adds exactly one entry to the dictionary. After enough rounds the stream is much shorter than what you started with. That is a compressor.

chunks.h: Byte-pair encoding began as a compressor
chunks.t: It knows nothing about grammar, morphology, or meaning. For twenty-one years it stayed a compressor. Then in 2015, Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch were preparing a neural machine translation system and hit a wall. Their model produced output one word at a time from a fixed vocabulary, and any word outside that vocabulary was unmappable. Rare names, compounds, inflections, and loanwords all collapsed into a single unknown token. Their fix was to borrow Gage's algorithm, run it on the training corpus, and let the model operate on subword units instead of words. Frequent words stay whole. Rare words get split into pieces that the model has seen before.

chunks.h: Byte-pair encoding began as a compressor
chunks.t: The paper was called "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units," it ran its experiments on the WMT 2015 shared translation task, and it appeared at ACL 2016. It made subword tokenization a standard part of neural translation and later language-model pipelines.

chunks.h: The merge loop and rank order
chunks.t: Almost every strange behavior downstream traces back to this merge procedure. You start with a corpus and a base alphabet. In the original formulation the alphabet was characters; in the byte-level variant that came later it is the 256 possible byte values. You count adjacent pairs across the whole corpus. Suppose the pair consisting of e followed by r is the most frequent. You write a merge rule, "e r → er," assign it rank zero, and rewrite the corpus so every er is now a single symbol. Then you recount, find the new most frequent pair, and write rank one. You do this tens of thousands of times. The output is an ordered list of merge rules, and that list is the tokenizer.

chunks.h: The merge loop and rank order
chunks.t: At inference time, production byte-level tokenizers first split the input into chunks via pre-tokenization and handle special tokens, then apply the merge rules in rank order, greedily, left to right, within each chunk; merges are not applied across chunk boundaries. Nothing about the process consults meaning. A small corpus makes the mechanics concrete. Take the words low five times, lower twice, and lowest once, with an end-of-word marker </w> appended to each word. The initial symbols are l o w </w>, l o w e r </w>, and l o w e s t </w>. The pair l o occurs eight times, and so does o w.

chunks.h: The merge loop and rank order
chunks.t: A deterministic tie-break, say lexicographic order, picks l o, assigns it rank 0, and rewrites every l o as lo. The corpus becomes lo w </w>, lo w e r </w>, and lo w e s t </w>. Now lo w occurs eight times, so rank 1 is lo w → low. The corpus becomes low </w>, low e r </w>, and low e s t </w>. The pair low </w> occurs five times, so rank 2 is low </w> → low</w>. Next low e occurs three times, so rank 3 is low e → lowe. The pairs lowe r and r </w> both occur twice; lexicographic order picks lowe r, rank 4. Then lower </w> occurs twice, rank 5. The ordered list is the tokenizer. At inference time the loop is short.

chunks.h: The merge loop and rank order
chunks.t: For rank r from 0 to N-1, scan the current symbol sequence left to right, and whenever the current pair equals the pair for rank r, replace it with the merged symbol. Continue until no rule applies. Rank order matters because merges can conflict. Suppose rank 0 is a b → ab and rank 1 is b c → bc. On the unseen string abc, rank order gives ab c. A left-to-right pass that applied the longest match first could give a bc. The ranks decide which merge wins. On an unseen string such as lowest, the same loop applies rank 0 to get lo w e s t </w>, rank 1 to get low e s t </w>, rank 3 to get lowe s t </w>, and then stops when no later rule matches. The final pieces are lowe, s, t, and </w>.

chunks.h: The merge loop and rank order
chunks.t: The model has never seen lowest as a whole word, but it has seen the pieces.

chunks.h: Byte-level BPE and SentencePiece
chunks.t: Byte-level BPE, introduced with GPT-2 in 2019 by Radford and colleagues, changed the base alphabet from characters to bytes. That matters because 256 byte values cover every string that can exist, including emoji, Cyrillic, and broken UTF-8. There is no unknown token, ever. GPT-2's vocabulary of 50,257 decomposes exactly into 256 base byte tokens, 50,000 learned merges, and one end-of-text marker. That arithmetic is the whole design. Before BPE runs, a pre-tokenization regex splits text into chunks. GPT-2's regex groups contractions, letter runs with an optional leading space, number runs, punctuation, and whitespace.

chunks.h: Byte-level BPE and SentencePiece
chunks.t: Llama 3's regex, described by Dubey and colleagues in 2024, differs in the number branch. It groups digits in runs of up to three, so 1234 is offered to BPE as 123 and 4. GPT-2's regex groups all consecutive digits into one chunk, so 1234 is offered as a single unit. Whether that unit becomes one token depends on the learned merges, but the regex decides what the merge model is allowed to see. Special tokens such as beginning-of-sequence, end-of-sequence, padding, and unknown markers are reserved before pre-tokenization and are never split by merges. SentencePiece, published by Taku Kudo and John Richardson at Google in 2018, attacked a different annoyance.

chunks.h: Byte-level BPE and SentencePiece
chunks.t: Character-based and byte-based tokenizers still required a pre-tokenization step that split on whitespace, and whitespace splitting is a language-specific decision that breaks for Chinese and Thai and is awkward for anything with unusual spacing. SentencePiece treats the raw input as a stream of characters after normalization, and it represents a space with a visible marker, conventionally ▁. Whitespace becomes an ordinary symbol the algorithm can merge across, and decoding replaces ▁ with a space. Normalization can change the string before tokenization, for example by applying Unicode compatibility rules, so round-tripping is not always byte-identical.

chunks.h: Byte-level BPE and SentencePiece
chunks.t: SentencePiece supports byte fallback, which encodes any character outside the vocabulary as a sequence of UTF-8 byte tokens such as <0xE4>, so the tokenizer remains reversible even for rare scripts. It also supports two training algorithms. BPE learns an ordered merge list. Unigram starts with a large candidate vocabulary, assigns each piece a probability, and prunes pieces that contribute little likelihood until the vocabulary reaches the target size; segmentation then chooses the most probable sequence of pieces. T5 and many open-weight families, including Llama 1 and 2, use SentencePiece or a descendant; Llama 3 switched to a tiktoken-style byte-level BPE tokenizer.

chunks.h: The vocabulary-size trade
chunks.t: Now the trade. Vocabulary size buys you shorter sequences and costs you parameters. A larger vocabulary compresses text into fewer tokens, which shrinks the attention matrix, since attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, and shortens generation, since every token produced requires a full forward pass. The price is paid at the two ends of the network. The input embedding table has one row per vocabulary entry, and the output projection has one column per entry. Llama 3 uses 128,256 tokens.

chunks.h: The vocabulary-size trade
chunks.t: At a model width of 4,096 and two bytes per weight, the embedding table alone is 128,256 × 4,096 × 2 = 1,050,673,152 bytes, just under a gibibyte, and the untied output projection is the same size again. GPT-2's 50,257 entries at the same width would cost 411,705,344 bytes each. Meta accepted roughly two and a half times the embedding cost in exchange for shorter sequences and better compression of non-English text, which had been a weakness of Llama 2. The attention saving follows from a stated workload rather than a measured one. Take a prompt of 131,072 tokens, the context length the book uses elsewhere. Attention work over a prompt scales with the square of that length.

chunks.h: The vocabulary-size trade
chunks.t: Halving the token count cuts attention work to a quarter. Generation savings are different: with KV caching, each new token attends to the current context, so attention cost per generated token grows with context length; the main saving from fewer output tokens is fewer forward passes. Take a reply of 600 generated tokens, where each generated token needs a forward pass. A 10% reduction removes about 60 forward passes per request. Those savings are real, but they are paid for with embedding parameters and with a vocabulary that must be trained on a corpus broad enough to cover the languages you care about.

chunks.h: Fertility and digit composition
chunks.t: Fertility is the average number of tokens a tokenizer spends per word, and it is not constant across languages. English sits comfortably; a language with rich inflection, or one written in a script that the merge process rarely encountered during tokenizer training, can cost more tokens for the same content. A byte-level example shows the worst case. The English sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog." is 44 UTF-8 bytes. With no merges, byte-level BPE spends 44 tokens on it. A 44-character Cyrillic sentence starts at 88 bytes, because Cyrillic characters take two bytes in UTF-8, so before merges it costs twice as many tokens.

chunks.h: Fertility and digit composition
chunks.t: Merges trained mostly on English may not cover those Cyrillic pairs, so the gap can persist. The same context window then holds less text, the same request costs more, and the model's effective capacity in that language is lower. Arithmetic fails for a related structural reason. If 1234 is a single token, the model has no access to the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 as separate objects. Gradient updates touch the embedding row for that whole numeral, and the model has no explicit digit-level token positions to compose over.

chunks.h: Fertility and digit composition
chunks.t: Its embedding can still encode digit-related features internally, but without separate digit subpieces, learning digit-wise procedures and generalizing to unseen numerals is substantially harder. Llama 3's regex groups digits in runs of up to three, so 1234 is offered as 123 and 4; 5678 is offered as 567 and 8. That gives the model repeated digit subpieces across many numbers and a chance to learn position-dependent digit operations. The tokenizer change does not guarantee arithmetic, but it changes what the model can learn compositionally.

chunks.h: Glitch tokens and trailing spaces
chunks.t: Then there are the glitch tokens. In 2023, Jessica Rumbelow and Matthew Watkins cataloged tokens in GPT-3's vocabulary that produced bizarre behavior when prompted, with SolidGoldMagikarp becoming the famous example. The tokenizer is trained on one corpus, the model on another. A token can survive into the final vocabulary because it was frequent in the tokenizer's data, then never appear in the model's training data at all. If input and output embeddings are untied, the input-embedding row for a token that never appears in the context receives no input-side gradient.

chunks.h: Glitch tokens and trailing spaces
chunks.t: But the softmax denominator still gives every output row a small nonzero gradient, and with tied embeddings the shared row is updated. So such a row is typically under-trained rather than frozen at initialization. In practice the boundary is blurrier than that: Rumbelow and Watkins reported only that these tokens had very little involvement in training, and later work by Land and Bartolo in 2024 characterized glitch tokens as under-trained rather than untouched, using embedding norms as the indicator. Either way the row is a slot in the table pointing at noise, and the model has no idea what to do when you hand it one. One more consequence surprises people.

chunks.h: Glitch tokens and trailing spaces
chunks.t: GPT-2-style byte-level BPE tokenizers attach an optional leading space to the following word chunk, so hello and hello are different token strings with different embeddings. A prompt that ends in a trailing space is asking the model to predict a continuation from a token boundary it did not expect. If an API normalizes trailing whitespace before tokenization, the final token changes before the model sees it, and the continuation shifts. Tokenizer training corpus selection is its own design decision. The corpus should sample the distribution the model will serve, with enough balance across languages and scripts that common pairs get merges.

chunks.h: Glitch tokens and trailing spaces
chunks.t: Deduplication matters because repeated text inflates pair counts. Normalization matters because it decides which strings are equivalent. Evaluation should go beyond fertility. Bits-per-byte on held-out text normalizes cross-entropy by UTF-8 bytes and lets you compare tokenizers with different vocabularies. Round-trip decoding checks reversibility. Downstream task accuracy checks whether the pieces preserve the distinctions the model needs. A common recipe is byte-level BPE or SentencePiece, vocabulary in the tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands, digit grouping chosen deliberately, and tokenizer training data balanced across languages.

chunks.h: Glitch tokens and trailing spaces
chunks.t: A tokenizer is a compression scheme with a vocabulary-construction procedure—such as a BPE merge list or unigram probabilities—and a normalization policy, and every model built on top of it inherits the choices made by whoever ran the merge loop. When the next chapter opens up the embedding table, remember that the rows in it are indexed by these arbitrary pieces, not by words.

chunks.h: Chapter 2: A vector is a coordinate, not a meaning
chunks.t: The tokenizer hands the model an integer, and that integer is a name badge. Byte-pair encoding builds it in a fixed order. Training starts with 256 single-byte symbols, then repeatedly counts adjacent pairs across the corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new symbol, and assigns that symbol the next free id. A token produced by an early merge gets a low number. One assembled late gets a high number. The id records when a merge happened and nothing else. The id for "cat" is not close to the id for "kitten," and the id for "the" sits wherever the merge order dropped it. Nothing in the number is ordered, weighted, or comparable to anything else.

chunks.h: The token id carries no geometry
chunks.t: So the first operation in every language model throws the integer away and replaces it with a vector. The obvious construction is one-hot. Give the vocabulary a hundred thousand entries and each token becomes a list of a hundred thousand numbers, all zero except a single one at the token's own position. The dot product of two distinct one-hot vectors is exactly zero, because no position holds a one in both. Every word is equally unrelated to every other word. The usual complaint about one-hot is imprecise, so the real problem deserves a careful statement. A linear layer over one-hot inputs does have a gradient. Feed it "cat" and the row at cat's index receives a nonzero update.

chunks.h: The token id carries no geometry
chunks.t: That row moves. What the loss never does is compare two input rows. "Cat" and "kitten" are trained against separate output slots, and no term in the objective pulls their input rows toward each other. Each row learns a private association with the output vocabulary. The table stays a lookup, and no geometry forms. The dense representation is the same linear layer viewed as a lookup table: one row per vocabulary entry, each row a few thousand numbers wide, learned rather than assigned. The geometry comes from training those rows under a shared prediction objective, not from replacing one-hot with dense.

chunks.h: The token id carries no geometry
chunks.t: Yoshua Bengio and colleagues did this in 2003 in "A Neural Probabilistic Language Model" (JMLR), learning a distributed representation for each word as a side effect of predicting the next one. Ronan Collobert and Jason Weston made the representation the point in 2008 in "A Unified Architecture for Natural Language Processing" (ICML). Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google turned it into a standard tool in 2013 with "Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality" (NIPS).

chunks.h: Scoring pairs with dot products and softmax
chunks.t: Two pieces of notation carry the rest of the chapter. The dot product of two vectors is the sum of their coordinatewise products, a single number that grows when the vectors point the same way. The softmax turns a list of scores into a probability distribution by exponentiating each score and dividing by the sum of all the exponentials. The skip-gram objective is worth walking through, because it explains why the resulting geometry is useful. Take a sentence, pick a center word, then pick a context word from a window around it. The model keeps two vectors per vocabulary item, one for when the word is the center and one for when it is context, and scores the pair with their dot product.

chunks.h: Scoring pairs with dot products and softmax
chunks.t: Write v_c for the center vector and u_o for the context vector. A softmax over the whole vocabulary would turn the score into a probability, but the denominator needs one exponential per vocabulary entry for every training pair. At fifty thousand tokens and a few billion pairs, that is on the order of a hundred trillion exponentials. Negative sampling avoids the denominator. For each real center-context pair, draw a handful of words from the corpus, label them noise, and train a binary classifier. The negatives come from the unigram distribution raised to the 0.75 power, which dampens the dominance of "the" and "of" without flattening the distribution entirely.

chunks.h: Scoring pairs with dot products and softmax
chunks.t: With k negatives the loss for one pair is L = -log σ(v_c · u_o) - Σ_{i=1}^{k} log σ(-v_c · u_{n_i}) where σ is the logistic function. The cost per pair is k+1 sigmoid evaluations instead of fifty thousand exponentials. With k=5 that is a factor of roughly eight thousand. The gradient on the positive term is what pulls the two vectors together. Differentiate L with respect to u_o and you get -(1-σ(v_c·u_o)) v_c. Put numbers on it. Let v_c = (0.5, -0.2) and u_o = (0.3, 0.4). The score is 0.15 - 0.08 = 0.07, and σ(0.07) = 1/(1+e^{-0.07}) = 0.517. The positive loss is -ln(0.517) = 0.659. The gradient with respect to u_o is -0.483 × (0.5, -0.2) = (-0.241, 0.097).

chunks.h: Scoring pairs with dot products and softmax
chunks.t: With a learning rate of 0.1, stochastic gradient descent updates u_o ← (0.3, 0.4) - 0.1 × (-0.241, 0.097) = (0.324, 0.390). The new score is 0.162 - 0.078 = 0.084, higher than before. The context vector has moved toward the center vector. The negative terms do the reverse, pushing noise vectors away. Do that over billions of pairs and the geometry settles. At equilibrium the positive gradient and the summed negative gradients balance, and the direction v_c settles into is pulled toward a frequency-weighted combination of the context vectors it actually co-occurred with, corrected by the negative-sampling term over frequency-sampled non-contexts—not simply their average.

chunks.h: Scoring pairs with dot products and softmax
chunks.t: Words that keep turning up in the same neighborhoods end up with similar averages, so their vectors point in similar directions. "Cat" and "kitten" share contexts, and their vectors converge because they are pulled toward the same mean.

chunks.h: Other routes to the same geometry
chunks.t: Jeffrey Pennington, Richard Socher and Christopher Manning reached a similar geometry in 2014 from the opposite direction. GloVe, published at EMNLP as "GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation," factorizes a word-word co-occurrence matrix instead of running a prediction task. Its objective is a weighted least-squares fit to the log of the co-occurrence counts, and the vectors it produces behave much like word2vec's. Two routes arriving at the same place suggests the geometry tracks language use rather than the algorithm.

chunks.h: Other routes to the same geometry
chunks.t: Piotr Bojanowski and colleagues added a third route with fastText, "Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information," which went up on arXiv in 2016 and appeared in TACL volume 5 in 2017. Each word's vector is the sum of vectors for its character n-grams, for n from 3 to 6, plus a vector for the whole word. "Running" is the sum of the vectors for <ru, run, unn, nni, nin, ing, ng>, with angle brackets marking word boundaries, plus a vector for the whole word. A word never seen in training still gets a vector, assembled from whatever n-grams it shares with known words.

chunks.h: Other routes to the same geometry
chunks.t: That is why morphology leaks into fastText's geometry, and why it handles rare and misspelled tokens better than a pure lookup table.

chunks.h: Cosine similarity and the anisotropic cone
chunks.t: Once you have vectors you need a way to compare them. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the two lengths. Take a = (3, 4) and b = (4, 3). The dot product is 12 + 12 = 24, both lengths are 5, and the cosine is 24/25 = 0.96. Now scale a by ten to (30, 40). The dot product with b is 120 + 120 = 240, the lengths are 50 and 5, and the cosine is 240/250 = 0.96 again. Length changed by a factor of ten and the angle did not move. Compare a with c = (0, 5) instead. The dot product is 20, the lengths are 5 and 5, and the cosine is 0.8, an angle of about 37 degrees.

chunks.h: Cosine similarity and the anisotropic cone
chunks.t: Training with an unnormalized dot product lets frequent words drift to large magnitudes, because a big vector scores high against everything. Cosine discards the length and keeps the angle. Then the trouble starts. Take two random words from a trained table and compute the cosine. You do not get something near zero. You get something comfortably positive. Kawin Ethayarajh measured this in 2019 in "How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations?" (EMNLP) and confirmed the pattern across layers of several models. The name for it is anisotropy. The vectors occupy a narrow cone rather than filling the space around the origin. A toy table shows the mechanism.

chunks.h: Cosine similarity and the anisotropic cone
chunks.t: Let the mean vector of the table be m = (1, 1), and let two rows be a = (1.6, 1.05) and b = (1.05, 1.6). Their dot product is 1.68 + 1.68 = 3.36. Each length is √(2.56 + 1.1025) = 1.914, so the cosine is 3.36/3.662 = 0.917. Now subtract m from both. The rows become a' = (0.6, 0.05) and b' = (0.05, 0.6). The dot product is 0.03 + 0.03 = 0.06, each length is √0.3625 = 0.602, and the cosine is 0.06/0.3625 = 0.166. Same two words, same table, and the similarity fell from 0.917 to 0.166 once the shared component came out.

chunks.h: Cosine similarity and the anisotropic cone
chunks.t: Where does the shared component come from? Negative sampling draws its negatives from the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power (the exponent flattens the distribution somewhat, but frequent words still dominate), so every center vector is pushed away from the same small set of very frequent words. That push adds a common direction to the whole table. The softmax denominator does something similar, since every prediction is normalized against the same vocabulary. Frequent words dominate both terms, and their direction spreads to everything else. The fix is unglamorous and takes two steps. First, compute the mean of all rows and subtract it from every row.

chunks.h: Cosine similarity and the anisotropic cone
chunks.t: Second, compute the top few principal components of the centered table and remove each vector's projection onto them, v' = v - Σ (v · p_i) p_i over the components you keep. Mu and Viswanath published this recipe in 2018 as "All-but-the-Top" (ICLR). To check whether it worked, sample ten thousand random word pairs, record the mean cosine before and after, and watch it fall toward zero.

chunks.h: Analogies and the embedding table
chunks.t: The famous demonstration is the parallelogram. Take man = (1.0, 0.2), woman = (0.9, 0.7), king = (0.8, 0.1), queen = (0.7, 0.6). The offset from man to woman is (-0.1, 0.5). Add it to king and you get (0.7, 0.6), which is queen exactly, so the cosine between the query and queen is 1.0. The arithmetic works because the training data made the two offsets nearly parallel. Anna Rogers, Aleksandr Drozd and Bofang Li showed in 2017, in "The (too many) problems of analogical reasoning with word vectors" (SEM), that the result is fragile. They took the standard analogy test set, added small random perturbations to the vectors, and re-ran the ranking.

chunks.h: Analogies and the embedding table
chunks.t: Accuracy fell sharply, which is a warning about reading too much into any single nearest neighbor. There is a second piece of housekeeping that matters more for memory than for linguistics. A transformer needs two matrices that touch the vocabulary. The input embedding E has shape V × d, where V is the vocabulary size and d is the model width. The output projection W has shape d × V, turning the final hidden vector h into a score per vocabulary item. If W = Eᵀ, the logits are h Eᵀ, which is the dot product of h with every row of E.

chunks.h: Analogies and the embedding table
chunks.t: Press and Wolf described the trick in a 2016 preprint published at EACL 2017, "Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models," and Inan and colleagues proposed it independently in a 2016 preprint that appeared at ICLR 2017, "Tying Word Vectors and Word Classifiers." Tying changes the gradient. The embedding lookup contributes a scatter of the incoming gradient into the rows that appeared in the batch. The output projection contributes an outer product of the logits gradient with h, transposed back into the same shape. Both land on E and sum. The direction that means "cat" when the model reads is the direction that scores "cat" when it writes, and both losses shape it.

chunks.h: Analogies and the embedding table
chunks.t: The savings are easy to count. GPT-2 small has V = 50,257 and d = 768, so the embedding matrix holds 38,597,376 parameters. GPT-2 ties its matrices, and its published 124 million parameters already count that matrix once. Untie them and the model would carry a second copy of the same 38.6 million, taking the total from about 124 million to about 163 million, so tying saves roughly 24 percent of the untied weight count. Not every model ties. LLaMA-7B has V = 32,000 and d = 4,096, an embedding of 131 million parameters, and it leaves the two matrices untied. Training the transformer table works differently from training word2vec.

chunks.h: Analogies and the embedding table
chunks.t: The embedding is optimized by the language-modeling loss, and the gradient reaches only the rows for tokens that appear in the batch. A batch of B sequences of length T touches at most B × T rows out of V, so the update is sparse. The row itself stays static. What changes across sentences is the output of the block stack, where attention mixes projected hidden states derived from those rows. "Bank" gets the same input row in both sentences, and a different contextual vector at the end, because the surrounding tokens pull different rows into the mix. Computationally the lookup is a gather.

chunks.h: Analogies and the embedding table
chunks.t: Multiplying a one-hot row by the table selects one row and adds a row of zeros, and every implementation notices this and indexes directly into a contiguous array. The memory cost is exactly V × d × bytes, with no sparsity tricks available. A vocabulary of 128,256 against 4,096 dimensions comes to 525,336,576 numbers. At two bytes each that is about 1.05 GB, and at four bytes it doubles. Vocabulary size is a design decision with teeth, and multilingual models pay for their coverage partly in this currency—larger vocabularies also raise output-layer/optimizer memory and softmax compute, and tokenizer fertility affects sequence length.

chunks.h: What cosine actually measures
chunks.t: One caveat belongs at the end. Nearest-neighbor and cosine benchmarks measure distributional overlap, not meaning. A high cosine says two vectors were pulled toward similar context averages. It does not say the model understands either word. Report the postprocessed number, the sample size, and the model, or you are reporting the cone.

chunks.h: The one lane everything writes into
chunks.t: In 2015 Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun at Microsoft Research put "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition" on arXiv, and it was published at CVPR in 2016. The idea inside it is one of the key enabling ingredients that lets you train a transformer with forty layers instead of four; normalization, initialization, attention scaling, and optimization also matter They were training convolutional networks on ImageNet and hit a wall that had nothing to do with overfitting.

chunks.h: The one lane everything writes into
chunks.t: In the 2015 ResNet paper, a 56-layer plain network on CIFAR-10 had higher training error than a 20-layer plain network on the same data; on ImageNet, a 34-layer plain net had higher validation error than an 18-layer one. Overfitting would show up as a gap between training and test error; here the training loss itself refused to come down. Adding layers had made the optimization problem harder.

chunks.h: The residual path and the gradient product
chunks.t: The fix was to stop asking a block to compute the whole transformation. Each block computes a correction F(x), and the layer outputs F(x) + x. The original input is added back, unchanged, at every block. Why that trains is a statement about the backward pass. A Jacobian is the matrix of partial derivatives of a vector output with respect to a vector input. Its spectral norm is its largest singular value, which bounds how much it can stretch a vector. For a plain stack, the gradient reaching the first block is a product of L Jacobians. If each has spectral norm s, the product has norm at most s^L. For two layers with s=0.9, the product norm is at most 0.81; with s=1.1, at most 1.21.

chunks.h: The residual path and the gradient product
chunks.t: At 56 layers, the bound is about 0.003 and 208 The first vanishes, the second explodes. With the residual, the layer map is x_{l+1}=x_l+F_l(x_l). Its Jacobian is I + J_l, where J_l is the Jacobian of F_l. The product over L layers is ∏(I+J_l). Expand for two layers: (I+J_1)(I+J_2)=I+J_1+J_2+J_1J_2. For L layers, the product is I plus every ordered product of a subset of the J_l, including the empty product I. The identity path has derivative exactly I. Even if each J_l is small, that term still delivers a gradient to the first layer.

chunks.h: The residual path and the gradient product
chunks.t: The expansion is usable when the J_l are small enough that the higher-order products do not dominate; initialization and normalization are chosen to keep them small at the start. He et al. trained a 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-10 and a 152-layer one on ImageNet, so depth stopped being a gamble. They were not first. Srivastava, Greff and Schmidhuber published highway networks earlier in 2015, with y=T(x)H(x)+(1-T(x))x, where T is a learned gate. ResNet dropped the gate and used a bare identity. A plain addition has no parameters, cannot be trained to close itself off, and costs nothing. The gated version could learn something richer, but the ungated one scaled further in practice.

chunks.h: Residual sublayers and the persistent stream
chunks.t: Vaswani and colleagues built the 2017 transformer on the same spine. Every sublayer in the encoder and decoder ends by adding its output to its input. Encoder layers have two residual sublayers—self-attention and the feed-forward network—so the encoder stream is written to twice per layer. Decoder layers have three—masked self-attention, cross-attention, and the feed-forward network—so the decoder stream is written to three times per layer. Here is where the picture changes. It is natural to draw a transformer as a stack of blocks, each handing a transformed representation to the next, the way a CNN hands feature maps up a hierarchy. That drawing misses the object that persists.

chunks.h: Residual sublayers and the persistent stream
chunks.t: There is one vector per token, its width is set once and never changes, and it lasts from the embedding lookup to the final unembedding. Attention and the feed-forward network do not replace it. They read from it and add to it. Concretely, attention projects the stream three ways into queries, keys and values. Each head computes a weighted sum over the values at all positions up to and including the current one (causal masking blocks only future positions). The heads' outputs are concatenated, projected back up to the stream's width by an output matrix, and added.

chunks.h: Residual sublayers and the persistent stream
chunks.t: The feed-forward network reads the stream, expands it into a wider hidden layer, applies a nonlinearity, projects back down, and adds. Neither sublayer carries state from one layer to the next. The only thing that survives the whole depth is the stream itself. The division of labor is clean. Attention is the only operation that moves information between positions; everything else in the block is per-token. The feed-forward network is where a token does its own computation, reading what attention brought in and writing conclusions back. Because the width never changes, any sublayer can read the stream at any depth without an adapter.

chunks.h: Residual sublayers and the persistent stream
chunks.t: The unembedding matrix at the end can be applied to the stream after layer three, provided the final layer norm is applied first, just as mechanically as after layer forty. That is what makes the stream a bus rather than a pipeline. Every component is wired to the same lane, at the same gauge. It is also why deleting a layer at inference time can still yield coherent text. Deleting a block removes the sublayer computation and its write; the identity path still carries the stream forward, but every later block now reads a different vector. Coherence after deletion is an empirical property of trained networks, not a theorem.

chunks.h: Pre-norm, post-norm, and stream growth
chunks.t: The placement of layer normalization determines what the stream looks like. The 2017 paper put the norm after the residual addition, so each block computed LayerNorm(x+Sublayer(x)). That renormalizes the stream at every layer, keeping its magnitude bounded, but it also puts a rescaling operation directly in the identity path. Post-norm transformers in practice used learning-rate warmup. GPT-2 in 2019 used pre-norm instead, normalizing the input to the sublayer and then adding the sublayer's raw output to the unnormalized stream.

chunks.h: Pre-norm, post-norm, and stream growth
chunks.t: Xiong and colleagues analyzed the two arrangements in 2020 and showed that pre-norm gives better-behaved gradients at initialization, which is why warmup can be dropped. GPT-3 in 2020 and LLaMA in 2023 also use pre-norm. The gradient argument is worth writing out. For pre-norm, the block is y=x+F(N(x)). Its Jacobian is I+J_F J_N. The identity term I is separate; the LayerNorm Jacobian J_N multiplies only the branch. For post-norm, the block is y=N(x+F(x)). Its Jacobian is J_N(I+J_F)=J_N+J_N J_F. The identity path is multiplied by J_N. LayerNorm's Jacobian is not the identity.

chunks.h: Pre-norm, post-norm, and stream growth
chunks.t: With scale γ=1 and ignoring the derivative of the variance for a moment, it is (1/σ)(I-(1/n)11^T), which subtracts the mean and scales the mean-zero part by 1/σ. That factor sits on the identity gradient path in post-norm but not in pre-norm; in pre-norm it multiplies only the sublayer branch At initialization, if the sublayer output is scaled small, J_F is small and the identity term dominates in pre-norm. That is the mechanism behind the warmup difference. The consequence is that the stream is never renormalized. Every sublayer adds its output, so the norm of the stream grows with depth.

chunks.h: Pre-norm, post-norm, and stream growth
chunks.t: If each write has variance v and the writes are independent, the sum of L writes has variance Lv and standard deviation √(Lv). With v=0.01 and L=40, the per-coordinate standard deviation is 0.1√40, about 0.63; the L2 norm also scales with √width. Positively correlated writes grow faster; negative correlations can make the variance grow more slowly A final norm before the unembedding has to undo that growth. This is a real wart. Wang and colleagues at Microsoft proposed DeepNorm in 2022, with x_{l+1}=LN(α x_l+G_l(x_l)), α=(2N)^{1/4}, and sublayer initialization scaled by β=(2N)^{-1/4}. They trained post-norm transformers with a thousand layers.

chunks.h: Pre-norm, post-norm, and stream growth
chunks.t: DeepNorm shows post-norm can be trained at that scale with a different residual scaling; it did not settle the practical choice.

chunks.h: Superposition and interference in a fixed-width stream
chunks.t: The fixed width has a cost that shows up in interpretability work. Every attention head and every feed-forward neuron writes into the same vector. There is no separate channel for separate concepts. Elhage and colleagues at Anthropic described the stream in 2021 as a communication channel of limited bandwidth, and in their 2022 work on superposition they showed what happens when a model needs to represent more features than the channel has dimensions. A toy case makes the interference concrete. Take a two-dimensional stream and three unit features placed at 0°, 120° and 240°. The dot product between any two feature directions is cos 120° = -0.5.

chunks.h: Superposition and interference in a fixed-width stream
chunks.t: If the stream holds a u1 + b u2 + c u3, reading feature 1 by projecting onto u1 gives a -0.5b -0.5c. The other features leak into the readout. The model can represent three features in two dimensions, but it pays interference. Width bounds how many linearly independent directions the stream can carry, and hence how many orthogonal features it can represent; superposition lets the model represent more features than that by using non-orthogonal directions, at a cost in interference Whether width is the binding constraint in a given model is an empirical question, but the arithmetic sets a hard ceiling on orthogonal features.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, attribution, and the logit lens
chunks.t: That same additivity is what makes the model tractable to inspect, with a caveat. At block boundaries the final stream is a sum of terms, and each term came from a specific head or neuron. But each write is a nonlinear function of the stream, so the terms are not independent. Zeroing a component changes the inputs to later sublayers and therefore changes their writes. Attribution is local and approximate. You can project a single term through the final layer norm and the unembedding and ask what it alone would predict, but the final norm blocks a clean linear decomposition. LayerNorm is nonlinear. Take x=(2,0), a=(1.5,0.5), b=(0.5,-0.5), γ=1, β=0.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, attribution, and the logit lens
chunks.t: For x, the mean is 1 and the standard deviation is 1, so LN(x)=(1,-1). For a, the mean is 1 and the standard deviation is 0.5, so LN(a)=(1,-1). For b, the mean is 0 and the standard deviation is 0.5, so LN(b)=(1,-1). Then LN(a)+LN(b)=(2,-2), while LN(a+b)=LN(x)=(1,-1). The norm does not commute with addition. A logit lens that applies the final norm and then the unembedding is not a sum of per-term logits. To attribute a term, you linearize the norm at the actual stream, or you compare ablations. Meng and colleagues used causal tracing (activation patching) in 2022 to follow factual associations through the layers.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, attribution, and the logit lens
chunks.t: The logit lens, posted by nostalgebraist in 2020, is the cleanest demonstration. Take the stream at an intermediate layer, apply the final layer norm and the unembedding matrix, and read off a distribution over next tokens. Early layers produce a broad, high-entropy distribution. Middle layers produce plausible continuations. Late layers sharpen them. The model has a usable guess long before its last layer, and the remaining depth refines it. That lens works when the stream stays in a consistent basis across depth. A basis here means the coordinate system in which the stream vector is expressed.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, attribution, and the logit lens
chunks.t: If the map from layer l to the final stream changes with l, applying the final unembedding early reads the vector in the wrong coordinates. Pre-norm helps because it leaves the stream unnormalized and preserves a clean identity path, but it does not guarantee a fixed basis. Belrose and colleagues introduced the tuned lens in 2023, training a small affine map per layer before the unembedding. In their paper, the tuned lens reported lower KL divergence from the model's final distribution than the raw logit lens across the layers they tested. That improvement is consistent with basis drift, but it does not isolate drift as the cause.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, attribution, and the logit lens
chunks.t: A trained affine map also adds capacity that the raw unembedding lacks. You would need a capacity-matched probe to separate the two.

chunks.h: Live stream versus KV cache at scale
chunks.t: For scale, take a long-document workload: a prompt of 100,000 tokens, the order of magnitude for a book-length document. During prefill the whole prompt is in flight at once. Every one of those tokens carries a live stream vector at whatever layer is being computed, and each layer reads and writes that vector twice. At the Llama-scale width of 4,096 dimensions and two bytes per element, the live stream is 100,000 × 4,096 × 2 = 819,200,000 bytes, about 0.82 GB. That figure scales with the number of tokens in flight, so a longer prompt costs proportionally more. The stream is transient. It exists only for tokens in flight.

chunks.h: Live stream versus KV cache at scale
chunks.t: The KV cache is persistent: it holds keys and values for every position in the context for the whole generation. A 32-layer model at d = 4,096 holds 32 × 4,096 = 131,072 values per position for one of the two tensors, and the cache stores both keys and values at two bytes each, so 2 × 131,072 × 2 = 524,288 bytes per position, half a megabyte. A 131,072-token context then costs 131,072 × 524,288 = 68,719,476,736 bytes = 68.7 GB. The stream is the smaller of the two at this length, but at long context it is the part that decides how many tokens can be pushed through at once, because it scales with the number of tokens in flight while the KV pool scales with the number of positions reserved.

chunks.h: Chapter 4: The bottleneck attention was invented to fix
chunks.t: By the end of 2014, neural machine translation had settled into a shape everyone used and a weakness everyone could see. The shape was the encoder–decoder. Cho, van Merriënboer, Gulcehre, Bahdanau, Bougares, Schwenk and Bengio described it in a paper posted in June 2014; Sutskever, Vinyals and Le published a version of the same idea that September. You feed the source sentence to a recurrent network one token at a time and let it run. At the end you have a single hidden state, a vector of a few hundred numbers. That vector is the entire sentence as far as the rest of the system is concerned.

chunks.h: Chapter 4: The bottleneck attention was invented to fix
chunks.t: A second recurrent network starts from it and emits the translation, one token per step, feeding each emitted token back in.

chunks.h: The fixed-vector bottleneck and its workarounds
chunks.t: The encoder's mechanism is worth stating plainly, because the bottleneck lives inside it. In a plain recurrent network, at each step the network takes the current token's embedding, multiplies it by a weight matrix, multiplies the previous hidden state by another weight matrix, adds the two results, and squashes the sum through a nonlinearity. The new hidden state replaces the old one. An LSTM or GRU does keep cell and gate state across steps; an LSTM carries a cell state \(c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t\) and a hidden state \(h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)\), while a GRU carries a single state with update and reset gates.

chunks.h: The fixed-vector bottleneck and its workarounds
chunks.t: Those internal states persist, but the decoder still receives only the encoder's final hidden state or a small set of final states, not the sequence of intermediate annotations. Whatever the network knows about the sentence after reading the tenth word is compressed into that final vector, and the decoder has no direct access to the earlier states. Two distinct failures follow as sentences get longer. The first is interference. Every step multiplies the state by a matrix and folds in a new token. Information about the first word has to survive that operation dozens of times, and each pass mixes it with everything else.

chunks.h: The fixed-vector bottleneck and its workarounds
chunks.t: A related failure appears in the backward pass Training pushes error backward through every step of the unrolled network, and each step contributes a Jacobian. For a scalar recurrence \(h_t = \tanh(w h_{t-1} + x_t)\), the derivative from the last step back to the first is \(\partial h_T/\partial h_1 = \prod_{t=2}^{T} w \tanh'(a_t)\). With \(w=0.5\) and \(\tanh'=0.8\) at each step, each factor is \(0.4\); over twenty steps the product is \(0.4^{19} \approx 2.7\times10^{-8}\). The earliest tokens receive almost no learning signal. If \(w=2\) and \(\tanh'=0.8\), each factor is \(1.6\) and the product grows instead.

chunks.h: The fixed-vector bottleneck and its workarounds
chunks.t: Whether a Jacobian product shrinks or explodes depends on the norms and eigenvalues of the matrices involved, so the vanishing-gradient story is a tendency, not a universal law. The second failure is capacity. A fixed vector has a fixed number of floats, and a sentence of five words and a sentence of fifty must both fit inside it. Take a hidden width of 256 floats. Five source tokens carry 1,280 floats of embeddings; fifty carry 12,800. The summary has 256 slots for either sentence. The decoder has no way to ask for a particular part of the source. It receives the summary or it receives nothing. Sutskever, Vinyals and Le reported a crude workaround.

chunks.h: The fixed-vector bottleneck and its workarounds
chunks.t: They reversed the source sentence before feeding it. That places the first source word at the last encoder step, next to the first decoder step, so the gradient from the first target token to the first source word passes through fewer recurrent steps. It shortened the path for early source-target pairs and helped in their experiments. It was also an admission that the architecture had a distance problem.

chunks.h: Bahdanau attention scores every annotation
chunks.t: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio attacked that problem directly in a paper posted in September 2014 and presented at ICLR the following spring. Their change fits in a paragraph. Stop discarding the encoder's intermediate states; keep every one of them and call them annotations. Their encoder ran in both directions. A forward RNN read the source left to right, a backward RNN read it right to left, and the annotation at position \(j\) was the concatenation \(h_j = \overrightarrow{h}_j; \overleftarrow{h}_j\). If each directional state has width \(d\), then \(h_j \in \mathbb{R}^{2d}\).

chunks.h: Bahdanau attention scores every annotation
chunks.t: The decoder's initial state was set from the final backward state, often through a learned projection. At each decoding step, compare the previous decoder state \(s_{i-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}\) against every annotation and produce a score for each. The scoring function they chose is a small feedforward network. For decoder state \(s_{i-1}\) and annotation \(h_j\), the score is \(e_{ij} = v^\top \tanh(W s_{i-1} + U h_j)\), where \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d'}\), \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times 2d}\), and \(v \in \mathbb{R}^{k}\) are learned.

chunks.h: Bahdanau attention scores every annotation
chunks.t: That is a two-layer network evaluated once per pair of decoder step and encoder position, and its only job is to emit a single number saying how relevant that annotation is right now. The score uses the previous decoder state because the current state has not been computed yet. A softmax turns the numbers into weights. Take three annotations scoring 2.0, 1.0 and 0.0. Exponentiating gives 7.389, 2.718 and 1.000, which sum to 11.107. Dividing gives weights of 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. The context vector handed to the decoder is 0.665 times the first annotation plus 0.245 times the second plus 0.090 times the third. Training pushes the score of whichever annotation would reduce the loss.

chunks.h: Bahdanau attention scores every annotation
chunks.t: If the decoder needs the verb it saw at position one, the gradient raises that score. Raise it to 4.0 while the others stay put. The exponentials are 54.598, 2.718 and 1.000, which sum to 58.316, and the weights become 0.936, 0.047 and 0.017. The distribution sharpens toward a hard choice without ever becoming one, and that is what keeps the whole operation differentiable. The gradient through the softmax is worth writing out. Let \(c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j\) be the context vector and let \(g = \partial L/\partial c_i\). Then \(\partial L/\partial \alpha_{ij} = g \cdot h_j\).

chunks.h: Bahdanau attention scores every annotation
chunks.t: Since \(\partial \alpha_{ij}/\partial e_{ik} = \alpha_{ij}(\delta_{jk} - \alpha_{ik})\), the score gradient is \(\partial L/\partial e_{ik} = \alpha_{ik}(g \cdot h_k - \sum_j \alpha_{ij} g \cdot h_j)\). The subtraction is a baseline that keeps the gradients across source positions summing to zero. That gradient then flows into \(W\), \(U\) and \(v\) through the tanh. For source padding, set \(e_{ij} = -\infty\) before the softmax so padded positions receive weight zero. The context vector is concatenated with the previous target embedding \(y_{i-1}\) and fed into the decoder cell, so \(s_i = f(s_{i-1}, y_{i-1}; c_i)\).

chunks.h: Bahdanau attention scores every annotation
chunks.t: The original formulation does not initialize the decoder with the context vector; initialization comes from the encoder's final backward state. Why a small network rather than a dot product? The annotation and the decoder state emerge from different weight matrices, may have different widths, and live in coordinate systems that were never trained to agree. A dot product presumes the two vectors are already comparable coordinate by coordinate. The tanh network learns the comparison rather than assuming it, and that matters most when the two sides are unaligned.

chunks.h: Luong's scoring functions and local attention
chunks.t: Thang Luong, Hieu Pham and Christopher Manning revisited the choice in a paper posted in August 2015 and presented at EMNLP. They set three scoring functions side by side. The dot product is \(e_{ij} = s_i^\top h_j\) and only applies when the vectors share a width. The general form is \(e_{ij} = s_i^\top W h_j\), which inserts a learned matrix between the two vectors and removes that width constraint at the cost of one matrix multiply. Bahdanau's additive form is the tanh network above. Their experiments found the simpler scores competitive.

chunks.h: Luong's scoring functions and local attention
chunks.t: They also introduced local attention, which predicts a single aligned position \(p_i\) for each decoder step and scores only a window from \(p_i-D\) to \(p_i+D\). With a source of 50 tokens and a window half-width of 2, each decoder step scores 5 positions instead of 50. The cost per step drops from \(O(m d)\) to \(O((2D+1)d)\), where \(m\) is the source length and \(d\) is the vector width.

chunks.h: Why dot-product attention won on hardware
chunks.t: Hardware pushed the field from additive toward multiplicative scoring. One practical reason is that additive attention evaluates a tanh over every pair, and those evaluations are elementwise and memory-bound; they do not collapse into one large matrix multiplication. Dot-product and general attention are matrix multiplies. For \(n\) decoder steps and \(m\) source positions, stack the decoder states into \(S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d'}\) and the annotations into \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 2d}\). A projected dot-product score matrix is \(S H^\top\), one GEMM producing an \(n \times m\) matrix.

chunks.h: Why dot-product attention won on hardware
chunks.t: Additive attention precomputes \(T = W S^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}\) and \(U H^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times m}\), which are also GEMMs, and then for every pair \((i,j)\) it forms \(T:,i + U:,j\), applies tanh, and dots with \(v\). The expensive part is not the projections but the \(n \times m \times k\) intermediate that no single GEMM can produce, because the tanh sits between the two reductions. With \(n=20\), \(m=50\), \(k=128\) and \(d=512\), the two projections cost \(128 \times 20 \times 512 + 128 \times 50 \times 1024 \approx 7.86\) million multiply-adds, and the per-pair \(v\)-dot adds \(20 \times 50 \times 128 = 128{,}000\), for roughly 8 million in total.

chunks.h: Why dot-product attention won on hardware
chunks.t: The dot product does \(20 \times 50 \times 1024 = 1{,}024{,}000\). So additive is about 16 times the arithmetic here rather than orders of magnitude more; the exact ratio depends on n and m because the projection cost amortizes as the sequence lengths grow. The real penalty is the shape of the work: additive produces a \(k \times n \times m\) intermediate that is typically materialised and reduced; a fused per-pair implementation can avoid materialising the full tensor, but then it cannot be expressed as one large GEMM. while the dot product is one contiguous GEMM the hardware is built for.

chunks.h: Why dot-product attention won on hardware
chunks.t: The note that \(H\) has width \(2d\) reflects Bahdanau's bidirectional encoder, which concatenates a forward and a backward state; Luong's encoder was a unidirectional two-layer LSTM of width \(d\), so his \(H\) has width \(d\) and the projection arithmetic differs accordingly. When Vaswani and colleagues built the transformer in 2017 they took the dot-product form and divided the result by the square root of the vector width. That scaling addresses dot-product variance. If the components of two independent \(d\)-dimensional vectors have variance \(\sigma^2\), their dot product has variance \(d\sigma^2\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{d}\) brings the variance back to \(\sigma^2\).

chunks.h: Why dot-product attention won on hardware
chunks.t: With \(d=512\) and \(\sigma^2=1\), raw scores have standard deviation about 22.6; scaled scores have standard deviation about 1. Large scores push the softmax into a region where its gradient is nearly flat. For scores 0 and 10, the softmax weights are \(4.5\times10^{-5}\) and \(0.99995\), and the derivative for the large weight is about \(4.5\times10^{-5}\). The scaling factor is a separate correction for the variance of a dot product, not an inheritance from Luong's general score. My view is that additive attention was dropped for reasons that had little to do with per-pair quality.

chunks.h: Why dot-product attention won on hardware
chunks.t: A learned nonlinear comparison has a different inductive bias from a fixed inner product; it is not a strict expressiveness ordering. Additive attention lost ground because it could not be batched into one big multiply as cleanly as dot-product attention. The transformer's dot-product attention maps to dense matrix multiplies, which is why it became the default in that architecture. The same trade shows up repeatedly in this book.

chunks.h: Attention weights are not explanations
chunks.t: Something else was lost along the way. Bahdanau's weights looked like alignments, and attention weights are sometimes read as explanations of what the model is doing. Philipp Koehn and Rebecca Knowles argued in their 2017 WMT paper on the challenges of neural machine translation that attention weights are a poor guide to what the model actually used, because they do not reliably behave like word alignments and can diverge sharply from what a human would call the correspondence. The weights are real numbers the model computed. The story we tell about them is ours.

chunks.h: The recurrence remained
chunks.t: What Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio did not do was remove the recurrence. The decoder still walked one token at a time and the encoder still read the source sequentially. They removed the bottleneck by letting the decoder consult every encoder state directly, and in doing so they made the cost of a translation grow with the product of source and target lengths. The score matrix has \(n \times m\) entries, and each entry costs \(O(d)\) work, so the attention layer costs \(O(n m d)\). Take a source of 50 tokens, a target of 20, and width 512.

chunks.h: The recurrence remained
chunks.t: The score matrix has 1,000 entries and costs about \(50 \times 20 \times 512 = 512{,}000\) multiply-adds for the scores, with a similar cost for the weighted sum. For self-attention, where source and target are the same length \(L\), the cost becomes \(O(L^2 d)\). The transformer kept the query-key-value lookup and replaced recurrence with self-attention, positional encodings, multi-head attention, residual connections, and layer normalization.

chunks.h: The 2017 move: drop the recurrence
chunks.t: In 2017, Vaswani et al. published "Attention Is All You Need." The paper was about machine translation, but its argument was larger. A sequence model does not need recurrence. Recurrent networks process tokens one at a time. To compute the hidden state at position t, you need the hidden state at t-1. That sequential dependency makes training on long sequences slow, and it forces gradients to travel through every step. The 2017 paper replaced the recurrence with attention, and attention has no such dependency. Every position can be computed at once.

chunks.h: Four facts the rest of the chapter leans on
chunks.t: Four pieces of background carry the rest of this chapter. A matrix multiply is a sum over an index, so an n-by-d matrix times a d-by-m matrix costs n m d multiply-adds. A multiply-add counts as two floating-point operations, which is the convention behind every FLOP figure below. The derivative of a softmax share a_ij with respect to a score s_ik is a_ij times (1 if j equals k, else 0, minus a_ik). And a GPU wants thousands of independent arithmetic operations in flight at once. An operation that must wait on its own previous step leaves most of those cores idle.

chunks.h: One token, three projections
chunks.t: Start with one token. In a transformer layer each token is represented by a vector x of length d_model. That vector is the residual stream. It runs the length of the network, and every sublayer reads from it and writes an addition back into it. The layer learns three weight matrices, W_Q, W_K and W_V, each of shape d_model by d_k. It multiplies x by each, giving q = x W_Q, k = x W_K and v = x W_V. These are the query, key and value for that token. The same three matrices apply to every token, so a sequence of n tokens yields n queries, n keys and n values.

chunks.h: What a block adds and why position must be injected
chunks.t: A block wraps attention in two pieces. The first is a residual connection. The sublayer's output is added to x rather than replacing it, so the gradient has a direct path back through the addition and information from earlier layers survives. The second is layer normalization, which rescales the vector to zero mean and unit variance across its d_model components, then applies a learned scale and shift. The original 2017 paper placed the norm after the residual addition, computing LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)); most later models moved it before the sublayer.

chunks.h: What a block adds and why position must be injected
chunks.t: After attention comes a feed-forward network, two linear layers with a nonlinearity between them and an inner width typically four times d_model. It is applied to each position independently. Attention mixes information across positions; the feed-forward layer transforms each position on its own. Attention itself is permutation equivariant. Shuffle the tokens and the set of dot products is unchanged, so the output is the same set of vectors in a different order. Order has to be injected. The 2017 paper added a fixed sinusoidal vector to each token embedding, with component 2i set to sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)) and component 2i+1 set to cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)).

chunks.h: What a block adds and why position must be injected
chunks.t: Different positions get different vectors, and the pair at any position is a fixed rotation of the pair at any other, so the model can learn to read relative offsets from the dot products. Later models learned the position vectors instead, and rotary position embedding (Su et al. 2021) rotates q and k by a position-dependent angle before the dot product.

chunks.h: Scores, softmax, and the lookup-table view
chunks.t: Now compare every query to every key. For tokens i and j the score is s_ij = q_i · k_j, a dot product that multiplies corresponding components and adds. The score is large when the query and key point in similar directions. Collect all n^2 scores into S = Q K^T. Row i holds the scores of token i against every token j. Softmax turns a row into shares. For row i, a_ij = exp(s_ij) divided by the sum over j' of exp(s_ij'). Take scores 2, 1 and 0. The exponentials are 7.389, 2.718 and 1.000, summing to 11.107, so the shares are 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. With values v_1 = (1, 0), v_2 = (0, 1) and v_3 = (1, 1), the output is 0.665 v_1 + 0.245 v_2 + 0.090 v_3 = (0.755, 0.335).

chunks.h: Scores, softmax, and the lookup-table view
chunks.t: That is a weighted average of the values, and the weights are the softmax shares. Written out, attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. The operation behaves like a differentiable lookup table. The query is a lookup key, the keys are the table's indices, the values are the table's contents. A hard table returns the value for an exact match. Attention returns a soft mixture of all values weighted by similarity. Because softmax and the dot product are differentiable, gradients reach the shares and the projections, and the table is learned end to end.

chunks.h: Multi-head attention and the scaling factor
chunks.t: Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. Split d_model into h heads of width d_k = d_model / h. Each head gets its own W_Q, W_K and W_V, computes attention in its d_k-dimensional subspace, and produces an output of width d_k. Concatenate the h outputs to width d_model and multiply by an output projection W_O. The total arithmetic matches a single full-width head, but the model can run h different attention patterns at once instead of one. The scaling factor deserves its derivation. The 2017 paper assumes the components of q and k are independent with mean zero and variance one. That is an assumption about initialization rather than a theorem.

chunks.h: Multi-head attention and the scaling factor
chunks.t: For the diagonal query-key pair, q and k come from the same token representation through different learned matrices, so they are correlated in general; for off-diagonal pairs they come from different token representations, and independence is still only an assumption. In either case the argument describes the scale at the start of training.; the argument describes the scale at the start of training. Under the assumption, each product q_a k_a has variance 1, and the sum of d_k such products has variance d_k. The score standard deviation is sqrt(d_k). Take d_k = 64, so the standard deviation is 8.

chunks.h: Multi-head attention and the scaling factor
chunks.t: A gap of two standard deviations between the top score and the next gives an exponential ratio of e^16, about 8.9 million. Softmax hands nearly all of the mass to the top score: if that top score sits 16 above every other, with n keys and all others 16 below, its share is 1/(1+(n−1)e^−16); for a single competitor this is approximately 1 − e^−16,, and its gradient a(1 − a) is about 1e−7. Even a milder concentration is enough to stall learning. At a = 0.999 the gradient is 0.000999, while in the unsaturated example above the top share was 0.665 and its gradient was 0.665 × 0.335 = 0.223, more than two hundred times larger.

chunks.h: Multi-head attention and the scaling factor
chunks.t: The point is not the exact share but that once one key wins by a wide margin, the gradient it receives collapses toward zero and the layer stops adjusting. Dividing the scores by sqrt(d_k) rescales the standard deviation to 1. The gap between top and next scores shrinks by a factor of 8, the exponential ratio falls from millions to single digits, and the shares stay spread out. There is a second reason to care about magnitude. In 16-bit floating point the largest representable value is 65,504, and exp overflows above about 11.1. Scores with standard deviation 8 cross that threshold routinely.

chunks.h: Multi-head attention and the scaling factor
chunks.t: Standard stable softmax implementations subtract the row maximum before exponentiating, which makes the largest exponent zero and everything else at most one, so the computation never overflows. Subtracting a constant from every score in a row leaves the shares unchanged, since the same factor cancels from numerator and denominator.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: The cost is quadratic in sequence length. For each pair, the score takes d_k multiply-adds, or 2 d_k FLOPs, and the weighted sum takes another 2 d_k. Per head that is about 4 n^2 d_k FLOPs, and with d_model = h d_k it is 4 n^2 d_model per layer. Take d_model = 4096 and h = 32, so d_k = 128. At the long-document length of 100,000 tokens, squaring gives 10^10 pairs. Per layer the attention arithmetic is 4 × 10^10 × 4096, roughly 1.6 × 10^14 FLOPs, or 160 trillion. The score matrix for one head at that length holds 10^10 entries; in 16-bit precision that is 20 GB.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: Materializing all 32 heads at once would need 640 GB, more than three times the 192 GB an H100 holds, so real implementations tile the computation and never hold the full matrix. Why accept the quadratic cost? A recurrent network is linear in sequence length. Each step costs O(d^2) and there are n steps, so O(n d^2). At n = 100,000 and d = 4096 that is about 1.7 × 10^12 multiply-adds per layer, against attention's 8.2 × 10^13, so roughly 49 times less arithmetic. (The 2n/d ratio is 2 × 100,000 / 4096 ≈ 48.8, which is the same answer from a shorter route.) But recurrence is sequential. Step t cannot start until step t-1 finishes.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: Attention hands the GPU a matrix multiply, and Q K^T is one wide operation with n^2 independent dot products. Softmax is row-wise. The weighted sum is another matrix multiply. The dependency chain is short even though the total work is large. Softmax and the weighted sum still reduce over n terms, so the graph depth grows with n, but those reductions are tree-shaped and the work inside them is parallel. The trade is more arithmetic in exchange for arithmetic the hardware can actually run at once. The 2017 paper chose the dot-product form over additive attention, which Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio introduced in 2014 for translation.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: Additive attention scores a pair with v^T tanh(W_1 h_j + W_2 s_i). The term W_1 h_j can be precomputed for all j, but the tanh and the final projection must be evaluated for every one of the n^2 pairs, as n^2 small matrix-vector products rather than one large matrix multiply. Dot-product attention collapses the whole score matrix into a single Q K^T. That is what makes the computation map onto hardware with thousands of cores. Generation changes the picture. A decoder cannot let token i see tokens after it, so before softmax every score s_ij with j > i is set to negative infinity, exp becomes zero, and the row sums only over the past.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: The mask is a triangular array, and applying it costs almost nothing. It also means the decoder's attention is masked self-attention, distinct from the encoder's bidirectional self-attention and from cross-attention, where the decoder's queries attend to keys and values produced by the encoder. At inference the model generates one token at a time. Recomputing keys and values for the whole prefix at every step would repeat work that has not changed, so the keys and values for positions already processed are stored in a KV cache and reused.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: At each decode step the model computes q_t, k_t, and v_t for the new token, appends k_t and v_t to the KV cache, and q_t attends over the cached keys and values through the current position—so t+1 entries if t tokens were already cached The cache is what makes decoding affordable, and it is also what limits concurrency. A serving engine runs several streams against a shared pool of positions, and each request reserves a reply budget out of that pool before generation starts. Decode at batch one reads the whole weight set once per token.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: Adding a stream lets one read of the weights serve every row in the batch, so aggregate throughput rises with concurrency, but the gain is never linear: every stream re-reads its own KV cache and they all contend for the same bandwidth ceiling. The scaling factor is the clearest case of a small numerical detail carrying a whole design. Without it the softmax saturates, the gradient for the winning share collapses toward zero, and the projections stop moving. With it, the shares stay in a range where gradients flow. At serving time the binding constraint shifts.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost and the shift to inference
chunks.t: Prefill is compute-bound, because each weight is read once and reused across every prompt token, so the arithmetic per byte stays high. Decode is memory-bound. Each generated token reads the cache and the weights, and the streams share one bandwidth ceiling. That is where the design's cost lands once training is over.

chunks.h: The fixed budget of one softmax
chunks.t: One attention operation produces one probability distribution over the sequence, then one weighted average of value vectors. That weighted average is the entire output the layer writes. Every relation the layer wants to express has to pass through that single distribution, and the distribution has a fixed budget of mass summing to one. Put numbers on it. Four positions carry scores 2.0, 1.0, 0.0 and −1.0. After exponentiation and normalization, e^2.0 = 7.389, e^1.0 = 2.718, e^0 = 1.000, e^−1.0 = 0.368, and the sum is 11.475, so the weights are 0.644, 0.237, 0.087 and 0.032. The output is 0.644 v_a + 0.237 v_b + 0.087 v_c + 0.032 v_d. The coefficients live inside the layer.

chunks.h: The fixed budget of one softmax
chunks.t: What crosses the layer boundary is the sum, not the coefficients, so a downstream layer receives a single 512-vector and cannot tell which position contributed which part of it. The information about position is carried by the weights, and the weights are not written anywhere the next layer can read. Now suppose two relations matter at once. To predict the token after "the cat sat on the", the model wants position i−1. To resolve "it" three clauses later, it wants the antecedent. A single head has to score both. Give both score 2.0 and the rest 0.0 and −1.0. The exponentials are 7.389, 7.389, 1.000, 0.368, summing to 16.146, so each relation gets 0.497.

chunks.h: The fixed budget of one softmax
chunks.t: The output is 0.497 v_prev + 0.458 v_ant + 0.062 v_c + 0.023 v_d. Each signal arrives at less than half strength, and the two are added into one vector.

chunks.h: Splitting attention into eight heads
chunks.t: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar and the rest of the 2017 transformer team split that competition eight ways. Head h gets its own projections Q_h = X W_Q^h, K_h = X W_K^h, V_h = X W_V^h, each W a 512×64 matrix, so each head works in a 64-dimensional subspace. The score of token i against token j in head h is (q_i^h · k_j^h) / √64, and √64 = 8. The softmax runs over j inside head h alone. The head's output is o_i^h = Σ_j a_ij^h v_j^h, a 64-vector. The eight outputs concatenate into a 512-vector, and W_O, a 512×512 matrix, maps that concatenation into the residual stream. All eight heads read the same x_i, so they run in parallel and add no depth. The parameter arithmetic shows what the split costs.

chunks.h: Splitting attention into eight heads
chunks.t: Eight heads of width 64 use 8 × 512 × 64 = 262,144 weights for the query projection. One head of width 512 uses 512 × 512 = 262,144. The same holds for K, V and W_O, so the layer carries 4 × 262,144 = 1,048,576 attention weights either way. Splitting rearranges the numbers; it does not add or remove them.

chunks.h: Rank expressiveness versus softmax scarcity
chunks.t: What changes is the number of softmaxes. A single 512-dimensional head can represent any bilinear query-key interaction of rank up to 512. A 64-dimensional head is capped at rank 64. Take B = I_512, the identity bilinear form. If B = U V^T with U and V both 512×64, then rank(B) ≤ min(rank U, rank V) ≤ 64, which contradicts rank(I_512) = 512. One wide head can express interactions that eight narrow heads cannot, in the bilinear sense. Raw expressiveness favors the wide head. The wide head loses because the softmax is the scarce resource. Return to the two-relation sentence. Head 1 scores the previous token at 5.0 and the antecedent at 0.0.

chunks.h: Rank expressiveness versus softmax scarcity
chunks.t: Head 2 scores the antecedent at 5.0 and the previous token at 0.0. With the other two positions at 0.0 and −1.0, head 1's exponentials are 148.4, 1.000, 1.000 and 0.368, summing to 150.8, so it puts 0.984 of its mass on the previous token. Head 2 does the same for the antecedent. Each signal now reaches the concatenation at 0.984 strength instead of 0.497, in its own 64-dimensional block.

chunks.h: What a head writes versus where it looks
chunks.t: The concatenation is not the end of the story. W_O is dense, so head h's contribution to the residual is W_O:, 64h : 64h+64 o^h, a 512-vector built from a 64-vector. Different heads write into different column subspaces of W_O, and those subspaces can overlap. A head's attention pattern is visible; its contribution to the residual is that pattern filtered through a learned 512×64 block. Saying "head 5 is a previous-token head" describes where head 5 looks, not what it writes.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: What heads learn has been mapped. Voita, Talbot, Moiseev, Sennrich and Titov (2019) trained a transformer on WMT English-Russian translation, put stochastic gates on the heads and penalised the number of gates that survived, and classified heads by their attention patterns into positional, syntactic and rare-word categories. They then pruned heads layer by layer and measured BLEU. Most encoder layers tolerated losing a large share of their heads with a small BLEU change, and the decoder was less prunable: their sparse model kept 14 of 48 encoder self-attention heads, but 31 of 48 decoder self-attention heads and 30 of 48 decoder-encoder heads.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: Clark, Khandelwal, Levy and Manning (2019) probed BERT-base by feeding a corpus through the model and clustering attention maps, finding heads that attend to the next token, to the SEP and CLS delimiters, to direct objects of verbs, and to coreferent mentions. Both papers point the same way: a minority of heads does most of the measurable work. Voita et al. showed that the rest can go The cleanest circuit is the induction head, described by Olsson and colleagues at Anthropic in 2022. It needs two layers. A previous-token head in layer 1 attends from position i to i−1 and writes a copy of x_{i−1} into position i's residual. Call that copy c_i.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: In layer 2, a head's query is q_i = W_Q(x_i + c_i + r_i), where r_i collects the other residual components. The term W_Q c_i is a 64-vector produced by the 64×64 matrix W_Q W_O^{h1} acting on the layer-1 head's output. That product is the composition. On the key side, a parallel shift puts x_{j−1} into position j's key. The layer-2 query then matches keys at positions j where x_{j−1} = x_i, meaning j−1 is an earlier occurrence of the same token.
