Attention lands on j, and the value at j is x_j, the token that followed the earlier occurrence.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: The one-position offset between the match and the value is what turns "find the earlier occurrence" into "predict the next token." Heads are not cleanly one thing. Elhage and colleagues at Anthropic (2022) studied toy models and showed that a network with more features to represent than dimensions to hold them will spread the features across near-orthogonal directions rather than drop them. A feature here is a direction in the residual stream; the model reads it by projecting onto that direction. In 512 dimensions, two features can be exactly orthogonal and interfere not at all.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: Three features in two dimensions cannot be mutually orthogonal; the best arrangement puts them 120° apart, and each pair has |cos θ| = 0.5, so reading one feature picks up half of another. Superposition buys capacity at the price of interference, and sparsity makes the price affordable, because features that rarely co-occur rarely interfere. The same pressure applies across heads. A head can act as a previous-token head on some inputs and as an induction component on others, and a probe returns an average of its behaviour. Pruning separates two regimes. At inference, removing head h subtracts W_O:, 64h:64h+64 o^h from the residual.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: If that term is small relative to the residual's norm, the layer's output barely moves, and Michel, Levy and Neubig (2019) found that many heads in a trained model can be removed this way with little task loss; they also found that some layers need nearly all their heads and others need only one, measured across checkpoints of a normally trained model rather than by retraining. Pruning during training is different in kind. The head's gradient path is gone from the first step, so the remaining heads must discover the layer's function without that route.

chunks.h: What heads learn and which ones matter
chunks.t: Voita and colleagues measured this directly: a model trained with L0 head gates and then pruned beat retraining from scratch with the same small head count by 0.2 to 0.6 BLEU, which is the cost of removing the route before the layer has learned what it is for.

chunks.h: Head count and the KV cache
chunks.t: The cost of many heads shows up in the KV cache. Per token per layer, the cache stores one key and one value vector of width d_model, so with 16-bit storage that is 2 × 512 × 2 = 2,048 bytes per token per layer, independent of how the 512 dimensions are divided among heads. Head count does not multiply the cache; d_model and layer count do. What multiplies is the number of independent key spaces. Multi-query attention (Shazeer, 2019) keeps the per-head queries but shares one key projection and one value projection across all heads, cutting the cache by a factor of eight in the eight-head case. Grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023) shares within groups, giving a factor of H/G.

chunks.h: Head count and the KV cache
chunks.t: The independence lost is the ability of each head to score against its own key subspace. In MQA all heads read the same keys, so diversity has to come from the queries alone; in GQA only heads within a group share keys and values, so different groups still contribute distinct key/value subspaces and diversity can come from both the queries and the group-specific projections Head count and context length meet in the KV cache. A grouped-query layer stores only the KV heads it declares. Llama 2 70B declares 8 KV heads at 128 dimensions, which is 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per layer.

chunks.h: Head count and the KV cache
chunks.t: Keys and values across 80 layers come to 2 × 80 × 1,024 = 163,840 values per position, and at two bytes each that is 327,680 bytes. A 131,072-token context then costs 131,072 × 327,680 = 42,949,672,960 bytes = 42.9 GB, and that is the number to watch when head count and context length grow together.

chunks.h: Chapter 7: The function that turns scores into shares
chunks.t: A query vector leaves the residual stream at one position, gets multiplied by that head's $W_Q$, and then meets every key in the context. Each meeting is a dot product. Each dot product is a scalar with no upper bound and no lower bound. At the 131,072-token context length used throughout this book, a single head at a single layer produces 131,072 of these scalars for one query. They are raw affinities, and attention cannot average value vectors with raw affinities. Softmax converts them. It exponentiates each score and divides by the sum of the exponentials. The output is non-negative and sums to one, which is exactly what a weighted average of value vectors requires.

chunks.h: Why exponentials and shift invariance
chunks.t: Why exponentials rather than a sigmoid, or squaring, or dividing by the sum of absolute values? The answer is a property only the exponential has. Add the same constant to every score in the row. The shares should not change, because a constant added to all affinities says nothing about which key is better. With exp that holds exactly: $\exp(s_i + c) = \exp(s_i)\exp(c)$, and the $\exp(c)$ appears in numerator and denominator and cancels. With any other monotone function it fails. Take $f(x) = 1 + x$ on scores 2.0, 1.0 and 0.1. The normalized shares are 3/6.1, 2/6.1 and 1.1/6.1, roughly 0.49, 0.33 and 0.18.

chunks.h: Why exponentials and shift invariance
chunks.t: Add 10 to each score and the shares become 13/36.1, 12/36.1 and 11.1/36.1, roughly 0.36, 0.33 and 0.31. The ranking survived. The distribution did not. The exponential is the unique continuous function, up to a change of base and a scale on the argument, whose normalized form depends only on differences of scores. That is the whole justification, and it is why the same function shows up in Gibbs' statistical mechanics in 1902 and in multinomial logistic regression decades before anyone pointed it at attention. John Bridle named it softmax in 1990, in a paper on interpreting classification network outputs. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio used it in 2014 to normalize their additive attention scores.

chunks.h: Why exponentials and shift invariance
chunks.t: Vaswani and colleagues used it in 2017 on scaled dot products, and the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor exists partly to keep scores in a range where the softmax does not saturate. Work the arithmetic on three scores: 2.0, 1.0, 0.1. $\exp(2.0) = 7.389$, $\exp(1.0) = 2.718$, $\exp(0.1) = 1.105$. The sum is 11.212. The shares are 0.659, 0.242 and 0.099. The first key gets two thirds of the value vector. Now add 100 to each score. The exponents become enormous and the shares are identical to three decimal places. A row has no idea what the absolute scale of its scores is, and that is by design.

chunks.h: Overflow and the row-maximum shift
chunks.t: The naive implementation of that arithmetic overflows. IEEE 754 binary16, which most inference kernels use for activations, tops out at 65,504. $\exp(11.09)\approx65{,}513$, already above the 65,504 maximum (fp16 overflows just above $\ln(65{,}504)\approx11.0899$). A row that reaches 12 produces inf in the numerator and inf in the denominator, and inf/inf is NaN. Once a NaN enters a softmax it propagates through every downstream layer and the request dies. Even in fp32 the ceiling arrives at $\exp(88.7)$. The fix is to subtract the row maximum before exponentiating. With scores 2.0, 1.0 and 0.1 the maximum is 2.0, so the shifted scores are 0, $-1.0$ and $-1.9$.

chunks.h: Overflow and the row-maximum shift
chunks.t: $\exp(0) = 1$, $\exp(-1.0) = 0.368$, $\exp(-1.9) = 0.150$. The sum is 1.518 and the shares are 0.659, 0.242, 0.099, unchanged. The largest exponent is now 1, so no numerator can overflow, and the denominator is at most the row length. The cost is one pass to find the maximum, which is cheap when the whole row sits in registers. When it does not, as in the tiled kernels Dao and colleagues introduced with Flash Attention in 2022, the maximum has to be tracked incrementally. Milakov and Gimelshein published that online normalizer in 2018, and it is the reason a kernel can stream a 131,072-token row through shared memory without ever materializing the full score vector.

chunks.h: Underflow and temperature
chunks.t: Underflow is the quieter failure. $\exp(-20)$ is about $2\times10^{-9}$, which fp16 flushes toward zero, and a share that underflows receives no gradient. The shift does not fix this: it caps the largest exponent at 1, so it prevents overflow, not underflow — a score 20 below the row maximum still yields exp(-20) and can vanish. Kernels therefore evaluate the exponentials in fp32 (or accept that vanishingly small shares lose their gradient), while the shift itself remains mandatory because overflow, unlike underflow, yields NaN and kills the request. Temperature is a divisor placed inside the exponent. Replace $\exp(s_i)$ with $\exp(s_i/T)$. At $T=1$ nothing changes.

chunks.h: Underflow and temperature
chunks.t: At $T=0.5$ the scores are doubled before exponentiating, so the leader pulls further ahead and the row concentrates. At $T=2$ the scores are halved and the row flattens toward uniform. As $T$ approaches zero the softmax approaches a one-hot vector on the argmax. Hinton, Vinyals and Dean used this in 2015 to soften targets in knowledge distillation, and the same knob appears in sampling, where it is called temperature for precisely this reason.

chunks.h: Entropy as a measure of concentration
chunks.t: Concentration can be measured. The entropy of a row, $H = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i$, is the number of nats of uncertainty the head carries about which key matters. For the three-score example above, $H$ is about 0.85 nats against a maximum of $\ln 3 = 1.10$. The row is moderately focused. A row collapsed onto one key has $H$ near zero, and a row uniform over $n$ keys has $H = \ln n$. Entropy is the honest way to say how concentrated a row is; whether that concentration reflects genuine selection or a degenerate sink is a separate question, taken up next.

chunks.h: The attention sink and the cost of normalization
chunks.t: Normalization has a consequence that took the field years to name. Softmax must put its mass somewhere. If no visible key is a good match, the head still has to emit a convex combination of values, and the best available behaviour is to attend to something inert. In 2023 Xiao and colleagues showed that many heads in pretrained models dump most of their mass on the first token of the sequence. They called it an attention sink. The mechanism is structural. Under causal masking the first token is the only position visible to every query, so it is always available as a null key, and gradient descent finds it.

chunks.h: The attention sink and the cost of normalization
chunks.t: Remove that token from the window and perplexity explodes, which is why streaming inference schemes keep a few initial tokens resident even after evicting everything else. The sink is a symptom of a design choice worth arguing about. Softmax forces competition: every unit of mass given to one key is taken from another, and there is no way to say "attend to nothing." Sigmoid attention, which Ramapuram and colleagues analyzed in 2024, drops the normalization and lets each key be weighted independently, at the cost of losing the shift-invariance argument above. Whether that trade is good remains unsettled.

chunks.h: The attention sink and the cost of normalization
chunks.t: What is settled is that the denominator couples every key in the row to every other key, and that coupling is why the sink exists.

chunks.h: Saturation, scaling, and the artifacts of softmax
chunks.t: Saturation is the other cost. The gradient of softmax with respect to a score is $p_i(1-p_i)$ along the diagonal and $-p_ip_j$ off it. When one share approaches 1, that gradient approaches zero, and the attention weights for that row stop being refined — though gradients to the value and output projections remain, so the head can still learn what to write, just not where to look. A head that locks onto a shortcut early in training can stay locked for the rest of it. This is the reason the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling matters. Without it, dot products of high-dimensional vectors have variance proportional to $d_k$, the softmax saturates almost immediately, and the gradients vanish.

chunks.h: Saturation, scaling, and the artifacts of softmax
chunks.t: Vaswani's 2017 paper included the factor for that reason, and it remains the cheapest logit-variance stabilizer in the architecture. Softmax won. It is differentiable, shift-invariant, has a clean gradient, and maps onto the categorical distribution that next-token prediction needs. It also brought two artifacts the field has spent a decade working around.

chunks.h: Saturation, scaling, and the artifacts of softmax
chunks.t: A head that appears to do nothing may be redundant, near-uniform, or attending to an attention sink; the softmax denominator helps explain why sink-attending heads arise, but diagnosing inactivity requires inspecting attention and value behavior rather than assuming a null-key mechanism, and a model that breaks when the first token is evicted is a model whose heads had learned to dump surplus attention on that first token as a sink — softmax still normalizes over the remaining keys, but the distribution the heads were calibrated on is gone.

chunks.h: Saturation, scaling, and the artifacts of softmax
chunks.t: The sink follows directly from the denominator; no-op heads often exploit the same need to allocate mass by collapsing onto a null key/value, but that is a common pattern rather than a general consequence of normalization alone.

chunks.h: Unmasked attention is permutation-equivariant
chunks.t: Take "the dog bit the man", run it through one bidirectional self-attention layer, then run "man the dog the bit" through the same layer. Compare the two outputs. Every vector from the first run appears in the second. The set is identical. Only the ordering changed. That follows from the arithmetic for a layer with no mask. For token i the layer produces a weighted average of value vectors, where the weight on token j is the softmax over q_i · k_j / √d_k across all j. Permute the input by some π and every query, key and value travels with its token.

chunks.h: Unmasked attention is permutation-equivariant
chunks.t: The collection of dot products is the same collection, so the softmax normalises over the same numbers and assigns the same weights, so the output that used to sit at position i now sits at position π(i). Unmasked self-attention is equivariant to permutation. No index is read in the score.

chunks.h: The causal mask makes a decoder order-sensitive
chunks.t: Decoder self-attention is different. A causal mask adds negative infinity to score i,j when j is greater than i, so token i can attend only to j less than or equal to i. The mask depends on i and j, so permuting tokens changes which pairs are allowed. A three-token example makes the break visible. Use scalar queries q=(1,2,3), keys k=(1,0,1), and values v=(10,20,30). Without a mask, token 2 scores against all keys as (2,0,2); softmax gives (0.468,0.063,0.468) and output 19.98. With a causal mask, token 2 sees only keys 1 and 2, scores (2,0); softmax gives (0.881,0.119) and output 11.19. Move token 2 to first position and the allowed set changes again.

chunks.h: The causal mask makes a decoder order-sensitive
chunks.t: The bag-of-tokens claim holds only for unmasked attention. A decoder is order-sensitive by construction. The consequence is blunt for a transformer with no positional signal and no mask. It sees a bag of tokens. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are the same input to it. Word order has to be inserted deliberately, and the four generations of doing that insertion explain a surprising amount of how modern models behave at long context.

chunks.h: Sinusoidal encodings and the offset property
chunks.t: The first generation is the sinusoidal encoding of Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin, published as "Attention Is All You Need" in 2017. For dimension pair i and position p they set one slot to sin(p / 10000^(2i/d)) and the next to cos of the same argument. The wavelengths form a geometric ladder. The fastest pair completes a full cycle every 2π positions; the slowest takes roughly 10000·2π. The design has a property worth pausing on. Because sin(a+k) equals sin a cos k plus cos a sin k, and cos(a+k) equals cos a cos k minus sin a sin k, the pair at position p+k is the pair at p multiplied by the matrix cos k, sin k, -sin k, cos k.

chunks.h: Sinusoidal encodings and the offset property
chunks.t: For k=1 and p=1, the pair (sin 1, cos 1) is (0.841,0.540); the matrix 0.540,0.841,-0.841,0.540 gives (0.908,-0.415), which is (sin 2, cos 2). The map depends only on k. A linear projection inside the attention layer can therefore learn to compare tokens by offset rather than by absolute address. The property gives a route, not a guarantee. The projections are fit on a finite range; at longer positions the phase pattern enters combinations not present in training, and high-frequency pairs wrap many times. The original paper trained and tested within a fixed range, so the property was a hope rather than a demonstrated long-context result.

chunks.h: Learned tables and relative position biases
chunks.t: The second generation dropped the sinusoids for a lookup table. BERT (Devlin, Chang, Lee and Toutanova, 2018) and GPT-2 (Radford, Wu, Child, Luan, Amodei and Sutskever, 2019) learned one vector per position and added it to the token embedding. This works well inside the training length. At position 1025 in a table built for 1024 positions there is no row. Clamping reuses a trained row, typically the last one, at an untrained position; inventing a row feeds a vector the model never trained on. Either way, the model sees a position encoding outside its training distribution A learned table also entangles where a token is with what it is.

chunks.h: Learned tables and relative position biases
chunks.t: The same word at position 5 and position 500 arrives at the first layer wearing different vectors. Because the position vector occupies the same dimensions as the token embedding, downstream layers that need position-invariant content must disentangle it from position; layers can also use the entangled signal, so this is a capacity trade-off rather than a hard requirement The third generation made position relative. Shaw, Uszkoreit and Vaswani proposed relative position representations in 2018, adding a learned vector indexed by the clipped offset i−j to each key before the dot product. The score becomes q_i · (k_j + a_clip(i−j,−k,k)), which equals q_i · k_j plus q_i · a_clip(i−j,−k,k).

chunks.h: Learned tables and relative position biases
chunks.t: Offsets beyond the maximum distance k share the same vector. Transformer-XL (Dai, Yang, Yang, Carbonell, Le and Salakhutdinov, 2019) built a similar bias out of sinusoids. The extra term is computable. It is not a plain q·k product, so you cannot fold the whole thing into one matmul over cached keys. A cached key vector no longer suffices because the same key needs a different added term for every query position. For a new query i, the q_i·k_j scores are one matmul over cached keys, but the relative term needs q_i·a_{i−j} for each j.

chunks.h: Learned tables and relative position biases
chunks.t: Naively that is O(nd) multiply-adds; with clipped offsets there are at most 2k+1 distinct a_r, so you can compute q_i·a_r for all r in O(kd) as a separate matmul against the relative-embedding table, then add the appropriate scalar bias to each of the n scores in O(n). So the whole score is not one matmul over cached keys alone

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: Rotary position embedding arrived in April 2021 from Jianlin Su and colleagues, in "RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding". It applies a rotation instead of an addition. Take the query and key vectors, split them into pairs of dimensions, and for pair m rotate the two components by an angle proportional to position, with frequency θ_m = 10000^(−2m/d). Do the same to the key at its own position. Consider one pair with frequency θ. A query whose unrotated value is (1,0), sitting at position i, becomes (cos iθ, sin iθ). A key with the same unrotated value at position j becomes (cos jθ, sin jθ). Their dot product is cos iθ cos jθ plus sin iθ sin jθ, which is cos((i−j)θ).

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: The absolute positions vanished. For general q and k the pair dot is a linear combination of cos and sin of (i−j)θ, still a function of offset alone. The full dot product is a sum over pairs of linear combinations of cosines and sines of the offset at a spread of frequencies Position enters the score as a function of distance and nothing else. Press, Smith and Lewis published ALiBi in 2021, in "Train Short, Test Long". ALiBi adds no positional vector at all. It subtracts a penalty proportional to distance from the attention score, m_h·|i−j|, with a different slope m_h for each head. For n heads, m_h = 2^(−8h/n) for h from 1 to n.

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: For 8 heads the slopes are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, 1/64, 1/128 and 1/256. The sequence is geometric because each head's penalty slope sets its effective range, and multiplicative spacing covers a log scale. A head with m=1/2 drops a score by 0.5 per token of distance; at 100 tokens the penalty is 50. A head with m=1/256 drops 0.39 at 100 tokens. Softmax turns that into near-zero weight for far tokens in fast-decay heads. Because the penalty grows linearly, far scores go to negative infinity; there is no periodic ambiguity. That is why ALiBi avoids RoPE's unscaled long-range failure. RoPE became the default for mechanical reasons.

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: The rotation is applied to the query and key once, at the moment they are produced, so the cached key is already rotated and the cache stays an ordinary matrix. It adds no parameters. And it exposes a knob, the base 10000, which turns out to be tunable at inference time. ALiBi is simpler and extrapolates more gracefully out of the box; its fixed linear decay does not blow up past the training length the way an unscaled rotation does. But ALiBi offers no equivalent knob. By early 2023 LLaMA (Touvron, Lavril, Izacard and colleagues) had adopted RoPE, many derivative models followed, and kernel libraries standardised around it.

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: Adoption is evidence about tooling and pretrained weights, not proof RoPE is better at every length. The knob is where the modern story lives. If you want a model trained on a shorter window to handle a longer one, the naive fix is position interpolation, published by Chen, Wong, Chen and Tian in 2023. Divide every position by a scale factor s so the extended sequence occupies the same angular range the model was trained on. It works, but with a cost. Take a training length L=1024 and a token at p=2048, with s=2. The interpolated position is 1024. For θ=0.01, the angle goes from 20.48 radians to 10.24 radians.

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: Adjacent long-range tokens p=2048 and p=2049 become 1024 and 1024.5, so the angle gap is 0.005 instead of 0.01. Low-frequency dimensions lose the resolution that distinguishes them NTK-aware scaling, circulated by bloc97 in 2023 as a community post rather than a paper, fixes that by changing the base instead of the positions. Raise the base and the frequency ladder stretches unevenly. The formula is b' = b·s^(d/(d−2)). For d=128 and s=2, the exponent is 128/126=1.016, so b'=10000·2^1.016=20220. The per-frequency effect is θ_m' = b^(−2m/d)·s^(−2m/(d−2)). The fastest dimension m=0 stays at θ=1. The slowest pair m=63 goes from 10000^(−126/128)≈1/8660 to about 1/17320.

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: Fast dimensions barely move; slow ones stretch a great deal. YaRN (Peng, Quesnelle, Fan and Shao, 2023) refined this into a per-dimension ramp between interpolated and extrapolated behaviour. Let λ_m=2π/θ_m and r_m=L/λ_m. With α=1 and β=32, the ramp is γ_m=clamp((r_m−α)/(β−α),0,1). When γ_m=0 the dimension is interpolated; when γ_m=1 it is extrapolated; values between blend the two angles. YaRN also adds a temperature correction on the attention logits because stretching changes the entropy of the softmax. The correction is t=0.1·ln(s)+1, and the logits are multiplied by 1/sqrt(t). For s=2, t=1.069 and the scale is 0.967. For s=8, t=1.208 and the scale is 0.910.

chunks.h: Rotary position embedding and the scaling knob
chunks.t: What breaks when you stretch is easiest to see in the slowest dimensions. Those pairs complete less than one full rotation across the training window. Push past it and two positions far apart map to nearly the same angle, so the model cannot separate them in that subspace. The fast dimensions keep working, which is why extended models still produce fluent local text while quietly losing the ability to track a fact from the beginning of a long document. No amount of rescaling creates information the model never learned.

chunks.h: KV cache memory and admission
chunks.t: Positional encoding sets what the model can distinguish. The KV cache sets what you can afford to store. A KV cache stores key and value vectors for past tokens so decode does not recompute them. Memory scales with positions. In general, KV bytes equal 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × dtype_bytes × positions divided by tensor_parallel. The factor 2 is K and V; layers, kv_heads, head_dim and dtype set bytes per position; tensor parallel divides the cache across ranks. A serving pool rarely reserves the full window. Suppose a pool holds 262,144 positions against a native window of 1,048,576, a quarter of what the model can address.

chunks.h: KV cache memory and admission
chunks.t: Raising it to the full window adds 1,048,576−262,144=786,432 positions, which is 786,432/1,048,576=0.75 of the window, so the cache grows by three quarters of its full-window size. That is the trade: context is a knob you pay for in cache bytes, linearly, and the price per position is set by layers, KV heads and head width. Admission reserves space before a request runs. With 4 streams, the equal share of the pool is 262,144/4=65,536 positions. The default reply budget is 32,768 tokens, the decode round batch width is 16 rows, and two rows are reserved, so the reservation is 32,768+16+2=32,786 positions. The per-stream ceiling is 65,536−32,786=32,750 tokens.

chunks.h: KV cache memory and admission
chunks.t: If the pool were raised to 1,048,576, the share would be 1,048,576/4=262,144 positions per stream. The ceiling would then be 262,144−32,786=229,358 tokens, seven times the original. Context length is where the two costs meet. Longer positions raise the cache linearly and the attention arithmetic quadratically. A window the model was trained on is not the same thing as a window a server can afford to reserve for every concurrent request, and the gap between the two is what admission control exists to manage. At 262,144 positions the pool is 786,432 positions short of the native window, and closing that gap costs three quarters again the cache bytes you already hold.

chunks.h: Chapter 9: The cost that defines the field
chunks.t: A request arrives carrying a long-document prompt of 100,000 tokens. The server has a shared KV pool of 262,144 positions and four concurrent streams. Admission reserves each stream an equal share of the pool, then subtracts the reply budget and round-batch overhead: 262,144 / 4 = 65,536; 65,536 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 32,750. The prompt does not fit inside that ceiling: 100,000 tokens is roughly three times the 32,750-token limit, so admission would reject or chunk the request. Now attention does its work.

chunks.h: The quadratic term in attention
chunks.t: A transformer block stacks an attention sublayer with a feed-forward network. The quadratic cost lives in the attention sublayer. For each token, the model produces a query vector, a key vector, and a value vector. For token i, attention scores its query against the key of every token j ≤ i (causal masking), so the score matrix is lower triangular with n(n+1)/2 entries; using n² as an upper bound for the quadratic scaling argument. The score is a dot product. Softmax turns the row of scores into weights that sum to one. The output for token i is the weighted sum of all value vectors.

chunks.h: The quadratic term in attention
chunks.t: The cost comes from the phrase "every token j." For a sequence of length n, the score matrix has n rows and n columns. At 131,072 tokens, the entry count is 131,072 squared, or 1.718 × 10^10. Every entry requires a dot product of length d, the head dimension. Take d = 128. The score computation costs 1.718 × 10^10 × 128 = 2.199 × 10^12 multiply-adds per head per layer. The value aggregation costs the same again. That is the quadratic term.

chunks.h: Why the score matrix never fits
chunks.t: Store that matrix as a dense fp16 array and the arithmetic becomes concrete. Each entry takes two bytes. 10^10 entries × 2 bytes = 20 GB for one head in one layer. The on-chip SRAM of a GPU is measured in tens of megabytes, so the matrix is hundreds of times larger than the memory that feeds the compute units. It is also about 10 percent of the 192 GB of HBM on an H100, since 20 / 192 comes to 0.104. Multiply by the head count and the layer count and the product passes the budget many times over — which is why no production kernel ever materializes this matrix; attention is computed in fused, streaming tiles. The n² figure is a compute-cost illustration, not a memory budget.

chunks.h: Why the score matrix never fits
chunks.t: The wall a real server hits is the KV cache: at long context the per-stream KV footprint, its bandwidth demand, and allocator fragmentation across concurrent streams are what bind admission, not score storage.

chunks.h: Flash Attention and the tiled softmax
chunks.t: The first response to the wall was a change in the memory schedule. The math stayed the same. Standard attention materializes the score matrix in HBM, the large but slow memory attached to the GPU. It writes scores, reads them back for softmax, writes probabilities, reads them back for the value multiply. Each pass moves n squared entries through an HBM bus delivering roughly 1.5–3.3 TB/s on datacenter GPUs that is far slower than the SRAM feeding the compute units. Tri Dao and colleagues introduced Flash Attention in 2022. The idea is to tile the score matrix.

chunks.h: Flash Attention and the tiled softmax
chunks.t: Load a block of queries and a block of keys into SRAM, compute the scores for that tile, apply softmax incrementally, multiply by the corresponding values, and write only the output. The n squared matrix never exists in HBM. The backward pass recomputes the tiles instead of storing them. The arithmetic is identical to standard attention. The memory footprint is linear in n. HBM traffic is still quadratic in n for a fixed tile size, but with a much smaller constant: it drops to O(n^2/M) for SRAM size M, because K and V tiles are re-read for each query tile rather than materializing the full score matrix Flash Attention is exact. It does not trade recall. It refuses to pay the HBM tax.

chunks.h: Flash Attention and the tiled softmax
chunks.t: The incremental softmax is the part that makes the tiling work. For a full row, softmax needs the maximum score to subtract before exponentiating, and the sum of exponentials to normalize. When you process a row in tiles, you do not know the global maximum until you have seen every tile. Flash Attention keeps a running maximum m and a running sum l. Start with m = −∞ and l = 0. For each tile, compute the tile maximum m_tile. The new running maximum is m_new = max(m_old, m_tile). Rescale the accumulated sum and output: l_new = l_old × exp(m_old − m_new) + Σ exp(s_tile − m_new); O_new = O_old × exp(m_old − m_new) + Σ exp(s_tile − m_new) × v_tile.

chunks.h: Flash Attention and the tiled softmax
chunks.t: The factor exp(m_old − m_new) is at most 1, so the rescale never overflows. At the end, divide O by l. The result is numerically identical to the full softmax, up to the rounding of the exponentials. Work through two tiles with numbers. Suppose the first tile yields scores 2, 4 and the second yields 6, 8. After tile one, m = 4, l = exp(2−4) + exp(4−4) = 0.135 + 1 = 1.135. After tile two, m_new = 8. Rescale: l = 1.135 × exp(4−8) + exp(6−8) + exp(8−8) = 1.135 × 0.0183 + 0.135 + 1 = 0.0208 + 1.135 = 1.156. The full softmax over 2,4,6,8 gives denominator exp(2−8)+exp(4−8)+exp(6−8)+exp(8−8) = 0.00248 + 0.0183 + 0.135 + 1 = 1.156. The running sum matches.

chunks.h: Flash Attention and the tiled softmax
chunks.t: The output accumulates the same way, with the same rescale applied to the partial value sum. Dao's contribution was to fuse that recurrence with the value multiply and the backward pass so that the score matrix never touches HBM. The backward pass recomputes the score and probability tiles from Q and K, using the saved logsumexp and output for gradient scaling, which costs a second pass over the same arithmetic but saves the memory. The tile order matters for rounding, not for the mathematical result.

chunks.h: Flash Attention and the tiled softmax
chunks.t: Summing in a different order changes the last bits of the floating-point result, and the recomputation in the backward pass uses the same order so the gradients are consistent with the forward pass.

chunks.h: Sparse, linear, and state-space alternatives
chunks.t: Sparse attention took a different route. Child, Gray, Radford and Sutskever introduced the Sparse Transformer in 2019. Longformer followed in 2020 from Beltagy, Peters and Cohan, and BigBird also in 2020 from Zaheer and colleagues. The mechanism is a mask. Each token attends to a local window of nearby tokens and to a small set of strided or global tokens. The score matrix still has n squared entries in principle, but most are masked out and never computed. Take a window of 4,096. At n = 131,072, the quadratic cost is 1.718 × 10^10 entries; the windowed cost is 131,072 × 4,096 = 536,870,912, a 32-fold reduction. The trade is recall.

chunks.h: Sparse, linear, and state-space alternatives
chunks.t: A token can no longer attend to every other token directly. Information must hop through intermediate tokens. For exact retrieval of a fact placed far away, that hop loses precision. The mask is a bet that most long-range interactions are mediated by local structure. Linear attention replaced the softmax with a kernel feature map. Katharopoulos and colleagues proposed this in 2020. Define phi as a positive feature map applied elementwise, for example phi(x) = elu(x) + 1.

chunks.h: Sparse, linear, and state-space alternatives
chunks.t: Instead of computing softmax(Q K^T) V, compute phi(Q) (phi(K)^T V), divided elementwise by the normalizer phi(Q)·Σ_j phi(K_j) — the row sums of phi(Q) phi(K)^T — which is what makes the result a weighted average rather than an unnormalized sum that grows with n. Associativity does the work: phi(K)^T V is a d by d matrix that can be computed once and reused for every query. The cost becomes O(n d^2) instead of O(n^2 d). With d = 128, the crossover is at n = 128. At n = 131,072, linear attention costs 131,072 × 16,384 = 2,147,483,648 operations, against 2.199 × 10^12 for the quadratic form, a thousand-fold difference. The trade is exactness.

chunks.h: Sparse, linear, and state-space alternatives
chunks.t: Softmax produces a sharp, competitive weighting; a kernel feature map produces a smoother weighted average. The model loses the ability to focus precisely on one token. That loss follows from the construction. State-space models are the most recent subquadratic family. S4, from Gu, Goel and Ré in 2021, and Mamba, from Gu and Dao in 2023, use a recurrence with a fixed-size state. The mechanism is a linear recurrence over the sequence: h_t = A_t h_{t−1} + B_t x_t, y_t = C_t h_t. Each token updates the state, and the output is read from the state.

chunks.h: Sparse, linear, and state-space alternatives
chunks.t: The recurrence itself is linear-time at inference, and Mamba’s selective scan is O(n); original S4 training uses an FFT convolution at O(n log n), so the family is subquadratic rather than uniformly linear The trade is memory. A fixed-size state cannot store every key and value. It must compress. For tasks that need exact recall of a token from 100k positions ago, a fixed state will forget. Mamba adds input-dependent selection: A_t, B_t and C_t are functions of x_t, so the state can decide what to write and what to drop at each step. That is a real improvement over the fixed linear recurrence of S4, but it does not recover exact recall. The honest comparison is this.

chunks.h: Sparse, linear, and state-space alternatives
chunks.t: Flash Attention is exact, so it does not trade quality for speed. Sparse attention, linear attention and state-space models trade exactness or recall for asymptotics. That trade is sometimes worth it. The field's dominant response to the quadratic wall has been to keep exact attention and optimize the memory hierarchy around it. Linear attention is simpler and asymptotically cheaper, though constant factors and kernel maturity mean it is not always faster at short or medium context lengths It has not displaced exact attention for quality-critical long-context work. The wall is still there. We have learned to tile around it.

chunks.h: The KV cache and the prefix cache
chunks.t: The KV cache is the other cost. It grows linearly with sequence length, not quadratically, but it dominates memory at long context. A 32-layer model at d = 4,096 holds 32 × 4,096 = 131,072 values per position for one of the two tensors, and both keys and values at two bytes each come to 2 × 131,072 × 2 = 524,288 bytes per position. A 131,072-token context then costs 131,072 × 524,288 = 68,719,476,736 bytes = 68.7 GB. That is the linear cost. The quadratic compute cost appears in attention both during prefill, which is quadratic in prompt length, and during decode, where each generated token reads the full KV cache, so total decode cost is also quadratic in context length. Both are real.

chunks.h: The KV cache and the prefix cache
chunks.t: A serving engine also uses a prefix cache. It hashes the prompt prefix, looks it up in a radix tree of stored KV blocks, and reuses the matching blocks instead of recomputing them. When many requests share a long system prompt or a retrieved document, most of the prompt is already computed and the cache turns a quadratic recomputation into a lookup. Caching attacks the quadratic cost by not recomputing what you already have. It does not change the asymptotics, but it changes the constant. The decode side has its own cost. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and pays the quadratic term once. Decode generates one token at a time and attends to the KV cache.

chunks.h: The KV cache and the prefix cache
chunks.t: For each new token, the query scores against n cached keys, which costs O(n d) per head per layer, not O(n^2 d). The cache itself is 2 × n × d × layers × bytes. At n = 131,072 and d = 128, one head stores 131,072 × 128 = 16,777,216 values per layer, and keys and values together double that. At two bytes each the pair is 67,108,864 bytes per head per layer, and across 32 layers that is 2,147,483,648 bytes = 2.1 GB per stream. Multiply by concurrent streams and the cache dominates the memory budget at long context, which is what a position pool is sized for, not the score matrix.

chunks.h: What actually binds admission
chunks.t: The pool is the binding constraint. At 262,144 positions shared across four streams, each stream gets 32,750 tokens after the reply budget and overhead. The model's native window is 1,048,576 positions, so a pool at a quarter of the window cannot serve even one stream at full length. Closing that gap is cheap in memory terms and expensive in scheduling terms, because the admission reservation has to hold the line for every stream.

chunks.h: The request profile this book assumes
chunks.t: Take a request carrying a 100,000-token prompt and asking for a 600-token reply. Prefill processes all 100,000 tokens in one pass. Decode then runs 600 passes, each producing one token and each reading the cache built so far. The asymmetry between those two phases is the subject of this chapter. Time to first token is not the same as prefill time. It starts when the request arrives, so it includes admission wait, tokenization, the prefill pass, and the first decode step that emits a token. Prefill itself is one batched pass whose cost grows with prompt length; the first token adds one decode step on top.

chunks.h: The request profile this book assumes
chunks.t: Once generation starts, each subsequent token costs a full decode step, so the per-token latency during decode is set by the memory-bound roofline rather than by the arithmetic.

chunks.h: Why decode advances one token at a time
chunks.t: Prefill advances the whole prompt in one pass; decode advances one position per pass. The gap between the two rates follows from that shape rather than from a hardware defect. A language model produces one token per forward pass. It reads the sequence so far, produces a distribution over the vocabulary at the final position, samples from it, appends the sample, and starts again. Token t+1 depends on token t, and token t did not exist when the pass began, so the loop cannot be unrolled in the naive exact-sampling sense — each token must be conditioned on the verified prefix.

chunks.h: Why decode advances one token at a time
chunks.t: Techniques such as speculative decoding can propose several draft tokens and verify them in one target forward pass, partially breaking this dependency, but the target model still advances one verified block at a time. A 600-token reply is 600 forward passes, each conditioned on everything before it. The naive way to run that loop feeds the whole sequence in every time. Pass one sees 100,000 tokens, pass two sees 100,001, and the last pass sees 100,599. Attention inside each pass lets every position attend to itself and all preceding positions, so the number of comparisons in one pass grows with the square of the sequence length.

chunks.h: Why decode advances one token at a time
chunks.t: Summed over the reply, the total grows as the reply length times the square of the prompt length. For a long prompt that product is catastrophic. The model would re-derive the same key and value vectors for the same 100,000 positions 600 times and discard each set.

chunks.h: What the KV cache stores
chunks.t: The fix is to keep them. Inside every attention layer, each position produces a query, a key, and a value. The query is consumed once, in the pass that created it. The key and the value are what later positions compare against and read from. So the cache stores exactly those two, per layer, per position, per key-value head, which is why it is called the KV cache and not the QKV cache. The omission of the query is the whole point. It is the one tensor with no future. To see the shapes, take one layer with h query heads, g key-value heads, and head dimension d. The hidden state at a position projects to a query of h×d numbers, a key of g×d numbers, and a value of g×d numbers.

chunks.h: What the KV cache stores
chunks.t: When g equals h the layer is ordinary multi-head attention. When g is smaller, several query heads share one key-value head, which is grouped-query attention. The cache holds the keys and values only, so its size per position per layer is 2 × g × d × b bytes, where b is the number of bytes per element. With the cache, pass k computes keys and values for one new position, then attends that position's query against the stored keys of every previous position. The feed-forward work per step is one token's worth. The attention work per step is a read over the cache. Generating n tokens after a prefill of length p costs roughly one prefill plus n small steps instead of n full passes.

chunks.h: What the KV cache stores
chunks.t: The transformer paper described the decoder as autoregressive from the start (Vaswani et al. 2017), and caching the keys and values is the standard way to run that decoder.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind the cache size
chunks.t: Now the size. The cache per position is 2 × L × g × d × b bytes, where L is the layer count, g the KV head count, d the head width and b the element size. Take Llama 2 70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads at 128 dimensions, and two bytes per element in FP16. Each layer holds 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per position, keys and values across 80 layers come to 2 × 80 × 1,024 = 163,840 values per position, and at two bytes each that is 327,680 bytes per position, a third of a megabyte. At a 131,072-token context the cache is 131,072 × 327,680 = 42,949,672,960 bytes = 42.9 GB, which is most of a 192 GB H100 once the 140 GB of FP16 weights are loaded.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind the cache size
chunks.t: That is why the same model in four bits leaves room for long context and in sixteen bits does not. The same multiplication answers the other sizes. A 100,000-token prompt needs 100,000 × 327,680 bytes = 32,768,000,000 bytes, or 32.77 GB. The pool's 262,144 positions would hold 262,144 × 327,680 bytes = 85,897,216,000 bytes, or 85.9 GB, and the native 1,048,576-position window would hold 1,048,576 × 327,680 bytes = 343,597,383,680 bytes, or 343.6 GB. Four concurrent 100,000-token streams would need 4 × 32.77 GB = 131.1 GB, which is more than the card has spare beside its FP16 weights. The multiplier on g matters here.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind the cache size
chunks.t: A model with 32 query heads and 8 key-value heads pays one quarter of what the same model would pay with 32 key-value heads, because the cache scales with g and not with h. That ratio is why grouped-query attention became standard, and it is what makes long context affordable at all. Every decode step re-reads the whole cache for its stream, so cache size sets the floor on step time as well as on memory.

chunks.h: Positions, rows, and admission
chunks.t: The pool itself is a shared resource. It holds 262,144 positions across 4 concurrent streams. Positions, tokens, and rows are three different things and the rest of this chapter depends on keeping them apart. A token is a unit of text. A position is one slot in the pool holding that token's key and value for every layer. A row is one entry in a decode batch, and the book assumes a round batch of at most 16 rows per step. The allocator is paged, following the design Kwon and colleagues described for vLLM in 2023. The pool is divided into fixed-size blocks, typically 16 positions each, and a block table maps each request's logical positions onto physical blocks.

chunks.h: Positions, rows, and admission
chunks.t: A request that grows does not need contiguous space, so the pool does not fragment the way a contiguous allocator would. The analogy to virtual memory is exact. The operating system maps contiguous virtual pages onto scattered physical frames through a page table, and the serving engine maps contiguous logical positions onto scattered physical blocks through a block table. That is what chapter 13 means by the page table fixing the allocation problem. Admission reserves the reply budget before generation starts.

chunks.h: Positions, rows, and admission
chunks.t: The scheduler admits a request only if the pool can supply blocks for the prompt plus the reply budget, which is a worst-case reservation so that a request never stalls mid-reply waiting for cache. With four streams an equal share of a 262,144-position pool is 65,536 positions each, though the pool is shared and a stream may use more if others use less. The reservation subtracts 32,768 for the reply, 16 for the round batch, and 2 for alignment, leaving 32,750 usable positions per stream. A 100,000-token prompt does not fit that ceiling, so it cannot be admitted at concurrency 4 at all.

chunks.h: Positions, rows, and admission
chunks.t: At concurrency 1 the whole pool is available: 262,144 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 229,358 positions, and the prompt needs 100,000 of them against that ceiling, leaving 129,358 spare. It fits with room to grow.

chunks.h: Batching, bandwidth, and the prefix cache
chunks.t: Decode is not compute-bound. The arithmetic per step is tiny: one token's worth of multiply-adds against a cache that may be hundreds of thousands of positions long, and against every weight in the model. Count the arithmetic intensity. Each weight participates in one multiply-add for the single new token, which is two floating-point operations, and it must be read from memory once, which is two bytes in half precision. That is one FLOP per byte. The KV read adds bytes and roughly proportional arithmetic, about one FLOP per byte in FP16, so it keeps the overall intensity near one rather than lowering it.

chunks.h: Batching, bandwidth, and the prefix cache
chunks.t: The intensity sits near one, far below the balance point of peak throughput divided by bandwidth, which for an H100 is 295 FLOPs per byte. The limit is therefore memory bandwidth. On an H100 that is 3,350 GB/s of HBM3, and a 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB of weights per token, so the floor is 35 GB / 3,350 GB/s = 10.4 ms per token, about 96 tokens per second for a single stream. The cache and the weights both have to come past the arithmetic units on every step, and a faster clock buys nothing because the units sit idle waiting on memory. Prefill sits on the other side of the roofline. A prefill pass processes p tokens at once, so each weight read is amortized over p tokens.

chunks.h: Batching, bandwidth, and the prefix cache
chunks.t: At p = 100,000 the intensity is roughly p FLOPs per byte, hundreds of times above the balance point of 295 FLOPs per byte, so the pass is compute-bound. That is why prefill and decode behave so differently on the same hardware: opposite bottlenecks. Batching is the whole game in serving. Adding a stream does not cost four times the work, because the weight read is shared across the batch: one pass over the weights serves every row. That sharing is where the gain comes from. Each stream's cache read is separate, though, and the attention kernel walks rows one at a time, so the gain is never linear. Write the step time as a shared term A plus a per-stream term B times the stream count s.

chunks.h: Batching, bandwidth, and the prefix cache
chunks.t: The speedup from one to four streams is 4(A + B) / (A + 4B), which is below 4 whenever B is not zero. At longer contexts the cache term grows and the multiplier falls further. A prefix cache is the mitigation that costs nothing in quality. It matches the beginning of a new request against blocks already in the pool. Each block is hashed together with the hash of the block before it, so a match requires the entire prefix to be identical, not just one block. On a hit the allocator increments the block's reference count and points the new request's block table at the existing physical block. Eviction is least-recently-used among blocks whose reference count has fallen to zero.

chunks.h: Batching, bandwidth, and the prefix cache
chunks.t: When many requests share a long system prompt or a retrieved document, most of the prefill is skipped. Nothing about the model changes. The same numbers are simply not computed twice. The remaining cost is structural. The pool is fixed at 262,144 positions and shared, so context becomes a resource to be allocated rather than a property of the model. A stream that reserves 32,768 tokens of reply budget has reserved the cache for them whether or not it uses them, which is why the per-stream ceiling is 32,750 and not 65,536. The KV cache began as an optimization and became the constraint.

chunks.h: Batching, bandwidth, and the prefix cache
chunks.t: Multi-query attention, which Shazeer proposed in 2019, and grouped-query attention, which Ainslie and colleagues published in 2023, both attack the same multiplier in the formula, the number of key-value heads. State-space models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) avoid a growing cache altogether, and the architectures that deploy at long context tend to carry some answer to the cache question. Nobody set out to make memory the bottleneck of inference. The field arrived there, then reorganized itself around it.

chunks.h: Why the KV cache exists
chunks.t: A decoder at step t has already emitted t−1 tokens, and to emit the next one it needs to attend over all of them. For each head, the model computes a score between the new query and each previous key. The score is q·k / sqrt(d_head). It masks positions after t−1 by setting their scores to negative infinity, applies softmax over the allowed positions, and uses the resulting weights to average the previous value vectors. The keys and values were computed on earlier steps and do not change, so recomputing them wastes work. Every serving stack stores them as the KV cache.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind the cache bill
chunks.t: The cache size per token is 2 × layers × kv_heads × d_head × dtype_bytes. The factor 2 is for one key vector and one value vector. kv_heads is the number of key-value heads, which equals the query head count in multi-head attention and can be smaller in the sharing schemes below. Take a representative model with 32 layers, 32 query heads, d_head=128, stored in FP16 at 2 bytes. Multi-head attention caches 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 524,288 bytes per token, or 512 KiB. At 4,096 tokens that is 2 GiB. MQA with one KV head caches 2 × 32 × 1 × 128 × 2 = 16,384 bytes per token, or 16 KiB, and 64 MiB at 4,096 tokens. The ratio is 32x. The saving compounds with context.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind the cache bill
chunks.t: DeepSeek-V2's MLA stores a 512-dimension latent plus 64 shared rotary values per layer per position, which is 576 values, or 1,152 bytes at two bytes each. A grouped-query layer at 8 KV heads of 128 dimensions stores 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per layer, or 2,048 bytes, so MLA is 2,048 / 1,152 = 1.78 times smaller per position. Multi-head attention at 32 heads of 128 dimensions stores 4,096 values per layer, or 8,192 bytes, and against that MLA is 8,192 / 1,152 = 7.1 times smaller. That is the shape of the problem: context is a knob you pay for in bytes per position, and every scheme here is a way to lower that price.

chunks.h: From multi-head to multi-query attention
chunks.t: The original transformer did not treat this as a problem, because it was not built for serving. Vaswani and colleagues, in "Attention Is All You Need" (2017), split the model dimension into several heads, and gave each head its own query, key and value projections. The reason is structural. A head learns what to look for and what to advertise as worth looking for, and those two learned subspaces are coupled. If head three wants to find previously-mentioned dates and head five wants to find syntactic heads of phrases, they need different key spaces to express that.

chunks.h: From multi-head to multi-query attention
chunks.t: Multi-head attention buys expressiveness by giving every head a private key-value vocabulary, and the cache bill for that expressiveness is one key-value pair per head per token per layer. Noam Shazeer looked at that bill in 2019 and asked what would happen if all the query heads read from a single shared key head and a single shared value head. His paper is called "Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need," and the title is the argument. The key and value projections are the write side of attention; the queries are the read side. Sharing the write side collapses the cache by a factor equal to the number of query heads.

chunks.h: From multi-head to multi-query attention
chunks.t: The attention score and value-aggregation FLOPs per token do not change, though the K/V projection FLOPs fall; the bytes read from the cache fall For the representative model, MHA reads 16,384 bytes per token per layer from the KV cache; MQA reads 512 bytes. The attention arithmetic intensity rises from 1 FLOP/byte to 32 FLOP/byte. The ridge point is peak FLOPs divided by memory bandwidth. Above it a kernel is compute-bound; below it, bandwidth-bound. That intensity is still below the ridge point for this class of GPU, so the kernel remains bandwidth-bound. Shazeer reported comparable BLEU on WMT14 English-German. The quality cost is real.

chunks.h: From multi-head to multi-query attention
chunks.t: With one shared key head, every query head retrieves through the same subspace. Chowdhery et al. (2022) reported that MQA training became unstable at PaLM's 540B scale and used query-key layer normalization to stabilize it. Falcon shipped MQA in 2023.

chunks.h: GQA as a dial and an uptraining recipe
chunks.t: Grouped-query attention arrived in 2023 as the obvious interpolation. Joshua Ainslie and colleagues at Google, in "GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints," proposed dividing the query heads into G groups, with one key-value head per group. Set G equal to the head count and you have multi-head attention back. Set G to one and you have multi-query attention. Everything between is a dial. For the representative model with 32 query heads and 8 groups, kv_heads=8. The cache per token is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, or 128 KiB, one quarter of MHA. At 4,096 tokens that is 512 MiB.

chunks.h: GQA as a dial and an uptraining recipe
chunks.t: What made GQA spread was the uptraining recipe rather than the memory saving. Ainslie's group showed that you can convert an existing multi-head checkpoint without pretraining from scratch. Within each group, mean-pool the key and value projection matrices across the query heads that will now share them, then continue pretraining for 5% of the original token budget. If original pretraining used D tokens, uptraining uses 0.05D tokens. With the standard 6ND FLOP approximation, uptraining costs 6 × N × 0.05D = 0.3ND FLOPs. The average is a warm start; continued pretraining adapts the shared projection to all its members. Ainslie et al.

chunks.h: GQA as a dial and an uptraining recipe
chunks.t: compared GQA with 1, 2, 4, and 8 groups and found 8 groups close to MHA on their summarization and translation benchmarks. Llama 2 70B uses 8 KV heads for 64 query heads; Mistral 7B uses 8 KV heads for 32 query heads. That adoption followed from kernel support and checkpoint conversion.

chunks.h: MLA compresses keys and values into a latent
chunks.t: DeepSeek went further in 2024. DeepSeek-V2 introduced multi-head latent attention, and the mechanism is genuinely different from head-sharing. Instead of giving groups of heads a shared key-value head, MLA compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent vector. A down-projection maps the model dimension into a much smaller latent dimension; two up-projections map the latent back out into per-head keys and per-head values. What you cache is the latent plus a separate rotary key, one small vector per token per layer, shared implicitly by every head because every head reconstructs its own key and value from it.

chunks.h: MLA compresses keys and values into a latent
chunks.t: Take a model with 32 layers, 32 heads, d_head=128, d_model=4096, latent rank 512, and a shared rotary key dimension 64. The cache per token per layer is 512 + 64 = 576 elements. In FP16 that is 1,152 bytes, or 1.125 KiB per token per layer. Across 32 layers that is 36 KiB per token, and 144 MiB at 4,096 tokens. MHA for the same model is 512 KiB per token and 2 GiB at 4,096 tokens. MLA is about 14.2x smaller

chunks.h: Absorbing projections and decoupling RoPE
chunks.t: The score between query q and key k is qᵀW_UKc, where c is the latent and W_UK is the up-projection. That equals (W_UKᵀq)ᵀc, so the up-projection can be folded into the query projection at load time. The same trick works on the output side: the weighted sum over values is W_UV times the weighted sum over latents, so W_UV folds into the output projection. At decode, the kernel multiplies the absorbed query against c and adds the rotary part. The full key and value matrices are not materialized. Rotary position embedding, RoPE, rotates queries and keys by position-dependent angles.

chunks.h: Absorbing projections and decoupling RoPE
chunks.t: A rotated key cannot be recovered from a shared latent by any fixed linear map applied to the query, because the rotation depends on where the key sits. DeepSeek's fix was to decouple the rotary key. The cache carries a separate small shared rotary key, one per token rather than per head, that receives RoPE, and the kernel concatenates it with the content part at score time. The cache therefore holds the latent plus that rotary key, which is still far smaller than a full per-head key and value pair.

chunks.h: The quality-versus-cache curve and adoption constraints
chunks.t: Across the three generations the quality-versus-cache curve has a consistent shape. Multi-query attention sits at the cheap end and pays for it. Grouped-query attention recovers most of the lost quality as soon as you have more than a couple of groups; Ainslie et al. found that 8 groups closely match MHA, so additional groups are generally unnecessary. MLA sits at the far end. Its latent is a learned compression, so each head can reconstruct a distinct key subspace from the shared latent.

chunks.h: The quality-versus-cache curve and adoption constraints
chunks.t: DeepSeek-V2's report compared against dense models on MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval and reported higher MMLU and HumanEval scores but a lower GSM8K score than DeepSeek 67B while shrinking the cache substantially. Which one you should use depends on what you are allowed to change. GQA is a drop-in: existing kernels handle it, existing checkpoints can be uptrained into it, and the code change is a reshape. MLA is better on the curve, but it is not a drop-in: adopting it requires either training with MLA or uptraining/converting an existing model, plus kernels written and validated for the absorbed-projection form. DeepSeek was building its own stack and could pay that cost.

chunks.h: The quality-versus-cache curve and adoption constraints
chunks.t: Most of the field could not, so GQA became the default. That outcome follows from engineering constraints rather than a pure quality ranking. None of these techniques remove the cache. They shrink the per-token cost, and then long context and high concurrency eat the savings back. You still have to decide where each request's cache lives, how much to reserve for it, and what to do when the pool fills. That is an allocation problem, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

chunks.h: The worst-case reservation and its arithmetic
chunks.t: Orca, the serving system Yu and colleagues described at OSDI in 2022, made a promise on every request it admitted. The scheduler reserved a contiguous stretch of GPU memory sized for the longest sequence the model could produce, and handed that stretch to the request for its entire life. The reservation happened before the first token existed. Nobody knew how long the answer would be. The engine had little choice. Keys and values accumulate one position per generated token, and a buffer cannot grow in place when the bytes after it belong to another request. Take a reserving engine. Its KV pool holds 262,144 positions and it admits four streams at a time.

chunks.h: The worst-case reservation and its arithmetic
chunks.t: The admission rule divides the pool equally, so each stream is entitled to 65,536 positions. From that share it subtracts three config constants. The first is the default reply budget, 32,768 tokens, because the rule reserves room for a reply that names no length. The second is the decode round batch width, 16 rows, the widest row kernel the scheduler can assemble. The third is two positions of slack for the position counter's boundary bookkeeping. 65,536 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 32,750. A request is admitted against that ceiling whether or not it intends to use it, and it holds the whole 65,536-position share for as long as it runs. The model's native window is 1,048,576 positions.

chunks.h: The worst-case reservation and its arithmetic
chunks.t: A pool of 262,144 positions covers a quarter of it. Raising the pool to the full window would add three quarters of the cache's full size, so the cost scales linearly with positions and nothing else. The per-stream ceiling then becomes 1,048,576 / 4 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 229,358 tokens. The ceiling is a function of the pool divided by the number of streams. It has almost nothing to do with what any particular request needs. Two kinds of waste follow. Internal fragmentation is the gap between what a sequence reserved and what it used. A request that finishes at 100 tokens still held its whole 65,536-position share until it finished, so 65,436 positions sat idle for its whole life.

chunks.h: The worst-case reservation and its arithmetic
chunks.t: External fragmentation is the gap between buffers. Each sequence needs one contiguous run, so a hole left by a departing request can only be reused by a new request whose worst-case length fits inside it. Large holes are rare, since they require a large request to leave first, and the allocator ends up holding plenty of free memory in pieces too small to admit anything. Kwon and his coauthors at Berkeley measured the cost in 2023, running against FasterTransformer and Orca. Between 20 and 40 percent of the memory reserved for KV cache actually held token state. The rest was a reservation against a future that mostly did not arrive.

chunks.h: The worst-case reservation and its arithmetic
chunks.t: Orca had already introduced continuous batching, which admits new requests as old ones finish and raises utilization considerably. Continuous batching fixed when memory was allocated. It did not fix how much.

chunks.h: Decode is bandwidth-bound
chunks.t: That distinction matters because decoding is bandwidth-bound. HBM3 on an H100 moves 3,350 GB/s. Every decode step reads the weights once and the KV cache of every active sequence. Write W for the bytes of weights, k for the KV bytes per token per sequence, and n for the batch. A step reads W + nk bytes and cannot finish faster than (W + nk) / 3,350×10⁹ seconds. The weights term is fixed; the cache term scales with n. Adding one more sequence adds k / 3,350×10⁹ seconds to the step and one more share of a weight read you were going to pay for anyway. Memory wasted on reservations is throughput you cannot buy back. Concurrency behaves the way the bandwidth arithmetic predicts.

chunks.h: Decode is bandwidth-bound
chunks.t: Four sequential 400-token requests pay four full weight reads, one after another. The same four fired concurrently share a single weight read across the batch, so the step is shorter than four steps would be. The gain is real and sublinear, because each sequence still reads its own cache and the attention kernel walks rows one at a time.

chunks.h: From page tables to PagedAttention
chunks.t: The fix came from an operating system textbook. In virtual memory a process sees a flat, contiguous address space that has nothing to do with where its bytes live. Physical memory is divided into frames of a fixed size. A per-process page table maps each virtual page number to a physical frame number, and the hardware translates every access, consulting a TLB of recent translations and walking the table only on a miss. Because frames need not be adjacent, allocation means finding any free frame rather than finding a contiguous run, and fragmentation collapses to the unused tail of the last page (10-kv-cache sizes the buffer this replaces).

chunks.h: From page tables to PagedAttention
chunks.t: PagedAttention, published by Kwon and colleagues at SOSP in October 2023 and shipped as vLLM, applies that arrangement to the KV cache. Physical memory is carved at startup into blocks holding a fixed number of token positions. Each physical block ID indexes the KV storage for those positions across all layers, with one per-layer slice per block, for one sequence. A sequence owns a single block table, an array indexed by logical block number whose entries are physical block numbers Growing a sequence past a block boundary means allocating one more block and writing one more pointer. Nothing is copied, and no contiguity is required.

chunks.h: From page tables to PagedAttention
chunks.t: Internal fragmentation is bounded by the unused tail of a single block per sequence. The kernel that reads this layout works one query at a time. For a query at position p, the logical block is p / B and the offset within it is p mod B. The kernel walks the sequence's logical blocks in order, reads each physical block number from the table, loads that block's K and V, and computes Q·Kᵀ over at most B keys. Softmax has to span blocks, so the kernel carries a running maximum m and a running normalizer l, the online-softmax trick from Milakov and Gimelshein in 2018 and Dao's FlashAttention in 2022.

chunks.h: From page tables to PagedAttention
chunks.t: For each block it computes the block's local max, rescales the accumulator by exp(m_old − m_new), adds the block's exponentials, and moves on. The final block is usually partial, so the kernel masks positions past the sequence length before taking the max. Block boundaries never split an attention computation; they only split the loop.

chunks.h: What the gather costs the kernel
chunks.t: Gathering through a table costs something. Each block is a separate memory transaction, and the table read is a dependent load that must complete before the K/V load can start. A contiguous run lets the prefetcher stream and lets the compiler emit one wide vectorized load; a gather cannot. The first paged kernels paid for this. One rewrite hoisted the block-table read into shared memory once per block per warp instead of once per query. Another double-buffered the next block's K/V while computing the current one, to hide the dependent-load latency. A third replaced a separate tail kernel with in-kernel masking of the partial block.

chunks.h: What the gather costs the kernel
chunks.t: In the reported benchmarks, those changes brought the paged kernel to parity with the contiguous one; parity is workload- and block-size-dependent, and small blocks or high concurrency can still make the dependent block-table gather lose

chunks.h: Copy-on-write sharing and prefix caching
chunks.t: The block table made sharing cheap. Two sequences that branch from the same prompt have block tables whose entries point at the same physical blocks, and each block carries a reference count. Take a prompt of 100 tokens with 16-position blocks. It occupies seven blocks, six full and one holding four tokens. Sequence A's table reads 7, 12, 3, 19, 22, 8, 41, and every one of those blocks has refcount 1. Fork into A and B, and both tables point at the same seven blocks with refcount 2. B generates token 101, which lands in logical block 6, physical block 41.

chunks.h: Copy-on-write sharing and prefix caching
chunks.t: Its refcount is 2, so the engine takes a free block, say 55, copies 41's contents into it, rewrites B's entry 6 to 55, and decrements 41 to 1. A's table is untouched. The copy is one block, not the prefix. This is fork() and copy-on-write, transplanted, and it is what makes parallel sampling and beam search affordable. The same mechanism extends across requests that were never related. vLLM added automatic prefix caching in 2024. The hash granularity is one block, and each block's hash is chained to the hash of the block before it, so a hash identifies the whole prefix up to that block rather than the block alone.

chunks.h: Copy-on-write sharing and prefix caching
chunks.t: On a hit the engine compares the stored token IDs against the incoming ones before reusing the block, which is how collisions are caught; a 64-bit hash by itself would not be enough. Only full blocks are cached. A partial tail block is never shared, because its contents change as tokens are appended. Eviction is LRU over blocks whose refcount has fallen to zero, and a cached block stays in the hash map until it is evicted or reused, at which point its refcount goes back to 1. When many requests share a long system prompt or a retrieved document, most of their prompt tokens are served from cache.

chunks.h: Copy-on-write sharing and prefix caching
chunks.t: A hash and a pointer chase replace the forward pass for every block that matches, and the saving grows with how much traffic shares a prefix. The cache does not change the model; it just avoids computing the same numbers twice.

chunks.h: Admission, block size, and where paging stops paying
chunks.t: Admission in a paged engine looks different from the reserved engine's ceiling. The scheduler admits a request when the free-block count covers the blocks its prompt needs; the next token may fit in the last partial block, and a new block is allocated only if that block is full. It does not reserve the reply budget. If the pool runs dry, the scheduler preempts the lowest-priority sequence, either swapping its blocks to CPU memory or dropping them and recomputing the prefix later. The ceiling becomes the pool itself, and no per-stream division applies. Block size is the tuning knob, and the trade fits in a short list.

chunks.h: Admission, block size, and where paging stops paying
chunks.t: Take a 100-token sequence and count the blocks a paged engine allocates: - Block size 8: 100 / 8 = 12.5, so 13 blocks. Twelve are full and the last holds the remaining 4 tokens, so 4 of tail waste and 13 table entries. - Block size 16: 100 / 16 = 6.25, so 7 blocks. 7 × 16 = 112 positions, so 112 - 100 = 12 of tail waste, and 7 entries. - Block size 32: 100 / 32 = 3.125, so 4 blocks. 4 × 32 = 128 positions, so 128 - 100 = 28 of tail waste, and 4 entries. - Block size 64: 100 / 64 = 1.5625, so 2 blocks. Two blocks cover 128 positions, and 128 - 100 = 28 of tail waste, with 2 entries.

chunks.h: Admission, block size, and where paging stops paying
chunks.t: Small blocks cut the tail waste and multiply the table entries the kernel must chase; large blocks do the reverse. Sixteen positions is the common default because it keeps the table small enough to cache and the waste small enough to ignore. The virtual-memory analogy has limits worth naming. There is no page fault. Blocks come from a pool allocated at startup, and the engine never migrates a block to disk mid-step. There is no TLB. The block table is read from global memory on each kernel launch and cached in shared memory or registers by hand, which is why the hoisting rewrite mattered. And the indirection has a real cost that reservation does not pay.

chunks.h: Admission, block size, and where paging stops paying
chunks.t: When sequences are short and uniform, reservation waste is small and the gather overhead dominates, so a contiguous allocator can win. Paging pays when lengths vary widely, which is the normal case for chat traffic. Against FasterTransformer and Orca, the vLLM paper reported two to four times the throughput on the same hardware. Memory capacity bounds the batch size, and in the bandwidth-bound decode regime batch size is the dominant throughput lever — though compute or attention bandwidth can cap it sooner. Paging cuts the waste per sequence from most of a worst-case buffer to at most one block, and a larger batch amortizes each weight read over more tokens.

chunks.h: Admission, block size, and where paging stops paying
chunks.t: NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM ships paged KV blocks, and SGLang's RadixAttention, described by Zheng and colleagues in 2024, manages the KV cache as a radix tree of token prefixes, a different allocation abstraction from vLLM’s fixed-size paged block table, so that shared prefixes are found by tree walk rather than by hash. The idea changed the KV cache from a private buffer into an addressable resource, and once memory is reached through a table, sharing, eviction, offloading and defragmentation become ordinary allocator problems rather than special cases. A reserving engine still caps what a request can ask for.

chunks.h: Admission, block size, and where paging stops paying
chunks.t: Its per-stream ceiling sits at 32,750 tokens while the model's window is 1,048,576, and the gap is a line in a config file. Raising the pool lifts the ceiling to 229,358, still well short of the full window, and the pool stops wherever memory runs out. The ceiling moves until it hits that floor. The silicon sits far above it.

chunks.h: Chapter 13: Why the second request is cheaper
chunks.t: A support bot answers a familiar question. The system prompt is identical to the last call. The user's question differs by a sentence. The engine receives the prompt, tokenizes it, and begins prefill. If it recomputes the system prompt from scratch, it has wasted most of the work. The second request should be cheaper because the keys and values for the shared prefix are already known, but only under conditions the mechanism must make explicit.

chunks.h: When a shared prefix is actually reusable
chunks.t: Start with the condition. In a decoder-only transformer, prefill processes the prompt tokens through every layer. At each layer, each token produces a query, a key, and a value. The key and value for token \(i\) depend on tokens \(1\) through \(i\). Attention is causal, so token \(i\) never sees tokens after \(i\). If two requests have the same token sequence up to position \(i\), then the key and value at position \(i\) are identical in both requests, layer by layer. The computation is deterministic; there is no randomness in the forward pass. The KV cache stores those tensors so decode can attend to them without recomputing.

chunks.h: When a shared prefix is actually reusable
chunks.t: The same storage can be shared across requests when the prefix matches. The match is stricter than “same tokens.” With rotary position embeddings, the key at a position depends on the absolute position through the RoPE rotation. The same token sequence at a different absolute position produces different keys. A prefix cache therefore requires the shared prefix to start at the same absolute position, usually position \(0\), because prompts begin there, and the cache key must include the model weights/version, tokenizer, adapter or LoRA identity, dtype, block size, and starting position or block index. If any of those differ, the cached KV is not valid.

chunks.h: When a shared prefix is actually reusable
chunks.t: A fixed system prompt is not literally free. The engine still pays for hash computation, tree lookup, block-table updates, and reference-count bookkeeping, and the cached blocks must still be resident and not invalidated. It is nearly free in prefill compute only while those conditions hold.

chunks.h: What a PagedAttention block stores
