chunks.t: The storage unit is the PagedAttention block. In PagedAttention, the KV cache is divided into fixed-size physical blocks, or pages, in GPU memory. A request’s block table maps each logical block index in its token sequence to a physical block ID. For each layer and each head, the cache stores key and value vectors for every token position in the block. A block is therefore a slice across every layer and every head. For layer \(l\), head \(h\), and offset \(o\) inside the block, the cache holds a key vector and a value vector of dimension \(d_{\text{head}}\). A physical block ID refers to the same offset in every layer/head’s K and V arrays.

chunks.h: What a PagedAttention block stores
chunks.t: PagedAttention gave the KV cache fixed-size blocks and a block table; prefix caching reuses those blocks across requests by pointing a new request’s block table at the same physical pages and incrementing the blocks’ reference counts.

chunks.h: How block hashes bind a block to its prefix
chunks.t: In block-based prefix caching, the lookup uses fixed-size token blocks and a hash table keyed by block content plus the prefix hash; radix-tree caches such as RadixAttention instead match variable-length token sequences along tree edges Take a block of consecutive tokens. Hash the token IDs in the block together with the hash of the previous block and the cache-key namespace fields above. The previous-block hash binds the block to its prefix, so the same tokens at a different place in a document do not collide.

chunks.h: How block hashes bind a block to its prefix
chunks.t: The hash table maps the hash to one or more candidate physical KV blocks; implementations may use a fast non-cryptographic hash such as xxHash or a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256, trading lookup speed against collision resistance. Because collisions are possible, the cache stores the full token IDs, or a strong fingerprint, for each block and verifies the incoming tokens against the stored tokens before reuse. If the stored tokens differ, the entry is a collision and is skipped; a new entry is inserted. The hash is a lookup accelerator; the tree walk and token verification are the correctness check. A worked example distinguishes the two cases. Suppose the block size is two tokens.

chunks.h: How block hashes bind a block to its prefix
chunks.t: Request A has prefix \(A_1, A_2B_1, B_2\), and Request B has prefix \(C_1, C_2B_1, B_2\). The second block contains the same tokens \(B_1, B_2\) in both requests, but its hash includes the previous-block hash: \(h(A_1,A_2)\) for A and \(h(C_1,C_2)\) for B. The block hashes differ, so B’s second block is not reused from A. Now suppose Request C has prefix \(A_1, A_2B_1, B_2\), exactly matching A. Its first block hash matches A’s first block, and its second block hash matches A’s second block, so both blocks are reused.

chunks.h: How block hashes bind a block to its prefix
chunks.t: Separately, if the same tokens \(B_1, B_2\) appear at position \(0\) in one prompt and position \(4\) in another, the chained previous-block hash prevents reuse, because the block is bound to its prefix; if the same tokens appeared at a different position, RoPE and the different preceding context would also make the KV values differ.

chunks.h: Radix-tree lookup and the block-size trade-off
chunks.t: The radix tree stores token sequences as edges, with each node representing a shared prefix. On a new request, the engine computes block hashes incrementally and walks the tree from the root. At each node, it compares the incoming tokens to the child edges. If the tokens match an edge, the walk follows it and reuses the KV blocks along that path. If the tokens match part of an edge, the tree splits the edge at the divergence point: the matched prefix becomes a node, and the unmatched suffix becomes a new edge. If the tokens diverge, the walk stops. The engine computes only the remainder, but “remainder” is block-aligned.

chunks.h: Radix-tree lookup and the block-size trade-off
chunks.t: KV blocks are fixed-size and atomic; the cache does not reuse a partial block’s KV. If divergence falls inside a block, the entire block containing the divergence is recomputed, even if some of its tokens matched. If the prompt ends inside a block, that partial block is computed for the request but is not shared as a reusable block. The tree split may happen at token granularity for lookup, but reuse happens only for complete blocks whose hashes and stored tokens match. The new request’s block table is updated accordingly. Matched logical blocks point to existing physical block IDs with incremented reference counts.

chunks.h: Radix-tree lookup and the block-size trade-off
chunks.t: The remainder gets newly allocated physical blocks, the engine writes their K/V, and the block table entries are appended. Block size is a trade-off. Larger blocks reduce hash-table entries and block-table metadata, and they reduce lookup overhead at block granularity; they do not reduce token-level radix-tree nodes when the tree splits at token granularity. and they improve contiguous reuse, but a divergence inside a large block wastes more recomputation and makes memory allocation coarser. Smaller blocks reduce wasted recomputation at divergence and allow finer sharing, but they increase metadata, hashing, lookup, and block-table overhead.

chunks.h: Radix-tree lookup and the block-size trade-off
chunks.t: The right size depends on prompt-length distribution and divergence patterns; a common choice is 16 tokens, but it is not universal.

chunks.h: Eviction, admission, and cache isolation
chunks.t: Eviction is where the design gets subtle. The cache cannot hold every block forever. The engine must evict blocks to admit new requests. The eviction policy is least recently used on blocks, not on requests. Each block has a reference count. A live request holds a reference to every block in its KV. When the request finishes, the engine decrements the counts. Blocks with zero references become eviction candidates. The least recently used zero-reference candidate is evicted first.

chunks.h: Eviction, admission, and cache isolation
chunks.t: Shared blocks are counted per block-table reference, not per token: if two requests both hold the same physical block, its reference count is two; when one request finishes, the count drops to one and the block remains. A concrete refcount/LRU example follows. Request A arrives with system-prompt blocks \(S_1, S_2\) and unique suffix block \(U_A\). \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) have refcount 1; \(U_A\) has refcount 1. Request B arrives with the same system prompt and a different suffix \(U_B\). The lookup matches \(S_1, S_2\), so their refcounts become 2, and \(U_B\) is allocated with refcount 1.

chunks.h: Eviction, admission, and cache isolation
chunks.t: Request A finishes: \(S_1, S_2\) drop to 1, and \(U_A\) drops to 0, so \(U_A\) becomes an eviction candidate. Request B finishes: \(S_1, S_2\) drop to 0 and become candidates. A request-level LRU would have evicted \(S_1, S_2\) when A finished, destroying the shared prefix while B still needed it. Block-level LRU separates the shared prefix from the unique suffix. The system-prompt blocks stay because they are touched by every request. The unique suffix goes because it is touched once. The radix tree imposes an order. A child block’s KV is only meaningful with its parent prefix. The cache enforces this by evicting leaves first. A parent block cannot be evicted while a child block is live.

chunks.h: Eviction, admission, and cache isolation
chunks.t: The enforcement is mechanical. Eviction considers only zero-reference leaf nodes. If a parent has zero references but a live child, the parent remains. If a parent must be invalidated, its descendants are invalidated first. Concurrency safety requires atomic reference-count updates under a per-block lock or a global cache lock. A lookup that finds a candidate must increment the block’s reference count before attaching it to the request’s block table; eviction checks that the count is zero and that the node is a leaf, and it cannot race with an attach. If admission fails after a partial attach, the engine decrements the counts it incremented.

chunks.h: Eviction, admission, and cache isolation
chunks.t: Admission control reserves blocks before admitting a request. The scheduler estimates the prompt blocks plus the reply budget; if free blocks are insufficient, it evicts zero-reference leaves; if still insufficient, it queues or rejects the request rather than admitting it and later evicting live blocks. Scheduling and batching interact with the cache. A high hit rate reduces the number of prefill tokens in a batch, so the scheduler can batch more requests or admit longer prompts. But cache lookup and block-table updates add CPU overhead, and eviction during scheduling can change the hit estimate. Continuous batching must account for both effects.

chunks.h: Eviction, admission, and cache isolation
chunks.t: Cache invalidation and isolation are part of correctness. When the model, tokenizer, adapter, dtype, block size, or position scheme changes, the cache namespace changes; old entries are not reused and may be cleared. If prompts from different tenants can share a cache, a tenant may infer another tenant’s prompt through hit timing or reuse. Production systems either include a tenant ID in the cache key, isolate caches per tenant, or disable cross-tenant sharing; they also verify stored tokens before reuse and clear a tenant’s entries on deletion.

chunks.h: Measuring token-level hit rate and uncached prefill throughput
chunks.t: The metrics must match the mechanism. The token-level hit rate is \( \text{cached tokens} / \text{queried tokens} \). The request-level hit rate is \( \text{requests with at least one cached token} / \text{requests} \). A numeric example follows. Request A has 100 prompt tokens and 90 are cached. Request B has 10 prompt tokens and 0 are cached. The token-level hit rate is \(90/110 = 81.8\%\); the request-level hit rate is \(1/2 = 50\%\). A request with one cached token counts as a request-level hit but saves almost no compute. That is why the useful metric is token-level.

chunks.h: Measuring token-level hit rate and uncached prefill throughput
chunks.t: It tells what fraction of prompt tokens skipped query-token processing; it is not the fraction of total prefill work removed, since uncached tokens still attend over cached KVs and other overhead remains. The counters are collected during lookup. For every prompt token considered for prefix matching, increment the query-token counter. For every token whose KV block is reused, increment the hit-token counter. The prefill timer wraps only the prefill kernel.

chunks.h: Measuring token-level hit rate and uncached prefill throughput
chunks.t: Cached tokens are not processed as queries in the prefill kernel, but their KV blocks are read as attention context when prefilling uncached tokens; prefill time therefore excludes cached-token query computation but not attention over cached KV. so the prefill-time denominator excludes them. Therefore the uncached prefill throughput uses prompt tokens minus cached tokens divided by prefill seconds.

chunks.h: Measuring token-level hit rate and uncached prefill throughput
chunks.t: The naive ratio of all prompt tokens divided by prefill seconds is an effective throughput that includes cache savings and overstates kernel compute throughput; it does not measure cache lookup For a sample window, take the prompt-token count, the cached-token count, and the prefill kernel time for the uncached tokens. The uncached throughput is the uncached token count divided by that time. A benchmark that reports prefill throughput without the hit rate is reporting the cache’s effect. The same applies to latency. Time to first token includes lookup, prefill of uncached tokens, and scheduling, so comparisons across engines need the hit rate and the uncached prefill throughput.

chunks.h: Measuring token-level hit rate and uncached prefill throughput
chunks.t: The second request is cheaper because the first request paid to build a path in the tree. SGLang’s RadixAttention is described in Lianmin Zheng et al. “SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs,” NeurIPS 2024; vLLM’s PagedAttention memory manager is described in Woosuk Kwon et al. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention,” SOSP 2023, and vLLM’s serving stack implements automatic prefix caching with block hashes. Prefix caching is implemented in several serving engines, but it is not universal and it is not free.

chunks.h: Measuring token-level hit rate and uncached prefill throughput
chunks.t: The honest report gives uncached prefill throughput and token-level hit rate separately, with the cache-key conditions and eviction policy stated. The accounting can obscure the mechanism; the mechanism should be stated first.

chunks.h: Attention That Never Builds the Matrix
chunks.t: A GPU is a stack of memories, and the distances between the layers explain most of what modern attention kernels do. Start with the execution model, since everything later leans on it. A kernel launches a grid of thread blocks. Each block runs on one streaming multiprocessor and contains some number of warps, each warp 32 threads that execute in lockstep. Registers belong to individual threads. Shared memory belongs to the block, is sized at launch, and is the only scratchpad a block has for sharing data between warps without going back out to global memory. Registers hold a few hundred bytes per thread and are effectively free to read.

chunks.h: Attention That Never Builds the Matrix
chunks.t: Shared memory runs to tens or a couple hundred kilobytes per SM, addressed in tens of cycles. Then L2, shared across the chip. Then the unified LPDDR5X pool, the large address space where tensors actually live.

chunks.h: The bandwidth gap and latency
chunks.t: The bandwidth gap is the number that matters. HBM3 on an H100 delivers 3,350 GB/s across the whole part. Shared memory on a single SM moves 128 bytes per clock, and a Hopper SM runs at roughly 1.8 GHz, so one SM's scratchpad sustains about 128 bytes per clock times that rate. Hopper packs 132 SMs into one package, so the aggregate scratchpad bandwidth outruns the memory system by more than an order of magnitude. That is the ratio in its bluntest form. Latency tells the same story from the other side. A shared-memory load retires in tens of cycles. A miss to HBM costs several hundred. A kernel that touches HBM pays per byte and pays again per round trip.

chunks.h: Why naive attention cannot materialize the score matrix
chunks.t: Standard attention, as Vaswani and colleagues specified it in 2017, does exactly that. Take one head with queries Q, keys K, values V, each of shape L × d. The first step forms S = QKᵀ, an L × L matrix. Take a long-document prompt of 100,000 tokens, so L = 100,000, and a typical head width of d = 128. Then L² is 10¹⁰ entries, and at two bytes each, S occupies 20 GB for a single head in a single layer. Run the roofline on that. Forming S costs 2L²d = 2.56 × 10¹² FLOPs. Materializing it is the problem. Stored in fp16 at L = 100,000 and d = 128, the score matrix for a single head occupies L × L × 2 bytes, 20 GB, so all d heads of one layer occupy L × L × d × 2 bytes, which is 2.56 TB.

chunks.h: Why naive attention cannot materialize the score matrix
chunks.t: No accelerator holds that, which is why naive attention is not merely slow but impossible at this length; the matrix must be produced tile by tile and consumed as it is produced. Softmax needs the row maximum before any element can be finalized, so a kernel that writes S out and reads it back four times moves five times the matrix through memory. At 3,350 GB/s of HBM3, moving 2.56 TB once takes 2.56 TB ÷ 3,350 GB/s = 0.76 seconds. Doing it five times costs 3.8 seconds for one layer, which is more than an H100 spends on a whole model pass at this length. The arithmetic intensity of that kernel comes to 8.74 × 10¹² FLOPs divided by 2.19 × 10¹³ bytes, or about 0.4 FLOPs per byte.

chunks.h: Why naive attention cannot materialize the score matrix
chunks.t: To be compute-bound at that intensity the machine would have to sustain 0.4 × 3,350 = 1.3 TFLOP/s from memory alone. It does not, because the kernel stalls on the four round trips. The matmuls are cheap by comparison. The materialization dominates.

chunks.h: FlashAttention's tiling fix
chunks.t: That diagnosis is what Tri Dao, Daniel Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra and Christopher Ré published in 2022 as "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness." The title states the method. Count the bytes, not the FLOPs. Their fix is tiling, borrowed from cache-aware numerical linear algebra. Split Q into row blocks of size Br and K, V into column blocks of size Bc. Load one Q block and one K block into shared memory, compute the Br × Bc score tile, apply the softmax pieces to it, multiply by the matching V block, and accumulate into a Br × d output block that also stays on chip. Advance to the next K block. The L × L matrix never exists anywhere.

chunks.h: FlashAttention's tiling fix
chunks.t: Tile sizes follow from the shared-memory budget rather than from taste. With d = 128 and fp16 operands, a Br = 128 Q tile takes 128 × 128 × 2 = 32 KB. A Bc = 64 K tile takes 64 × 128 × 2 = 16 KB, the matching V tile another 16 KB, and the Br × Bc score tile 128 × 64 × 2 = 16 KB. That totals 80 KB. NVIDIA's Hopper tuning guide lists a maximum of 228 KB of shared memory per SM, so one block fits comfortably and leaves room for double buffering, which is what lets the next K tile load while the current one is being multiplied.

chunks.h: FlashAttention's tiling fix
chunks.t: The Ampere tuning guide lists 164 KB per SM, which fits the same configuration with room for double-buffered K and V, and even double-buffered Q, though not comfortably for all four buffers. That shared-memory budget—together with register/accumulator pressure and occupancy—is what sets the tile shape, not the arithmetic alone; a 16×128 fp32 accumulator slice already costs 64 registers per thread per warp The block runs 8 warps.

chunks.h: FlashAttention's tiling fix
chunks.t: Each warp owns a 16-row strip of the Q tile and the corresponding 16 × d accumulator slice for those rows, held in registers The QKᵀ product issues as warp-level matrix multiply-accumulate instructions, and the score tile stays in registers, where row-wise softmax is computed with warp-level reductions/shuffles. One detail bites here. Shared memory is banked in 32 banks of 4 bytes, a 128-byte period. A row of the score tile at Bc = 64 fp16 is 128 bytes, exactly one period,, so every row starts on the same bank and a column-wise read serializes into 32-way conflicts. Padding the row stride to 136 elements moves each row's start by 16 bytes and spreads the accesses across banks.

chunks.h: Online softmax and the rescaling identity
chunks.t: One obstruction stands in the way, and it is why this is an algorithm rather than a loop reorganization. Softmax needs two quantities per row, the maximum score and the sum of exponentials, and neither is known until every key has been seen. Process keys in tiles and the maximum arrives late. Online softmax, published by Maxim Milakov and Natalia Gimelshein in 2018 and adopted by Dao's group, resolves it. Keep a running maximum m and a running sum l. When a tile arrives carrying a larger maximum, rescale the accumulated state by α = exp(m_old − m_new). The validity of that rescaling is a one-line derivation. The accumulator after the old tiles is O_old = Σ_j exp(s_j − m_old) v_j.

chunks.h: Online softmax and the rescaling identity
chunks.t: Rewriting each term in the new scale gives exp(s_j − m_new) = exp(s_j − m_old) · exp(m_old − m_new), and since the factor is constant across the row it factors straight out of the sum, so O_new = α · O_old + Σ_{j∈tile} exp(s_j − m_new) v_j. The same factor applies to l, because l is a sum of the same exponentials. Here is the loop. A numeric pass makes the rescaling concrete. Suppose the first tile yields scores 1.0 and 2.0 for one row, and the second tile yields 3.0 and 0.5. After tile one, m = 2.0, the exponentials are exp(−1) = 0.3679 and exp(0) = 1.0, and l = 1.3679, with O holding 0.3679·v₁ + 1.0·v₂. Tile two brings a larger maximum, so α = exp(2.0 − 3.0) = 0.3679.

chunks.h: Online softmax and the rescaling identity
chunks.t: The running sum becomes 1.3679 × 0.3679 = 0.5033 and O is scaled by the same 0.3679. Adding tile two's contributions, exp(0) = 1.0 and exp(−2.5) = 0.0821, gives l = 1.5854. The full-matrix softmax with the global maximum of 3.0 gives 0.1353 + 0.3679 + 1.0 + 0.0821 = 1.5853. The two agree once intermediate values are not rounded; using unrounded intermediates gives l = 1.5853 On the question of exactness, the running maximum is a max over values that are already exactly representable, so it is exact. Every exponent argument is therefore ≤ 0, so no exponential overflows.

chunks.h: Online softmax and the rescaling identity
chunks.t: Underflow happens only for scores more than about 103 below the maximum in fp32 (with subnormals beginning around 87 below). and those terms contribute nothing to the sum in any case. What remains is rounding. Each rescale multiplies the accumulator by a factor and rounds, so relative error grows with the number of tiles, on the order of one unit in the last place per tile in fp32. The naive kernel accumulates the same class of error over its single pass. Flash Attention adds a small multiple of it and nothing else.

chunks.h: Backward pass recomputation and linear footprint
chunks.t: The backward pass is where the memory savings turn dramatic. Ordinary attention stores the L × L matrix from the forward pass so the gradient can reuse it. Flash Attention stores none of it and recomputes the score tiles from Q, K and V during the backward pass, then applies the chain rule through softmax using the recomputed scores and the stored row normalization. The cost is one extra QKᵀ per head-layer, 2.56 × 10¹² FLOPs, against 20 GB of storage saved. That trade is not close on any single GPU. An H100 holds 192 GB of HBM in total, and dividing 192 by 20 gives 9.6, so the full score matrices for nine head-layers would consume the entire card.

chunks.h: Backward pass recomputation and linear footprint
chunks.t: A 100,000-token prefill touches thousands of head-layers. The footprint drops from quadratic to linear in sequence length. Per head, the quadratic term is 2L² bytes and the linear term is the K and V themselves, 4Ld bytes. The ratio is L/2d, which at L = 100,000 and d = 128 comes to 390×. Concretely, the score matrix for one head of one layer is 20 GB in fp16, while the keys and values it summarizes are 100,000 × 128 = 12,800,000 values per tensor, so keys and values together at two bytes each are 2 × 12,800,000 × 2 = 51,200,000 bytes. That is what made long-context models practical.

chunks.h: Backward pass recomputation and linear footprint
chunks.t: A KV pool holding 262,144 positions would need a stored score matrix larger again by the square of the ratio between the two lengths.

chunks.h: Scheduling rewrites and the decode wall
chunks.t: Flash Attention 2, published by Dao in 2023, is a scheduling rewrite. The first version rescaled the Br × d accumulator on every tile iteration and divided by l inside the loop. Both operations are elementwise work on 128 × 128 = 16,384 values, against 2·128·64·128 = 2.1 × 10⁶ FLOPs in the matmul for the same tile, so by count they look negligible. They are not, because exp and the elementwise multiply issue on units that run at a small fraction of the matrix-multiply rate, and they serialize behind the matmul. The second version keeps O unnormalized and defers the division to the end, and it rescales only when the running maximum actually changes, which after the first few tiles is rare.

chunks.h: Scheduling rewrites and the decode wall
chunks.t: It also reverses the loop so the K and V tile stays resident in shared memory while Q blocks stream past, cutting shared-memory traffic on K and V. and it partitions causal attention so that blocks working on early rows, which have few keys to visit, are paired with blocks working on late rows. Flash Attention 3, from Jay Shah and colleagues in 2024, targets Hopper. Three mechanisms carry it. The Tensor Memory Accelerator is a copy engine that takes a descriptor giving a tile's shape and strides and moves it from global to shared memory in one instruction, asynchronously, without occupying registers or the load-store units.

chunks.h: Scheduling rewrites and the decode wall
chunks.t: Warp specialization splits the block into producer warps that issue those copies and consumer warps that run the matrix multiplies, synchronized through mbarriers that track TMA copy completion, so copy and compute overlap without a software pipeline inside a single warp. And the matmuls run in fp8, e4m3, with a per-tile scale factor applied before the multiply and undone after, which doubles throughput against fp16 at a precision cost the scaling keeps bounded. What Flash Attention does not fix is decode. During decode the model emits one token at a time and attention is a single query against a long row of cached keys and values.

chunks.h: Scheduling rewrites and the decode wall
chunks.t: There is no L × L matrix to avoid, and the kernel is bandwidth-bound on the cache instead. Layout matters here. Keys and values are stored per layer, per KV head, per position, contiguous along the head dimension, so a decode step reads one long run rather than chasing a stride. At d = 128 in fp16, one KV head at one layer over the full 262,144-position pool occupies 262,144 × 128 × 2 = 67.1 MB for keys and the same for values, and 67.1 MB × 2 = 134.2 MB together, so every decode token reads that slab once per layer and per KV head — layers × KV heads × 134.2 MB in total, which is why the kernel is bandwidth-bound. Prefix sharing sits on top of that layout.

chunks.h: Scheduling rewrites and the decode wall
chunks.t: Requests that begin with the same tokens map onto the same physical blocks through a radix tree over token blocks, so a shared system prompt is stored once and read by every request that uses it. When a workload shares a long system prompt, most prompt tokens hit the prefix cache and the prefill work they would otherwise cost is skipped. Flash-Decoding, also from Dao's group in 2023, splits the key sequence across blocks and merges the partial results with the same online rescaling, which helps long-context decode, though the dominant cost stays the bytes moved over the cache. The same reasoning sets the shape of decode.

chunks.h: Scheduling rewrites and the decode wall
chunks.t: A single stream reads the weights once per token and is bound by bandwidth, not arithmetic. Adding streams shares that read across the batch, so throughput rises sublinearly with concurrency. Prefill is the opposite: one pass over the weights serves every prompt token, so the arithmetic per byte stays high and the pass is compute-bound. The next chapter picks up at the cache, where the question becomes how many of those bytes a decode step actually has to touch.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost of full attention
chunks.t: A request lands with a long prompt. Somewhere near the beginning is a clause the user cares about. The model generates an answer one token at a time. For each generated token, full attention compares it against every prompt token and every token generated so far. That is the baseline, and it is expensive. Take a long-document prompt of 100,000 tokens. At that length, the causal mask leaves n(n+1)/2 query-key pairs, where n is the prompt length. For n=100,000, that is 100,000 times 100,001 divided by 2, or 5,000,050,000 pairs. Each pair is a dot product of a query vector and a key vector. The scores go through a softmax, and the result weights a sum of value vectors.

chunks.h: The quadratic cost of full attention
chunks.t: The previous chapter explained that writing the attention matrix to memory and reading it back is the bottleneck. Sparse attention reduces the number of scores computed and the number of keys read. The prefix cache saves work when two requests share a prefix. Sparse attention saves work within a single request by reducing the keys each token reads.

chunks.h: Local, dilated, and global sparse patterns
chunks.t: Sparse Transformer, by Child, Gray, Radford and Sutskever in 2019, factored attention into local and strided patterns. The design bet was that many of the n squared interactions carry little information. A token needs its neighbors and a few long-range connections, but it does not need every other token. Longformer, by Beltagy, Peters and Cohan in 2020, turned that idea into a practical encoder. It combined a sliding window, dilated windows, and global tokens. The sliding window is the simplest. Each token attends to a fixed number of previous tokens. In a causal model, token i attends to the W positions ending at i. The cost per token is W instead of n. Take n=131,072 and W=4,096.

chunks.h: Local, dilated, and global sparse patterns
chunks.t: At the last position, full attention reads 131,072 keys. The window reads 4,096 keys. Over the whole prompt, full causal attention has 131,072 times 131,073 divided by 2, or 8,589,869,056 pairs. A sliding window has at most n times W pairs, or 131,072 times 4,096, which is 536,870,912 pairs. The ratio is 8,589,869,056 divided by 536,870,912, or about 16. The window caps each token's read at W, so the total cost grows linearly with n instead of quadratically. Stack the layers and the receptive field grows. With a window of W positions including the current one, one layer lets token i see i-W+1 through i.

chunks.h: Local, dilated, and global sparse patterns
chunks.t: Two layers let token i see the union of the windows around those positions, which reaches back to i-2W+2. After L layers, the earliest visible position is i-L(W-1). The receptive field size is L(W-1)+1. Take W=4,096 and L=32. The receptive field is 32 times 4,095 plus 1, or 131,041 positions. A 131,072-token prompt is longer than that by 131,072 − 131,041 = 31 positions, so a token at the final position reaches back to position 32 through the chain. The path is indirect. A token at position 1 reaches the final token through a chain of 32 attention operations. At each layer, the representation of the earlier token is mixed with up to 4,095 other tokens by a softmax that sums to one.

chunks.h: Local, dilated, and global sparse patterns
chunks.t: The final hidden state can carry a compressed trace of the clause, but it has no addressable slot for the exact string. A name or a number that appears once is averaged with everything else along the path. The residual stream keeps the token's original embedding, but later layers add updates to that stream, and the exact key-value pair from the first layer is not stored as a lookup key in the final layer. Longformer added two refinements. A dilated window attends to every d-th token in a wider span. With 4,096 scores and dilation 2, the window covers 8,191 positions. A dense window with 4,096 scores covers 4,096 positions. The score count is the same, and the span doubles.

chunks.h: Local, dilated, and global sparse patterns
chunks.t: Global tokens are a few positions that attend to every token and are attended by every token. Longformer marks task-specific positions as global, such as the classification token or the question in a question-answering task. BigBird in 2020 adds random attention edges alongside the same global-token pattern; the global tokens themselves are fixed or task-specific, not randomly selected. Training includes the global attention mask, so gradients flow through the global token. The global token gives every position a two-hop path to every other position: position → global token → other position That path passes through the global token's hidden state, which is a weighted sum of values.

chunks.h: Local, dilated, and global sparse patterns
chunks.t: It is not a copy of each key-value pair. The graph is connected, and the information is lossy. With g=4 global tokens and n=131,072, the extra dense component is about 2 times g times n, or 1,048,576 pairs. That is about 0.012 percent of the causal full count. The cost is small. The benefit is a direct path. The cost in information is that the global token carries a summary.

chunks.h: Attention sinks and the softmax denominator
chunks.t: Attention sinks are a separate mechanism. StreamingLLM, by Xiao and colleagues in 2023, found that a pure sliding window fails when it evicts the first few tokens. The softmax has to sum to one. If no key is strongly relevant, the model needs a place to put the remaining probability mass. Initial tokens often receive high attention regardless of semantic content. Because softmax must sum to one, the model can dump leftover probability mass on them. They need not be identical across sequences or semantically empty; the sink is an empirical behavior, not something learned from their stability You can see the effect in a toy softmax.

chunks.h: Attention sinks and the softmax denominator
chunks.t: Suppose a query has scores 4.0 for the sink key, 2.0 for a relevant key, and 1.0 for an irrelevant key. The exponentials are 54.598, 7.389, and 2.718. The sum is 64.705. The sink gets 54.598 divided by 64.705, or 0.844. The relevant key gets 0.114. The irrelevant key gets 0.042. Remove the sink key and the softmax runs over 2.0 and 1.0. The sum is 10.107. The relevant key gets 0.731, and the irrelevant key gets 0.269. The attention mass redistributes. The sink key matters because it holds the denominator open. Its value matters less if the sink's value vector is near zero or if later layers ignore it. You can separate the roles with a diagnostic. Keep the sink key but set its value to zero.

chunks.h: Attention sinks and the softmax denominator
chunks.t: The denominator still includes the sink, so the relevant key keeps 0.114 of the mass. Remove the sink key but keep its value. The value is never read because the key is gone. The first case changes the content added. The second changes the normalization. StreamingLLM reported that keeping a small number of initial tokens plus the recent window recovered the full-cache perplexity on their streaming benchmark. The fix follows from the softmax. The sink keys keep the denominator close to what the model saw in pretraining.

chunks.h: Rolling KV cache and position IDs
chunks.t: Mistral 7B in 2023 applied sliding window attention in every layer and used a rolling buffer for the KV cache. The cache holds only the last window of keys and values. Mistral 7B’s fp16 KV cache is about 128 KiB per token (32 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 2 for K/V × 2 bytes). A 4,096-position window therefore needs about 512 MiB of KV cache per stream. The same 128 KiB multiplies out over longer spans: 65,536 positions come to 65,536 × 128 KiB = 8 GiB, and a full 131,072-token prompt comes to 131,072 × 128 KiB = 16 GiB. The rolling buffer is a circular array. For token i, the slot is i modulo W. The attention mask maps logical positions to slots.

chunks.h: Rolling KV cache and position IDs
chunks.t: When the buffer wraps, the kernel must gather the valid slots in order and mask the rest. Position IDs are absolute, not slot indices. With rotary position embeddings, the dot product between query i and key j depends on i-j. If you renumber positions after eviction, the model sees a different relative distance. The rolling buffer keeps the original position IDs so the rotation stays consistent. Sparse attention and KV eviction are different. Sparse attention changes the score matrix. A block-sparse kernel can skip reads from a full cache. KV eviction deletes entries from the cache. The first preserves the option to read old keys if a later query needs them. The second does not.

chunks.h: Rolling KV cache and position IDs
chunks.t: Mistral combines a local attention pattern with a rolling buffer, so the score matrix is sparse and the cache is evicted. The model computes a softmax over the window, so the attention distribution is normalized over a smaller set. In Mistral

chunks.h: Pool arithmetic and hybrid attention
chunks.t: A shared pool makes the same point at serving time. Suppose a pool of 262,144 positions is split across 4 request slots, which gives 65,536 positions per stream. A request that fills its slice reserves a 32,768-token reply budget, leaves 16 round-batch rows, and keeps 2 positions of slack, so it can admit 65,536 - 32,768 - 16 - 2 = 32,750 prompt tokens. Full causal attention over 65,536 positions has 65,536 times 65,537 divided by 2, or 2,147,516,416 pairs per stream. A 4,096-position sliding window over the same 65,536 positions has at most 65,536 times 4,096, or 268,435,456 pairs per stream. The window cuts the pair count by about 8 times. The arithmetic is the argument for sparsity.

chunks.h: Pool arithmetic and hybrid attention
chunks.t: The question is whether the discarded pairs mattered. Hybrid layers mix local and full attention. Gemma 2 in 2024 alternated sliding-window layers with full-attention layers. The full layers give every token a direct edge to every other token. The local layers keep most of the cost down. Take L=32 layers, half local and half full, with W=4,096. At the last token, a full layer reads 131,072 keys. A local layer reads 4,096 keys. The 16 full layers cost 16 times 131,072, or 2,097,152 key comparisons. The 16 local layers cost 16 times 4,096, or 65,536. The total is 2,162,688. All 32 full layers would cost 32 times 131,072, or 4,194,304.

chunks.h: Pool arithmetic and hybrid attention
chunks.t: The hybrid is 2,162,688 divided by 4,194,304, or 51.6 percent of the full cost. The full layers are arranged every few layers, and training uses the same pattern. A full layer gives a direct edge from query i to key j, so the exact key-value pair is available at that layer. The architecture removes the information bottleneck that a pure local stack imposes, though it does not guarantee that the model learns to use the edge. For retrieval, that edge is the difference between reading the clause's key and reconstructing the clause from a summary.

chunks.h: Block-sparse kernels and retrieval evaluation
chunks.t: Implementation matters. A GPU attention kernel tiles queries and keys. It loads blocks of keys and values from high-bandwidth memory into shared memory, computes the query-key products for the tile, updates the online softmax running max and denominator across live key blocks, and accumulates the weighted value block; final normalization happens after all live key blocks are processed. Full attention reads every key-value block for every query block. A block-sparse pattern marks some blocks as entirely masked. The kernel skips those blocks. It does not load their keys and values from memory, does not compute their query-key products, and does not include them in the softmax denominator.

chunks.h: Block-sparse kernels and retrieval evaluation
chunks.t: That is how fewer scores become fewer memory reads. The pattern has to align with the kernel's block shape. If the mask is irregular, the kernel may still load a full block or use a gather, and the memory saving shrinks. Coalesced loads want contiguous blocks. A sliding window is contiguous, so it maps well to block masks. A strided or dilated pattern is less contiguous, so it may need a different kernel or a gather. FlashAttention tiles the attention computation and avoids materializing the full score matrix, but it still reads all keys and values. A sparse kernel skips tiles. The two techniques compose.

chunks.h: Block-sparse kernels and retrieval evaluation
chunks.t: The sparse mask decides which tiles are live, and the tiled kernel computes only those tiles. Evaluation separates two questions. Language modeling asks whether the next token is predicted well. Retrieval asks whether an exact string from a distant position can be recovered. A sliding-window model can have low perplexity on ordinary prose and still fail a needle-in-a-haystack test that asks for a clause beyond the window. The two metrics test different paths through the computation graph. Perplexity mostly exercises local continuation. Retrieval exercises the direct edge from the question token to the clause token.

chunks.h: Block-sparse kernels and retrieval evaluation
chunks.t: If no layer provides that edge, the answer must come through hidden-state summaries. A summary often preserves the gist of the clause but not the exact string; residual connections can in principle carry token identity along indirect paths, so exact copying through summaries is possible but generally unreliable That is why a hybrid with at least one full layer is a different architecture from a pure sliding window, even when most layers are local. For a 131,072-token prompt, the question token at the final position needs an edge to a clause at position 32, the earliest position its receptive field reaches.

chunks.h: Block-sparse kernels and retrieval evaluation
chunks.t: In a pure sliding-window model with W=4,096 and L=32, the edge exists only through 32 layers of averaging. The receptive field reaches the clause, but the path is indirect. In a hybrid with one full layer, the edge exists directly at that layer. The difference is whether the key-value pair for the clause is read by the question's query at some layer. If it is, the model can copy the exact string. If it is not, the model can only use what survived in the hidden states. That is the test to run on a long-context model. Find the layer where the question token's query reads the clause token's key.

chunks.h: Block-sparse kernels and retrieval evaluation
chunks.t: If no such layer exists, the model must rely on indirect, multi-hop propagation through intermediate hidden states. That path can sometimes carry exact strings, but it is less reliable and often degrades to gist-level summarization. So the direct-edge test is strong evidence for retrieval, not a proof against it

chunks.h: Chapter 16: Where most of the parameters actually live
chunks.t: In 2021, Mor Geva, Roei Schuster, Jonathan Berant and Omer Levy published a paper titled "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories." The title made a claim about mechanism, and it landed on the part of the Transformer that most of the field had treated as plumbing. Attention was where the ideas were, where the papers were, where the interpretability work went. The feed-forward network was the thing you appended to attention because a block needed a second sublayer. Then you count the matrices, and the emphasis looks badly placed.

chunks.h: Counting the matrices in a block
chunks.t: Start with the block. A Transformer of depth L carries a residual stream, a vector of width d that runs from the embedding layer to the unembedding. Each sublayer reads that vector, computes something, and adds the result back. Attention lets positions exchange information; it projects the stream into queries, keys and values, mixes across positions, and writes the mixture back. The feed-forward sublayer does no mixing. It reads one position's vector, transforms it in place, and adds the result back at that same position.

chunks.h: Counting the matrices in a block
chunks.t: At the end, the final stream state is multiplied by an unembedding matrix of shape d by V, where V is the vocabulary size, and the resulting scores become the logits that pick the next token. A standard block holds two sublayers. Attention has four projections of size d by d, for queries, keys, values and the output mix, so 4d² parameters. The feed-forward sublayer takes the d-dimensional residual vector, expands it to an inner width m, applies a nonlinearity, and contracts back to d. Two matrices, d by m and m by d, holding 2dm entries. With m = 4d, that pair holds 8d², twice the attention sublayer, in every layer, at every scale.

chunks.h: Counting the matrices in a block
chunks.t: Layer norms and biases add a few d each, which is rounding error against d² terms. Across a model, the feed-forward share of the parameters is 8Ld² / (12Ld² + cVd) where c is 2 when the embedding and unembedding matrices are separate and 1 when the weights are tied. Take d = 4096, L = 32 and V = 128,000. Attention comes to 32 × 4 × 16,777,216 = 2,147,483,648 parameters. The feed-forward pair comes to 32 × 8 × 16,777,216 = 4,294,967,296. Untied embeddings add 2 × 128,000 × 4096 = 1,048,576,000, for a total of 7,491,026,944 and a feed-forward share of 57.3 percent.

chunks.h: Counting the matrices in a block
chunks.t: Tie the embeddings and one matrix is shared, so the embedding term halves to 128,000 × 4096 = 524,288,000, and the total drops to 6,966,738,944, lifting the share to 61.7 percent. The fraction climbs toward two thirds as d grows, because the per-layer terms scale with d² while the embedding term scales with d.

chunks.h: The four-times inner width and its gated variants
chunks.t: The four-times expansion is old. Vaswani and colleagues set the inner width to four times the model width in "Attention Is All You Need" in 2017, and their Table 3 varies individual hyperparameters—including d_ff 2048 vs 4096 and d_model 512 vs 1024—and reports BLEU/perplexity alongside parameter counts, not perplexity per parameter. Table 3 mostly varied model and inner widths together, but row (A) did test the ratio in isolation by raising d_ff from 2048 to 4096 at d_model = 512; that 8× inner width performed slightly worse than the 4× base (PPL 4.41 vs. 4.33, BLEU 26.0 vs. 26.4), so the 4× choice was not strongly established by that table. GPT-2 in 2019 and GPT-3 in 2020 kept it.

chunks.h: The four-times inner width and its gated variants
chunks.t: T5, from Raffel and colleagues in 2019, kept four times in its base and large sizes but widened the inner layer to sixteen times at 3B parameters and sixty-four times at 11B, buying capacity with parameters rather than with depth. The gated variants that Shazeer described in 2020 change the count. A gated linear unit multiplies the expanded vector by a second projection of the same shape, so the sublayer holds three matrices of d by m instead of two. To keep the parameter budget at 8d², the inner width has to shrink to 8d/3, about 2.67d. That is where LLaMA's inner width comes from. With d = 4096, 8d/3 is 10,922.67, and LLaMA rounds it up to 11,008, a multiple of 256.

chunks.h: The four-times inner width and its gated variants
chunks.t: The ratio is 2.69, and the parameter count matches a plain four-times FFN. The four-times rule is really a rule about 8d² of parameters per layer (see 19-moe|the mixture-of-experts chapter for where that arithmetic goes next), and the inner width is whatever satisfies it.

chunks.h: The feed-forward block as a key-value memory
chunks.t: What does the pair compute? Take one token's residual vector, call it x. The first matrix has m rows, each a direction in the same d-dimensional space as x. Row i produces a scalar s_i = k_i · x, the dot product of that row with x, which measures how much the token's state points along that direction. Geva's group called those rows keys. A nonlinearity φ then acts on each scalar separately. In the original Transformer φ was ReLU, so any s_i below zero became exactly zero and that slot contributed nothing to the output.

chunks.h: The feed-forward block as a key-value memory
chunks.t: Modern blocks usually use GELU, which attenuates small negative scores instead of zeroing them, or SwiGLU, which multiplies the expanded vector by a second gated projection before the contraction. Under ReLU, roughly half the slots are silent for a given token. Under GELU, almost all of them contribute something, most of it tiny. The second matrix supplies, for each of the m hidden units, a vector v_i in d-space. Those are the values. The sublayer's output is y = Σ_i φ(k_i · x) v_i a weighted sum of value vectors, with the weights set by how well the token matched the corresponding keys. That is a memory read. The keys are addresses, the values are contents, and the read is soft.

chunks.h: The feed-forward block as a key-value memory
chunks.t: A slot whose key aligns strongly with x contributes a large multiple of its value vector; a slot whose key is orthogonal contributes nothing; a slot whose key points the other way is suppressed by the nonlinearity. Each layer has m slots. A model with 32 layers and m = 16,384 has 524,288 of them, and the residual stream carries the sum forward to be read again by the next layer's keys. Geva and colleagues followed up in 2022 by projecting each key and each value into vocabulary space, multiplying by the unembedding matrix and reading off the tokens with the largest scores.

chunks.h: The feed-forward block as a key-value memory
chunks.t: A key whose top projections are "the", "a" and "an" is a determiner detector, and it tends to fire when the residual at the current position carries determiner features, which may come from a determiner at that position or nearby (e.g. the previous token). A key that projects onto "France", "Paris" and "Europe" fires on country names. That projection gives an operational definition of a key pattern, the set of input contexts that maximize k_i · x, which you can find by gradient ascent on the dot product or by scanning a corpus for the contexts where the slot's activation is largest. The values, projected the same way, tend to promote words related to the entity under discussion.

chunks.h: The feed-forward block as a key-value memory
chunks.t: The pairing is what you would design if you wanted a lookup table keyed on context and returning content.

chunks.h: Causal evidence and editing the memory
chunks.t: This is where factual knowledge sits, and the causal evidence is specific. Meng, Bau and colleagues published ROME in 2022. Their procedure runs the model twice. The clean run uses a prompt like "The Eiffel Tower is located in" and assigns high probability to "Paris". The corrupted run replaces the subject tokens with noise, and the probability of "Paris" collapses. Then, for each layer and each token position, they take the corrupted run and overwrite one component's output with the value it had in the clean run, letting the rest of the network run forward.

chunks.h: Causal evidence and editing the memory
chunks.t: The score is the probability the model then assigns to the correct answer token, averaged over a set of facts and normalized against the clean and corrupted baselines. Plotted as a heatmap over layers and positions, the recovery concentrates at the last token of the subject and peaks in the middle layers, and the component that carries most of it is the feed-forward block. Restoring attention outputs at the same position recovers less, and the attention effect sits at the final token position in later layers, where the model moves the answer into place. The mechanism explains the result.

chunks.h: Causal evidence and editing the memory
chunks.t: Attention moves information between positions; by the time a subject like a country name has been resolved into the residual stream at its own position, the attribute lookup is a local operation. The feed-forward block is the only sublayer that transforms a single position Editing follows from the structure. If a fact is a key-value pair, you can change the value by writing to the second matrix. ROME computes a rank-one update. Let k be the key direction you want to steer, taken as the FFN’s intermediate key vector at the subject’s last token—the input to the down-projection matrix—averaged over many prompts. and let v be the vector you want the sublayer to add to the residual.

chunks.h: Causal evidence and editing the memory
chunks.t: The current output along that direction is W k, where W is the down-projection matrix. The update is ΔW = (v − W k) kᵀ / (kᵀ k) and after the write, (W + ΔW) k = W k + (v − W k)(kᵀ k)/(kᵀ k) = v. The key now returns exactly the value you asked for, which is what makes the memory addressable in the first place. The outer product (v − W k)kᵀ has rank one, so every row of the update is a multiple of k and the write changes the matrix only along one direction in input space. The size of the write is small. With d = 4096 and m = 16,384, W holds 67,108,864 entries.

chunks.h: Causal evidence and editing the memory
chunks.t: If the key has norm 20 and the desired change has norm 1, the update has Frobenius norm 1/20 = 0.05, spread across that many entries, so the root-mean-square change per entry is 0.05/8192 ≈ 6.1 × 10⁻⁶. The layer is chosen by sweeping candidates and measuring the edit's success rate on held-out prompts; the paper reports the best results in a middle band of layers, which matches where the causal trace peaks. The fragility comes from superposition. In d dimensions there are at most d mutually orthogonal directions, and a layer has m = 4d keys, so the keys cannot all be mutually orthogonal; many must have nonzero cosine similarity and therefore interfere.

chunks.h: Causal evidence and editing the memory
chunks.t: Two keys with cosine similarity c interfere. After the edit above, the output for a second key k' changes by (v − W k)·c, because the update's effect on k' is (v − W k)(kᵀ k')/(kᵀ k). At c = 0.3 and equal key norms, a neighbouring key's readout shifts by 30 percent of the edit vector. Currency facts illustrate it. "The currency of France is" and "the currency of Germany is" share the pattern "the currency of X is", so their keys point in similar directions, and rewriting the franc entry drags the mark entry with it. MEMIT, from the same group later in 2022, spreads thousands of edits across several layers to keep any single layer's interference below the point where neighbours drift.

chunks.h: Quantization and outlier weights
chunks.t: Quantization has the same shape of implication, from the other direction. Because the feed-forward matrices hold most of the bytes, they are where quantization saves the most memory; where quantization errors do the most damage depends on each component’s sensitivity, and the feed-forward layers are not necessarily the most sensitive. Group quantization stores each weight as a b-bit integer q and reconstructs it as w ≈ s·q, with one scale s shared by a run of G consecutive weights. The scale is set from the largest magnitude in the group. A group of 128 weights at 4 bits with a 16-bit scale costs 4 + 16/128 = 4.125 bits per weight.

chunks.h: Quantization and outlier weights
chunks.t: Shrink the group to 32 and the cost rises to 4.5 bits; widen it to 256 and it falls to 4.0625. Finer groups track the local range better and pay more overhead. The failure mode is a single large weight inside a group. Take a group of 128 weights whose typical magnitude is 0.02 and one outlier at 0.5. With 4-bit signed integers spanning −8 to 7, the scale must be 0.5/7 ≈ 0.0714. A weight of 0.02 then quantizes to round(0.02/0.0714) = round(0.28) = 0, and it is reconstructed as zero. Without the outlier, the largest magnitude might be 0.03, giving a scale of 0.03/7 ≈ 0.00429. The same weight quantizes to round(0.02/0.00429) = 5 and is reconstructed as 0.0214, an error of 7 percent.

chunks.h: Quantization and outlier weights
chunks.t: Every small weight in that group suffers the same fate. Outlier weights are common enough that the quantization literature organized around them. LLM.int8(), from Dettmers and colleagues in 2022, found that a handful of feature dimensions in large Transformers carry values an order of magnitude above their neighbours, and handled those dimensions in higher precision. AWQ in 2023 singles out a small fraction of weights, chosen by activation magnitude, for gentler treatment, and its authors report that protecting that fraction accounts for most of the quality gap at 4 bits.

chunks.h: Quantization and outlier weights
chunks.t: GPTQ, also from 2023, takes a different route: it quantizes every weight, using second-order information from activations to compensate for the quantization error column by column These methods protect outlier dimensions or salient weights across the model’s linear layers rather than singling out one matrix; the feed-forward down-projection is nonetheless a sensitive site, because its output is written straight into the residual stream An error δy there becomes an error in the stream that every later sublayer reads. It is projected by W_Q and W_K into the next layer, and finally in the logits as w·δy for each unembedding row w.

chunks.h: Quantization and outlier weights
chunks.t: The stream also holds the attention outputs and the token embedding, so δy competes with them rather than replacing them, but attention does carry δy to other positions through the value vectors, but the error at position i itself is not averaged away, because the feed-forward output is written at one position and read at that same position by the next feed-forward sublayer.

chunks.h: Bandwidth and sparse experts
chunks.t: The bandwidth argument points the same way. Decode reads the whole weight set once per token, because each token needs every matrix. That read, not the arithmetic, sets the floor on step time. A 70-billion-parameter model at four bits reads 35 GB per token, and on an H100 with 3,350 GB/s of HBM3 that is 35 GB / 3,350 GB/s = 10.4 ms per token for a single stream. The feed-forward block holds the large majority of those parameters, so most of that read is feed-forward weights. Splitting the weights across two GPUs halves the bytes each one reads per step, which is the reason tensor parallelism pays for itself on decode. Concurrency shows the loop is not purely bandwidth-bound.

chunks.h: Bandwidth and sparse experts
chunks.t: Batching four streams lets one read of the weights serve four tokens, so aggregate throughput would approach four times the single-stream rate if weights dominated the cost. It never does, because the rest of the per-token cost is the KV cache read, and at a 100,000-token prompt that read is enormous. Prefill behaves differently: it is matrix-matrix work that reuses each weight across many tokens, so it is compute-bound, though at very long prompts quadratic attention takes over the prefill cost and the rate becomes context-length dependent. Decode is matrix-vector work that reuses each weight once, so it is bandwidth-bound. Here is the part worth arguing about.

chunks.h: Bandwidth and sparse experts
chunks.t: The four-times ratio is a default that most papers no longer justify, but it is not arbitrary. It sets how much of the parameter budget goes into memory capacity rather than into token mixing, and Vaswani. Because the parameters live in the feed-forward block, the obvious way to add capacity without paying per-token compute proportional to the added capacity is to add many feed-forward blocks and route each token through only a few of them—capacity grows with the number of experts, while per-token compute grows only with the routing fan-out.

chunks.h: Bandwidth and sparse experts
chunks.t: Shazeer's sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts in 2017 and Switch Transformer in 2021 are that move, and the sparse models that followed, from GShard in 2020 to Mixtral in 2023, keep the shape. The arithmetic is plain. Take d = 4096 and eight experts per layer, each a plain four-times FFN holding 8d² = 134,217,728 parameters. The layer then holds 8 × 134,217,728 = 1,073,741,824 feed-forward parameters, eight times the dense layer, while a top-2 router sends each token through two experts, so per-token compute is 2 × 134,217,728 = 268,435,456 multiply-adds against 134,217,728 for the dense layer. Capacity grows eightfold and compute doubles.

chunks.h: Bandwidth and sparse experts
chunks.t: Attention got the name on the architecture, and the feed-forward block got the parameters, with a router of about 32,768 parameters (plus bias) deciding which of them a token reads.

chunks.h: Chapter 17: ReLU, GELU, and the gated turn
chunks.t: A transformer block does two things to a token's vector. It lets tokens look at one another through attention, and then it passes the vector through a feed-forward network. The feed-forward network is two matrix multiplies with a bend between them. The residual stream has width d. The first matrix projects the d-dimensional vector up to an intermediate width m. The activation bends each coordinate. The second matrix projects back down to d. The result is added back to the residual stream.

chunks.h: Why the nonlinearity cannot be removed
chunks.t: Remove the bend and the two matrices collapse into one. Matrix multiplication is associative, so W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. A product of matrices is a matrix. Two linear layers stacked without a nonlinearity have exactly the expressive power of one. The model's depth in the width direction buys nothing. That identity is the reason the activation exists. The intermediate layer is the model's private scratch space, wider than the residual stream, and the nonlinearity stops the scratch space from being a relabeling of the input. Everything else in this chapter is about which bend to use.

chunks.h: Saturation and the vanishing gradient
chunks.t: For most of the pre-2010 era the answer was sigmoid or tanh. Both saturate. The sigmoid derivative is σ(x)(1−σ(x)), which has a maximum of 1/4 at x=0. If a network has L sigmoid layers, the activation-derivative factor in the backpropagated gradient is at most (1/4)^L. For L=10, that factor is 1/1,048,576, about 9.5×10⁻⁷. The signal dies on the way down. Tanh has derivative 1−tanh²(x). For |x|>3, tanh²(x) is above 0.99, so the derivative is below 0.01 Ten such layers multiply the gradient by less than 10⁻²⁰. Saturation is the mechanism behind the vanishing gradient.

chunks.h: ReLU and the dead-unit problem
chunks.t: Nair and Hinton proposed the rectified linear unit in 2010, and Glorot, Bordes and Bengio made the case for it in 2011. Krizhevsky's AlexNet in 2012 made it standard. ReLU is max(0,x). Its derivative is exactly 1 for any positive input and exactly 0 for any negative one. There is no saturation on the positive side, so gradients pass through undiminished. The operation is a compare and a select, which is why it was cheap. The cost is the dead unit. If a unit's pre-activation is negative for every input in the training set, its gradient is exactly zero. The weights never move.

chunks.h: ReLU and the dead-unit problem
chunks.t: Its own incoming weights and bias receive zero gradient and stay put, but the unit can revive if upstream weights or data shift its pre-activation above zero. While dead, its output is zero, so it contributes nothing to the next layer Take a unit with weight w=0.1 and bias b=−1. For inputs x=1,2,3, the pre-activations are 0.1−1=−0.9, 0.2−1=−0.8, and 0.3−1=−0.7. All are negative. The output is zero for every input, and the derivative is zero for every input. The gradient with respect to w and b is zero, so the unit stays dead. A single large learning-rate step can push a whole slice of units into that state. Suppose a unit has w=1 and b=0, and the training inputs are x=1 and x=2.

chunks.h: ReLU and the dead-unit problem
chunks.t: The pre-activations are 1 and 2, both positive. A gradient step that sets b=−3 makes the pre-activations 1−3=−2 and 2−3=−1. Both are negative. The derivative is zero, so the unit cannot recover. Leaky ReLU and its relatives let a small fraction of the negative input through, which keeps a gradient alive. They never displaced plain ReLU in practice.

chunks.h: GELU as a probabilistic gate
chunks.t: GELU arrived in 2016 from Dan Hendrycks and Kevin Gimpel. Its construction is worth stating precisely because it explains why it behaves differently. GELU multiplies the input by the standard normal cumulative distribution function evaluated at that input: GELU(x)=xΦ(x). The standard normal CDF is Φ(x)=0.5(1+erf(x/√2)). So GELU(x)=0.5x(1+erf(x/√2)). Read that as a probabilistic gate. Φ(x) is the probability that a standard normal draw comes out below x. The unit's output is the input scaled by how likely that input is to be kept. For large positive x, Φ approaches 1 and GELU is the identity.

chunks.h: GELU as a probabilistic gate
chunks.t: For large negative x, Φ approaches 0 and GELU approaches zero from below; for any finite x it remains slightly negative with a small nonzero gradient, so GELU does not produce exact zero-gradient dead units the way ReLU does The derivative is Φ(x)+xφ(x), where φ(x) is the standard normal density. At x=0, Φ(0)=0.5 and φ(0)=0.3989, so the derivative is 0.5. At x=1, Φ(1)=0.8413 and φ(1)=0.2420, so GELU(1)=0.8413 and the derivative is 0.8413+0.2420=1.0833. At x=−1, Φ(−1)=0.1587 and φ(−1)=0.2420, so GELU(−1)=−0.1587 and the derivative is 0.1587−0.2420=−0.0833. At x=−2, GELU(−2)=−0.0455 and the derivative is 0.0228−0.1080=−0.0852.

chunks.h: GELU as a probabilistic gate
chunks.t: At x=−3, GELU(−3)=−0.0040 and the derivative is 0.00135−0.0133=−0.0119. At x=−4, the derivative is about −0.0005. The derivative is zero at the minimum near x=−0.75, and it approaches zero as x→−∞. GELU lacks ReLU's hard zero region, yet it saturates for large negative inputs. A unit whose pre-activation is consistently below −3 learns very slowly. The difference from ReLU is the smooth transition and the negative dip. For inputs just below zero, GELU outputs a small negative value, and the derivative stays nonzero until the minimum. That gives the unit a gradient signal in the region where ReLU would be flat.

chunks.h: GELU as a probabilistic gate
chunks.t: The dip helps because it keeps the unit responsive for moderately negative inputs, but it does not make the unit immortal. Practical dead-unit behavior still exists under GELU when the input distribution drives a unit far into the negative tail. The exact form needs the error function. The tanh approximation is 0.5x(1+tanh(√(2/π)(x+0.044715x³))). The factor √(2/π) matches the slope of erf(x/√2) at zero, and the cubic term improves the fit in the tails. At x=1, the exact value is 0.8413 and the approximation gives 0.84125. At x=−1, the exact value is −0.1587 and the approximation gives −0.15875.

chunks.h: GELU as a probabilistic gate
chunks.t: The maximum absolute difference over the range where the gradient is nonzero is on the order of 10⁻⁴. That is the sense in which the difference is negligible. GELU appeared in BERT (Devlin et al. 2018), and GPT-2 and GPT-3 followed. That adoption made it the default in many later models. The original GELU paper reported modest gains over ReLU and ELU on some tasks when substituted into fixed architectures; later adoption evidence does not separate architecture from activation It is smooth, it does not kill units outright, and it costs one transcendental function per element. That cost is more than a compare and select.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: The gated turn came from a different direction. Yann Dauphin and colleagues at Facebook AI Research introduced gated linear units in 2017 for convolutional language models. The idea is to split the up-projection into two halves and multiply them elementwise. Write the up-projection as a matrix W₁ of size 2m×d. Split W₁ into two d×m matrices, W_g for the gate and W_v for the value. The GLU is GLU(x)=(W_v x+b_v)⊗σ(W_g x+b_g), where ⊗ is elementwise multiplication. The gate half goes through a sigmoid and becomes a soft switch between 0 and 1. The value half passes through unchanged. The product is what the down-projection sees. The down-projection is a matrix W_d of size m×d.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: The mechanism is worth more attention than the benchmark table. In a plain feed-forward network, the output is a weighted sum of univariate functions of the input. Each hidden unit computes σ(w·x), and the next matrix adds those up. The gate changes that. If the gate unit computes g(x) and the value unit computes v(x), the contribution to the next layer is g(x)·v(x), a product of two functions of the input. That product can represent a multiplicative interaction. Suppose the input has two features a and b. Let the gate be g=σ(a) and the value be v=b. The product is σ(a)b. When a is negative, the gate is near 0 and the product is near 0.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: When a is positive, the gate is near 1 and the product is close to b. The value b passes only when a is present. That is the sense in which the gate is a soft switch. The gate and value are separate projections, so g_i and v_i can depend on different combinations of input features. If both were functions of the same scalar, the product would be univariate. The GLU uses separate projections to create the interaction. A sum of one-dimensional bends can approximate a product given enough width. The gated form builds the product into the layer with fewer parameters. That is an architectural shortcut.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: Noam Shazeer's 2020 paper, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer," took the construction and swapped the sigmoid for other activations. He tested ReLU, GELU and Swish as the gate. Swish is defined as Swish(x)=x·σ(x). The SwiGLU is SwiGLU(x)=(W_v x)⊗Swish(W_g x)=(W_v x)⊗(W_g x·σ(W_g x)). SwiGLU won on the T5 language-modeling benchmarks. Shazeer writes that he offers no explanation for the result and attributes the success to "divine benevolence" (Shazeer, 2020, arXiv:2002.05202). The price is a third matrix. The original Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) set the intermediate width to four times the model width. That choice became a default rather than a derivation.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: The plain feed-forward network is two matrices, one of size d×4d and one of size 4d×d. The weight count is 2·d·4d=8d² per layer. The multiply-adds per token are the same 8d². Now gate it. Two d×m matrices for the gate and value, plus one m×d down-projection matrix; each has dm parameters, so the total is 3dm. Holding the parameter count at 8d² requires 3dm=8d², so m=8d/3, about 2.67d. That is two-thirds of the original 4d width, a one-third reduction in width.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: The linear-layer multiply-adds land in the same place, since 3dm=8d²; the Swish gate adds a sigmoid and elementwise multiplications, so total FLOPs are somewhat higher Leave m at 4d instead and the layer grows from 8d² to 12d², a fifty percent increase in FFN parameters. Biases change the count slightly. The plain FFN has 4d biases in the up-projection and d in the down-projection, for 5d total. The gated FFN has two up-projection biases of size m each and one down-projection bias of size d, for 2m+d. With m=8d/3, that is 16d/3+d=19d/3, about 6.33d. So the gated layer has slightly more parameters when biases are present.

chunks.h: Gated linear units and the SwiGLU budget
chunks.t: Many modern models omit biases, which makes the equal-parameter calculation exact. Initialization does not change the count, but it changes whether the gate starts near open or closed. Implementations round 8d/3 up to a multiple that suits the kernel. For d=4096, the exact value is 10922.67. Rounding to a multiple of 256 gives 11008, which is 0.78% above the exact value. Llama 2 7B uses 11008. That is one concrete example; the overshoot depends on d and the chosen kernel/tensor-parallel multiple, so other models can sit closer to or much further above the exact value

chunks.h: Where each activation still lives
chunks.t: Where each activation still lives tells you what each one is good for. ReLU survives in vision models, in cheap inference stacks where a single compare beats a transcendental, and inside some mixture-of-experts implementations where the expert FFNs are kept deliberately simple. GELU is in BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3, ViT, and many of the models that inherited from them. SwiGLU is in PaLM (Chowdhery et al. 2022), Llama (Touvron et al. 2023), Mistral, and Qwen. GeGLU, the GELU-gated variant, appears where a team preferred it. My view is that SwiGLU won for a reason that is only half about quality.

chunks.h: Where each activation still lives
chunks.t: The gated form does seem to be better at equal parameters, and the multiplicative interaction is a real mechanism rather than a lucky initialization. The decisive fact is that Shazeer re-derived the intermediate width to keep the budget fixed, and that re-derivation changed the shape of gated feed-forward networks built afterwards. The activation itself is a small lever. The parameter accounting around it is the large one. The next chapter applies that counting to mixture-of-experts, where the FFN is split into many expert blocks.

chunks.h: 18. Keeping the residual stream in range
chunks.t: A transformer block has two sublayers. The first is attention, the second is a feed-forward MLP. Each sublayer reads the residual stream, computes a function, and adds its output back onto the stream. For block l with input x_l, the pre-norm form is a_l = x_l + Attn(LN(x_l)) x_{l+1} = a_l + MLP(LN(a_l)) The post-norm form is a_l = LN(x_l + Attn(x_l)) x_{l+1} = LN(a_l + MLP(a_l)) The residual stream is the shared vector that every block reads and writes. Anthropic's 2021 "A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits" gave it that name. Nothing overwrites the stream; each block adds to it. The stream is the only path connecting the first layer to the last.

chunks.h: The identity path through residual additions
chunks.t: The residual addition gives backpropagation an identity path. For a vector function f, write J_f for its Jacobian, the matrix of partial derivatives. A pre-norm block has output y = x + f(LN(x)), so ∂y/∂x = I + J_f(LN(x)) J_LN(x). The identity matrix I is the direct path. Through N blocks, the chain rule multiplies these Jacobians. Expanding the product gives the identity term plus terms with one or more J_f factors. The identity term carries a gradient component through every addition without multiplying it by a sublayer Jacobian. That identity path gives gradient a route through every block that does not multiply by a sublayer Jacobian.

chunks.h: The identity path through residual additions
chunks.t: It is one reason deep stacks can train, though it does not guarantee that the gradient at the first block is at least as large as the gradient at the last. The total Jacobian is a sum, and the other terms can cancel the identity term. Take a scalar simplification. Let LN have derivative s and the sublayer function have derivative a. For one pre-norm block, ∂y/∂x = 1 + a s. For two blocks with derivatives a and b, the gradient at the input is (1 + b s)(1 + a s) times the upstream gradient. Set s = 1, a = -1, b = 0. The product is zero. The identity term in the first block is present, but the sublayer derivative cancels it.

chunks.h: The identity path through residual additions
chunks.t: A depth comparison therefore has to look at the whole product, not just at the presence of I.

chunks.h: How the residual stream's norm recurses
chunks.t: The stream's norm also needs a recurrence, not an assumption. With x_{l+1} = x_l + f_l(x_l), ||x_{l+1}||^2 = ||x_l||^2 + 2 x_l·f_l(x_l) + ||f_l(x_l)||^2. The cross term decides the direction. If f_l points along x_l, the norm grows. If it points against x_l, the norm can shrink. If it is orthogonal, the squared norm grows by ||f_l||^2: ||x_{l+1}||^2 = ||x_l||^2 + ||f_l||^2. Over N blocks with a constant additive f_l = a, x_N = x_0 + N a, so the vector grows linearly; its norm is ||x_0 + Na|| = sqrt(||x_0||^2 + 2N⟨x_0,a⟩ + N^2||a||^2), which grows asymptotically linearly in N (exactly linear only in special cases such as x_0 parallel to a).

chunks.h: How the residual stream's norm recurses
chunks.t: With f_l = -x_l/2, x_{l+1} = x_l/2, so the norm halves each block. A model can have either behavior; the initialization and the learned functions decide which.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and the invariances that matter
chunks.t: LayerNorm arrived in July 2016 from Jimmy Lei Ba, Jamie Ryan Kiros and Geoffrey Hinton. Their problem was recurrent networks. Batch normalization computes statistics across the batch for each feature separately, which is awkward when every timestep has a different effective batch and sequences have different lengths. Ba and colleagues normalized per token and across the feature dimension. For a vector x with d components, μ = (1/d) Σ x_i σ = sqrt((1/d) Σ (x_i - μ)^2 + ε) y_i = γ_i (x_i - μ)/σ + β_i. The mean and variance come from one token's own vector, so the result does not depend on what else is in the batch. That is a batch-invariance property. It does not make the KV cache safe.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and the invariances that matter
chunks.t: The KV cache stores, for each layer and each past token, the key and value vectors produced by that layer. Future tokens attend to those stored vectors under a causal mask. Cache safety comes from causal masking and from treating past entries as read-only, not from the normalization's per-token statistics. The gamma and beta matter. Without them the layer would emit zero-mean, unit-variance output and throw away a deliberate offset that a later layer might detect. With them, normalization becomes a reparameterization. Take x = 2, 4, 6, 8. The mean is 5, so the centered vector is -3, -1, 1, 3.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and the invariances that matter
chunks.t: The variance is (9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5, the standard deviation is about 2.236, and the normalized vector is -1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342. Set gamma to all ones and beta to all zeros and that is the output. Ignoring ε (or in the limit ε→0), multiplying the input by 10 leaves the output unchanged; with ε>0, scale invariance is only approximate. Adding 100 to every component still leaves the output unchanged exactly. LayerNorm makes a layer's input invariant to scale and to shift. Zhang and Sennrich asked in 2019 which half of that invariance was doing the work. Their paper, "Root Mean Square Layer Normalization", dropped the mean subtraction and kept the scaling.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and the invariances that matter
chunks.t: RMSNorm divides x by the root mean square of its components, r = sqrt((1/d) Σ x_i^2 + ε) y_i = γ_i x_i / r. On the same vector, the mean of squares is (4 + 16 + 36 + 64)/4 = 30, the root mean square is about 5.477, and the output is 0.365, 0.730, 1.095, 1.461. That output has mean 0.913, so RMSNorm does not center anything. It is invariant to scaling and not to shifting. Zhang and Sennrich argued from their experiments that re-centering contributed little and re-scaling did the work. Dropping the mean removes one reduction, one elementwise subtraction and the beta parameters at every normalization site. LLaMA used RMSNorm in 2023.

chunks.h: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and the invariances that matter
chunks.t: The operation count falls; whether that shows up as wall-clock time depends on the kernel and the model.

chunks.h: Pre-norm, post-norm, and the Jacobian on the residual path
chunks.t: Placement changes which Jacobian multiplies the residual path. Pre-norm puts normalization inside the sublayer input, so the residual addition is outside the norm.
