chunks.t: During decode, the head runs once per decode step—one fewer than the generated-token count, because the first token’s logits come from prefill. Attention during decode reads the cached keys and values and costs O(n d_model) per layer per token for the query-key product and value sum, where n is the current context length. The head costs O(d_model V) per token. The relative cost depends on n, d_model, and V. The asymmetry is structural. A 1,000-token prompt is consumed in one prefill pass, so the head runs once for the whole prompt. A 600-token reply is produced one token at a time, so the head runs 600 times.

chunks.h: Decoding rules and failure modes
chunks.t: The head is invoked once per prompt and once per generated token, and that ratio is what makes it a target for optimisation on the decode path. The invocation count does not by itself prove that the head dominates cost, because the attention work and the head work scale with different variables.

chunks.h: The head as a fixed interface
chunks.t: The head is a fixed interface. It maps a d_model vector to V scores, and its matrix has d_model × V parameters. That can be a large block, sometimes comparable to a transformer layer and sometimes larger. The real constraint is readout. Everything the model has built in the residual stream must be legible through one linear map and a softmax. Whatever the model knows about syntax, arithmetic, or reference has to become a direction before the softmax can act on it. The softmax is where the model commits. Before it, the vector could still support many continuations. After it, there is a distribution, and a decoding rule has to choose. The next chapter takes up that choice.

chunks.h: Chapter 24: Temperature, top-k, top-p, and what each one does
chunks.t: The final projection has run. Out of the residual stream comes a vector with one score per vocabulary entry, and now something has to turn that list into a single token. It is a few lines of arithmetic, and it decides, more than any other part of the serving stack, whether the output reads as prose or as a stutter.

chunks.h: Greedy decoding and the degeneration loop
chunks.t: The simplest rule is to take the argmax. Greedy decoding picks the highest-scoring token at every step, appends it, and runs the model again. It is deterministic, it is cheap, and it degenerates. Ari Holtzman and colleagues documented the failure in April 2019 in "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration", where maximising likelihood step by step produced text that looped, drifted, and contradicted itself. The mechanism is self-reinforcement. Suppose the context ends with "the the". The model has seen that pattern in training, so the next-token scores put "the" above "cat" and "dog". Greedy takes "the".

chunks.h: Greedy decoding and the degeneration loop
chunks.t: The context becomes "the the the", an even stronger match for the repeated pattern, so the score for "the" rises again relative to the alternatives. The argmax locks the loop in. Nothing in the objective asks for variety, so nothing supplies it.

chunks.h: Temperature rescales logits without reordering
chunks.t: Temperature is the first fix, and it comes from statistical mechanics. Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski used it in Boltzmann machines in 1985. The operation is a division applied before the softmax. For logits \(z_i\), the probability of token \(i\) is \(p_i = \exp(z_i/T) / \sum_j \exp(z_j/T)\). Take three logits of 4.0, 2.0 and 1.0. At \(T = 1\) the probabilities are 0.844, 0.114 and 0.042. At \(T = 0.5\) the logits become 8, 4 and 2, and the probabilities become 0.980, 0.018 and 0.002. At \(T = 2\) the logits become 2, 1 and 0.5, and the probabilities flatten to 0.628, 0.231 and 0.140.

chunks.h: Temperature rescales logits without reordering
chunks.t: As \(T\) goes to zero the distribution collapses onto the argmax, so greedy decoding is the limit of temperature zero. As \(T\) goes to infinity it approaches the uniform distribution over the whole vocabulary. Temperature never reorders the candidates. The logits 4.0, 2.0 and 1.0 stay in that order at every positive \(T\), because division by a positive scalar and exponentiation both preserve order. What changes is the mass assigned to the tail, the lower-probability entries below the top few. High temperature gives the tail more mass; low temperature gives it less. Mathematically, no entry is removed at any positive T, so temperature has no explicit cutoff.

chunks.h: Temperature rescales logits without reordering
chunks.t: In finite precision, however, a very small positive T can underflow tail exponentials to zero, effectively dropping those tokens; this is a numerical artifact rather than an explicit top-k cut At \(T=0\) the division is undefined. Implementations special-case it as argmax, or clamp \(T\) to a small positive value; the limit is greedy, but the arithmetic needs the special case.

chunks.h: Count-based and mass-based truncation
chunks.t: Top-k sampling, introduced by Angela Fan, Mike Lewis and Yann Dauphin in their 2018 paper on hierarchical story generation, attacks that directly. Sort the distribution, keep the \(k\) highest entries, discard the rest, and renormalise what remains so it sums to one. With our three logits and \(k = 2\), the kept mass is \(0.844 + 0.114 = 0.958\), and renormalisation gives 0.881 and 0.119. The third token is gone entirely. The weakness is that \(k\) is a count, and the right count depends on the shape of the distribution, which changes at every step. When the model is confident, one token holds almost all the mass, and \(k = 10\) still admits nine tokens that are essentially impossible.

chunks.h: Count-based and mass-based truncation
chunks.t: When the model is uncertain, fifty continuations might be plausible, and \(k = 10\) throws away most of the probability mass and forces a choice among a fifth of the real options. Holtzman's nucleus sampling, from the same 2019 paper, replaced the count with a cumulative target. Sort descending, add probabilities until the running total first reaches or exceeds \(p\), keep that set, renormalise. With \(p = 0.9\) and our three logits, the first token gives 0.844, which is short of 0.9, so the second is admitted and the total reaches 0.958. Two tokens survive, and the result is identical to top-k with \(k = 2\). The difference shows up elsewhere.

chunks.h: Count-based and mass-based truncation
chunks.t: Ten equally likely tokens at 0.1 each: top-p at 0.9 keeps nine of them, while top-k at 5 keeps five and discards half the mass. One token at 0.95 with the rest spread thin: top-p keeps exactly one, while top-k at 50 keeps fifty entries, forty-nine of which are noise. The truncation width now adapts to the shape of the distribution rather than a fixed count; it is not determined by \(p_{\max}\) alone—two distributions with the same top-token probability can yield different nucleus sizes The cost is a sort over the vocabulary, which is why implementations use partial selection or a threshold scan rather than a full ordering.

chunks.h: Min-p sets a floor relative to the top token
chunks.t: Min-p, described by Minh Nguyen and colleagues in their 2024 preprint "Min-p sampling", takes a third approach. Instead of a cumulative target, it sets a floor relative to the top token: keep everything whose probability is at least \(\text{min\_p}\) times the maximum. With \(p_{\max} = 0.844\) and \(\text{min\_p} = 0.1\), the threshold is 0.0844, so the 0.844 and the 0.114 survive and the 0.042 does not. After thresholding, divide the surviving probabilities by their sum. Here the sum is 0.958, so the renormalised probabilities are 0.881 and 0.119. When the model is confident and \(p_{\max} = 0.99\), the threshold becomes 0.099 and only the top token survives.

chunks.h: Min-p sets a floor relative to the top token
chunks.t: When the model is genuinely uncertain and \(p_{\max} = 0.12\), the threshold drops to 0.012 and many more tokens survive than in the confident case, though at production vocabulary sizes the 1.2% floor still discards most of the long tail. The cutoff scales with confidence automatically, without a fixed count and without a cumulative target that can slice through a flat distribution at an arbitrary point. It does have a subtlety. Temperature rescales the logits before softmax, so \(p_{\max}\) changes nonlinearly and the effective floor moves when you change \(T\) At \(T=1\) with our three logits, \(p_{\max}=0.844\) and \(\text{min\_p}=0.1\) gives a threshold of 0.0844, keeping two tokens.

chunks.h: Min-p sets a floor relative to the top token
chunks.t: At \(T=0.5\), \(p_{\max}=0.980\) and the threshold becomes 0.098, so only the top token survives. At \(T=2\), \(p_{\max}=0.628\) and the threshold becomes 0.0628, so all three tokens survive. People who tune the two independently often end up with a sampler that behaves differently from what they intended.

chunks.h: Penalties and the order of operations
chunks.t: Penalties work on a different surface. The repetition penalty from Keskar and colleagues' CTRL paper in September 2019 walks the logits for tokens already present in the context and divides the positive ones by a factor \(r\) while multiplying the negative ones by \(r\). For a token with positive logit, dividing by \(r>1\) lowers it; for a negative logit, multiplying by \(r>1\) makes it more negative. The map is monotone on each side of zero, so two repeated tokens keep their relative order. A repeated token can fall below a non-repeated token, which is the point. The factor \(r\) is a scalar greater than 1; values below 1 would reward repetition.

chunks.h: Penalties and the order of operations
chunks.t: Frequency penalties subtract an amount \(\alpha\) proportional to how many times a token has already appeared; presence penalties subtract a flat amount \(\beta\) the first time. The scope matters. Repetition penalty applies to tokens already in the context, and implementations differ on whether the prompt counts. Many apply penalties only to generated tokens so that prompt words are not suppressed. All of these act on logits, before the softmax, so they reshape the entire distribution rather than trimming its tail. A worked example with logits 4.0, 2.0 and 1.0 and a repetition penalty \(r=1.2\) on the first token gives logits 3.333, 2.0 and 1.0.

chunks.h: Penalties and the order of operations
chunks.t: The probabilities become 0.735, 0.194 and 0.071: the first falls from 0.844, while the other two rise from 0.114 and 0.042 as the distribution renormalizes A frequency penalty with \(\alpha=0.5\) and count 2 on the first token gives logits 3.0, 2.0 and 1.0, and probabilities 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. A presence penalty with \(\beta=0.5\) gives logits 3.5, 2.0 and 1.0, and probabilities 0.766, 0.171 and 0.063. Order matters when you stack them. Penalties first, then temperature, then truncation.

chunks.h: Penalties and the order of operations
chunks.t: The reason is that mass-based truncation such as top-p/min-p is a function of the final probabilities; top-k is rank-based and temperature-invariant, so its selected set is unchanged by temperature Take logits 4.0, 2.0 and 1.0 and a repetition penalty \(r=2\) on the first token. Penalties first give logits 2.0, 2.0 and 1.0 and probabilities 0.422, 0.422 and 0.155. Top-p at 0.9 now keeps all three, because the cumulative reaches 0.999. Truncate first on the unpenalised distribution and top-p at 0.9 keeps only the first two, excluding the third token that the penalty made competitive.

chunks.h: Penalties and the order of operations
chunks.t: Temperature belongs between penalties and truncation because it changes the probabilities that the cumulative target or the min-p floor reads. If you truncate before temperature, you choose a set using the wrong mass. After truncation and renormalisation, the token is drawn from the remaining categorical distribution. The draw is random; argmax is a different decoder. A sampler with \(T=1\) and no truncation samples the full softmax.

chunks.h: Beam search and length normalisation
chunks.t: Beam search keeps \(B\) hypotheses alive at once, expands each, and retains the \(B\) highest-scoring partial sequences by cumulative log-probability. The raw score of a hypothesis \(Y\) is \(\sum_t \log p(y_t \mid y_{<t})\). Length normalisation, introduced for neural machine translation by Wu and colleagues in 2016, divides that score by a length penalty. In the GNMT formulation, \(\text{lp}(Y) = ((5+|Y|)^\alpha)/(6^\alpha)\), with \(\alpha=0.6\), and the beam score is the log-probability divided by \(\text{lp}(Y)\). Take two hypotheses. \(H_1\) has length 2 and log-probability -1.2. \(H_2\) has length 4 and log-probability -1.3.

chunks.h: Beam search and length normalisation
chunks.t: Raw scores favour \(H_1\), because -1.2 is greater than -1.3. With length normalisation, \(\text{lp}(H_1)=7^{0.6}/6^{0.6}=1.097\), so \(H_1\) scores -1.094. \(\text{lp}(H_2)=9^{0.6}/6^{0.6}=1.275\), so \(H_2\) scores -1.020. The longer hypothesis wins. When a beam emits an end-of-sequence token, that hypothesis is completed and removed from the active set; its score is stored. The search stops when \(B\) hypotheses are complete or the length cap is reached, and length normalisation is applied at completion. Beam search remained the default in statistical machine translation through Koehn's Moses in 2007 and in neural machine translation systems such as Wu et al.'s 2016 system.

chunks.h: Beam search and length normalisation
chunks.t: It is rarely used for open-ended generation, and the reasons are mechanical as well as qualitative. Maximising likelihood selects the mode of the sequence distribution, and Holtzman et al. showed that mode-seeking decoding tends to loop and drift, so beam search inherits the failure that greedy decoding has. The cost is also real. Continuous batching lets the scheduler add and remove requests at each decode step. Each request carries its own KV cache, and the batch is assembled from whatever requests are active. A beam search request is one request with several hypotheses, each needing its own KV cache and its own next-token computation.

chunks.h: Beam search and length normalisation
chunks.t: Take a pool of 262,144 positions split across four request slots, which gives 65,536 positions per stream. A request that fills its slice reserves a 32,768-token reply budget plus a few positions of round-batch and bookkeeping overhead, so it admits 32,750 prompt tokens. Each beam needs its own cache and its own reply budget, so four beams at that ceiling would need 4 × 32,750 = 131,000 positions of context plus four reply budgets, which is the whole 262,144-position pool. Beam search either shrinks the context per beam or blocks admission. Beams also finish at different times.

chunks.h: Beam search and length normalisation
chunks.t: A beam that emits end-of-sequence is complete, but the other beams continue; the request cannot be retired until the search finishes, so the scheduler holds its KV cache and its slot while other requests wait or share the batch. The sampler cannot add information to the distribution it is given. It can only decide how much of the model's uncertainty reaches the categorical draw, and each parameter above makes that decision at a different point in the arithmetic. When you tune, change one parameter at a time and re-run the same prompt. A change in \(T\) can move the min-p floor, and a change in penalties can move the truncation set.

chunks.h: Chapter 25: Guessing ahead and checking cheaply
chunks.t: A decode step on a large model is mostly a memory errand. During decode, each layer’s weight matrices, the attention projections and the MLP matrices, are streamed from memory and multiplied by one token’s activation vector. A transformer decoder stores, for each past token, a key and value vector per layer. That store is the KV cache. Decode appends one token at a time and reads the whole cache. Prefill processes many prompt tokens at once. Decode processes one token per stream per step unless a kernel packs rows from several streams. A kernel is memory-bound when the bytes it moves per arithmetic operation exceed the machine’s bandwidth-to-compute ratio.

chunks.h: Chapter 25: Guessing ahead and checking cheaply
chunks.t: It is compute-bound when arithmetic saturates. On an H100 the ratio is 989 TFLOPS against 3,350 GB/s of HBM3, or 295 FLOPs per byte. A single-stream decode step sits near one FLOP per byte, so it is memory-bound by a wide margin, and adding a faster clock buys nothing while the units wait on memory. That is why speculative decoding targets the number of steps rather than the speed of any one step. A batch of 16 rows per weight load amortises that read across the batch, so throughput rises sublinearly with concurrency rather than linearly.

chunks.h: How speculative decoding works
chunks.t: Speculative decoding attacks the decode gap. A cheap drafter guesses several tokens ahead. The target model checks all of them in one forward pass. The drafter can be a smaller model from the same family, a set of auxiliary heads, or a separate network trained for the job. It generates k candidate tokens autoregressively with its own weights. The drafter’s own decode is also bandwidth-bound, but its weights are smaller, so it usually runs faster than the target. The target model then runs a forward pass over the prompt plus the k candidates.

chunks.h: How speculative decoding works
chunks.t: Because attention is causal, the target’s logits at position i are conditioned on tokens up to and including i; the distribution used to score the draft token at position i is therefore conditioned only on the tokens before i. One pass gives a target distribution for every draft position at once. The target scores candidates. It does not generate them.

chunks.h: The verification pass is a batched GEMM
chunks.t: A verification pass over k draft tokens is a batched GEMM. The kernel loads each weight matrix once and multiplies it by a k-row activation matrix. Weight traffic is the same as a one-token decode step. Arithmetic grows by roughly k. Attention and KV writes also grow by k. For each draft token, the target computes attention over the prompt and all preceding draft tokens (acceptance is decided after the pass; KV entries for rejected drafts are discarded), then writes a key and value vector per layer. At a 100,000-token context, attention over the context is a real term. A k=4 pass does four rows of attention over 100,000 keys per layer plus four KV writes.

chunks.h: The verification pass is a batched GEMM
chunks.t: The wall-clock cost is one weight stream plus that attention and write work. It is about one decode step only when the extra k-row attention and KV-write work is small compared with the weight stream, that is, when context length is short relative to model size, not merely when k is small relative to context. At long context the verification pass costs more than the weight stream alone, and the speedup shrinks.

chunks.h: The acceptance rule and its exactness proof
chunks.t: The verifier walks the draft left to right. Let q(x) be the probability the draft assigned to token x, and let p(x) be the probability the target assigns to that same token. The draft samples x from q. The verifier accepts x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). If p is at least q, the token is always accepted. If p is smaller than q, the token is accepted only part of the time, in proportion to how much the target believes in it relative to the draft. When the verifier rejects a token, it samples a replacement from the residual distribution proportional to max(0, p(x) - q(x)). The accepted mass and the residual mass add up to p exactly. Here is the derivation.

chunks.h: The acceptance rule and its exactness proof
chunks.t: The accepted branch contributes min(q(x), p(x)). The reject probability is R = Σ_y max(0, q(y) - p(y)). Since Σ p = Σ q = 1, R equals Z = Σ_y max(0, p(y) - q(y)). The reject branch contributes R times the normalized residual, which is max(0, p(x) - q(x)). The sum is min(p(x), q(x)) + max(0, p(x) - q(x)) = p(x). That is the exactness proof for one token. A numeric example makes the residual sampler concrete. Let the vocabulary have three tokens A, B, C. Let q = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) and p = (0.2, 0.5, 0.3). The draft samples A with probability 0.5. The target assigns A probability 0.2, so the accept probability is min(1, 0.2/0.5) = 0.4.

chunks.h: The acceptance rule and its exactness proof
chunks.t: If the draft samples A and the verifier rejects it, the residual is max(0, p - q) = (0, 0.2, 0.1). The normalizer is Z = 0.3, so the normalized residual is (0, 2/3, 1/3). The verifier samples B with probability 2/3 or C with probability 1/3. The output probabilities are A: 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2; B: 0.3 × 1 + 0.5 × 0.6 × (2/3) = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5; C: 0.2 × 1 + 0.5 × 0.6 × (1/3) = 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3. The output distribution is p. To implement this, compute p and q over the vocabulary, draw u from Uniform(0,1), accept if u ≤ min(1, p(x)/q(x)); otherwise compute r_i = max(0, p_i - q_i), sum Z, and draw from r/Z. Temperature and top-p need care. Apply temperature and top-p to p and q before the ratio.

chunks.h: The acceptance rule and its exactness proof
chunks.t: The q in the ratio must be the draft’s actual sampling distribution after its own temperature and top-p. Different truncation does not break exactness, provided q is the draft’s actual post-truncation distribution and p is the target’s post-truncation distribution; it only changes the acceptance rate The residual must be over the target’s support. A token that the target’s top-p sets to zero can still appear in the draft, and the verifier will reject it with probability one. For k > 1, apply the same rule left to right. Conditional on the accepted prefix, the draft’s next-token distribution q_i and the target’s p_i are the distributions at that position.

chunks.h: The acceptance rule and its exactness proof
chunks.t: The single-token argument says the next output token is distributed as p_i. If token i is rejected, the procedure samples from the residual and stops. Later draft tokens are discarded because they were conditioned on a token the target would not have produced. If all k pass, the target samples one bonus token from p_{k+1}. By induction on positions, each output token conditional on the prior output is target-distributed. The joint distribution of the output prefix is the target’s autoregressive distribution. This is the theorem in Leviathan et al. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding,” ICML 2023, and Chen et al.

chunks.h: The acceptance rule and its exactness proof
chunks.t: “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling,” arXiv 2302.01318, 2023. Both prove exactness, not approximation. The target model remains the authority. The drafter only supplies candidates.

chunks.h: The arithmetic of the speedup
chunks.t: The arithmetic of the gain follows from the prefix accounting. If acceptance is independent with probability α, the expected number of output tokens per round is E = 1 + α + α^2 + … + α^k = (1 - α^{k+1}) / (1 - α). Let t_d be draft time per token, t_v verification time for k tokens, and t_t baseline target decode time per token. Round time is k t_d + t_v. Speedup over target decode is E t_t / (k t_d + t_v). Take k = 4, α = 0.7, t_d = 0.2 t_t, and t_v = 1.0 t_t. Then E = 1 + 0.7 + 0.49 + 0.343 + 0.2401 = 2.7731. Round time is 4 × 0.2 t_t + 1.0 t_t = 1.8 t_t. Speedup is 2.7731 / 1.8 = 1.54. A faster drafter with α = 0.3 and t_d = 0.05 t_t gives E = 1 + 0.3 + 0.09 + 0.027 + 0.0081 = 1.4251.

chunks.h: The arithmetic of the speedup
chunks.t: Round time is 4 × 0.05 t_t + 1.0 t_t = 1.2 t_t. Speedup is 1.4251 / 1.2 = 1.19. The faster drafter loses to the slower, higher-acceptance drafter. If t_v = 1.2 t_t and α = 0.1, E = 1.1111 and round time is 1.24 t_t, so speedup is 0.896. That drafter loses to no speculation at all. Choose k by this formula. Increase k while α^k remains high and k t_d stays small relative to t_v. If acceptance decays with k, a smaller k wins. Choose the drafter by measured end-to-end speedup on your traffic, since acceptance, draft time, k, and verification time interact; high acceptance is a strong signal but not sufficient by itself A drafter with higher α but slower t_d can win when t_v is large.

chunks.h: The arithmetic of the speedup
chunks.t: Measure α on your traffic, not paper numbers. The phrase “accepts only one token” hides two cases. If the verifier rejects the first draft token, the round outputs one token, the replacement. That round bought one token and paid draft plus verification, so it loses ground. If it accepts the first token and rejects the second, the round outputs two tokens, the accepted first plus the residual second. That round bought two tokens for one verification pass. The accounting is prefix length plus one replacement or bonus. The verification pass writes KV entries for draft tokens. If token i is rejected, entries for i and later are discarded. The cache truncates to the accepted prefix length.

chunks.h: The arithmetic of the speedup
chunks.t: If all k pass, the bonus token is sampled from the final logits, but its KV entry is not written during verification; it must be computed in a later forward pass. The cache after the round holds the accepted draft prefix Tree verification needs branch-aware rollback. Keep the KV entries on the accepted path and free the rest.

chunks.h: Drafting with heads, trees, and features
chunks.t: Medusa, from Cai et al. “Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads,” arXiv 2401.10774, 2024, removed the separate draft model. It attaches several decoding heads to the target model’s final hidden state. Each head predicts a token at a different offset. One head predicts the next token, another predicts the token after that, and so on. At inference, the heads produce a tree of candidate continuations. A tree attention mask lets the target model verify all branches in one pass.

chunks.h: Drafting with heads, trees, and features
chunks.t: The heads are trained with cross-entropy against the ground-truth next tokens from the training data, using the frozen target model’s hidden states as input; conditioning on those hidden states lets them approximate the target model’s continuation distribution rather than a separate draft model’s. A tree example shows the mask. Take a draft tree with root prompt and four draft positions. Position 1 is token A. Position 2 is B, child of A. Position 3 is C, child of A. Position 4 is D, child of the root. The attention mask rows for the four draft positions are row 1: 1 0 0 0; row 2: 1 1 0 0; row 3: 1 0 1 0; row 4: 0 0 0 1. Every row also attends the prompt. Row 2 attends A and B.

chunks.h: Drafting with heads, trees, and features
chunks.t: Row 3 attends A and C. Row 4 attends D only. The mask is a lower-triangular pattern on each branch, with zeros across sibling branches. The kernel computes A once and shares its KV entry between the B and C branches. After verification, if B is accepted and C and D are rejected, the cache keeps prompt, A, B and frees C, D. That is branch dedup plus rollback. EAGLE, from Li et al. “EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty,” arXiv 2401.15077, 2024, drafts at the feature level. The draft model takes the target model’s hidden state at position t together with the embedding of the next token, and predicts the hidden state at t+1.

chunks.h: Drafting with heads, trees, and features
chunks.t: The target’s LM head converts that predicted state to a token distribution. Training minimizes a regression loss against the target’s hidden states, with a token-level cross-entropy term. The draft operates in the target’s feature space. A sampled token ID is a single choice from a distribution. The hidden state that produced it contains the context that shaped the choice. Drafting from features gives the drafter a richer signal, and that can raise acceptance. EAGLE’s draft model is still small, but it operates in the target model’s feature space rather than in vocabulary space. Multi-token prediction trains the capability into the model itself. Gloeckle et al.

chunks.h: Drafting with heads, trees, and features
chunks.t: “Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction,” arXiv 2404.19737, 2024, showed that auxiliary heads predicting several future tokens improve training. DeepSeek-V3, “DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report,” arXiv 2412.19437, 2024, built multi-token prediction modules into pretraining. With heads at offsets 1, 2, and 3, head 1 predicts token t+1 from hidden state h_t. Head 2 predicts t+2 from h_t and the embedding of t+1. Head 3 predicts t+3 from h_t and the embeddings of t+1 and t+2. The heads share the embedding and output head. Training adds cross-entropy at each offset to the main next-token loss. At inference, those heads draft a chain and the target verifies it.

chunks.h: Drafting with heads, trees, and features
chunks.t: There is no separate small model to train or load. The target model’s own weights produce the draft, and the same weights verify it. Joint training gives the heads the target’s own distribution, which can raise acceptance.

chunks.h: What acceptance rates look like in practice
chunks.t: Reported acceptance rates vary widely with the drafter, the sampling settings, and the traffic. A draft model trained on the same data as the target and sampling at the same temperature can reach acceptance well above half on ordinary prose; a generic small model asked to continue another model's distribution does worse, and highly open-ended prompts do worse still. Papers in this area typically report acceptance per draft position rather than a single number, because acceptance decays as the draft chain lengthens: the first drafted token is usually right, the fourth is often not.

chunks.h: What acceptance rates look like in practice
chunks.t: That decay is why k is usually small, and why a drafter trained to match the target's distribution beats a larger generic one. The number to optimise is end-to-end speedup on your own traffic, not acceptance on someone else's benchmark. Measure acceptance at the k you intend to use, with your temperature and top-p, and multiply by the draft cost. A faster drafter that is accepted less often can lose ground, because the target pass is the expensive unit. Draft cost enters the break-even at every acceptance level. The speedup is roughly the accepted tokens per target pass divided by 1 + k·c, where c is the drafter's cost per token as a fraction of the target's decode step.

chunks.h: What acceptance rates look like in practice
chunks.t: The first thing to measure before enabling speculation is a per-k verification kernel timing at your real context length. Without it, acceptance and concurrency are guesses about the payoff rather than bounds on it.

chunks.h: Two regimes in one machine
chunks.t: A request arrives carrying 100,000 tokens of prompt. The engine answers it in two phases that share a machine and almost nothing else. Prefill runs the whole prompt through every layer and emits no visible text. Decode then emits one token per step, each depending on the one before it. Time the request end to end and you get one number, and that number describes neither phase. The two phases differ in what limits them. Prefill has many rows of work per weight read and is bound by arithmetic. Decode has one row per weight read and is bound by memory bandwidth. Almost every serving decision follows from that split.

chunks.h: Prefill is compute-bound
chunks.t: Start with prefill. The prompt is a matrix of activations, N rows by d_model columns, where N is the prompt length. Take one weight matrix in a layer: the attention projections are d_model by d_model, while the MLP up and down projections are d_model by d_ff, typically four times d_model. Each such matrix computes Y = XW + b. The GPU tiles this matmul into blocks of rows and columns. For each output tile, the kernel loads a block of X and a block of W into shared memory, computes the dot products, and accumulates. The weight block is loaded once and reused for every row of X that falls into the tile's row range.

chunks.h: Prefill is compute-bound
chunks.t: In prefill, N is 100,000, so a weight block is reused across a large number of rows. The cost of fetching the weights from memory is amortized across the whole prompt. The currency for that trade is arithmetic intensity, measured in floating-point operations per byte of memory traffic. Williams, Waterman, and Patterson formalized it in the roofline model in 2009 ("Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures," Communications of the ACM). Consider a bf16 weight. It occupies two bytes and takes part in two floating-point operations per token that uses it, one multiply and one accumulate.

chunks.h: Prefill is compute-bound
chunks.t: During prefill with N tokens in flight, that weight does 2N operations for the same two bytes, so intensity is N operations per byte. With N at 100,000, every byte hauled from memory feeds 100,000 FLOPs. The arithmetic units are the constraint and the memory bus has room to spare. Prefill is compute-bound.

chunks.h: Decode and the KV cache
chunks.t: Decode inverts every term. A stream that has already eaten its prompt generates one token at a time, and each token depends on the one before it, so there is no matrix–matrix multiply; the same weight matrix now meets a single row of activations in a matrix–vector product. It still has to be read from memory in full, two bytes at a time, and now those two bytes feed exactly one multiply-accumulate. Intensity is one operation per byte. The arithmetic units finish long before the memory system delivers the next weight, so they sit idle. Decode is bandwidth-bound. On an H100, HBM3 moves 3,350 GB/s.

chunks.h: Decode and the KV cache
chunks.t: A 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB per token, so the floor is 35 GB / 3,350 GB/s = 10.4 ms per token for a single stream. At sixteen bits the same model reads 140 GB per token and the floor becomes 41.8 ms. A decode step also reads the KV cache. In every layer, for every stream, the attention block pulls the keys and values of all previous positions. The cost per position per layer is one key vector and one value vector, each with H_kv heads times d_head elements. In bf16 each element is two bytes, so the cost per layer per position is 4 × H_kv × d_head bytes. Sum over L layers and divide by the tensor-parallel rank count R.

chunks.h: Decode and the KV cache
chunks.t: Take Llama 2 70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads at 128 dimensions, two bytes per element. Each layer holds 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per position, keys and values across 80 layers come to 2 × 80 × 1,024 = 163,840 values per position, and at two bytes each that is 327,680 bytes per position, a third of a megabyte. A 100,000-token context therefore needs 100,000 × 327,680 = 32,768,000,000 bytes of cache. At the 32,750-token per-stream ceiling derived later, the same cache is 32,750 × 327,680 = 10,731,520,000 bytes. The difference is 32,768,000,000 − 10,731,520,000 = 22,036,480,000 bytes per stream.

chunks.h: Decode and the KV cache
chunks.t: That increment is the mechanism behind the familiar complaint that long-context decode gets slower as the conversation goes on: the extra cache read per token is comparable to the weight read itself, and it grows with context while the weight read stays fixed.

chunks.h: The ridge point
chunks.t: Every accelerator has a balance point, the intensity at which a kernel stops waiting on memory and starts waiting on the ALUs. It is the peak floating-point rate divided by achievable bandwidth. On an H100 that is 989 TFLOPS against 3,350 GB/s, or 295 FLOPs per byte. Kernels below the line are bandwidth-bound, kernels above it are compute-bound. For a weight-bound matmul, intensity is proportional to batch size: B × (FLOPs per MAC) / (bytes per weight). Under the common convention of two FLOPs per MAC, it equals B operations per byte; with fp8 weights it would be twice that, so the balance point is a batch size. Here the balance point is roughly 300 rows.

chunks.h: The ridge point
chunks.t: That number tells you where each phase sits. Prefill runs at N rows, and N is 100,000, two orders of magnitude above the ridge, so the arithmetic units bind. Decode at batch one sits at one operation per byte, three hundred times below the ridge, so the memory system binds. Batching moves decode toward the ridge but does not cross it at the batch sizes a server actually runs: at batch 4 the intensity is four operations per byte, still far below 295. Clock speed matters to the compute-bound regime and barely at all to the bandwidth-bound one. Prefill can use every megahertz because it is waiting on the ALUs.

chunks.h: The ridge point
chunks.t: Decode is dominated by memory bandwidth, so SM clock is not the main throughput lever, though it still affects the SM-side softmax, normalization, sampling, and scheduling work and can influence decode latency and tail throughput. Anyone tuning SM clocks to improve decode throughput is tuning the wrong phase.

chunks.h: Time to first token and prefix reuse
chunks.t: Time to first token tracks prefill, since nothing can be emitted until the prompt has been through every layer. It is prefill plus queueing, a cache lookup, and one decode step. The prefill term dominates whenever the prompt is long, which is why the two numbers usually differ by little. Shazeer named this problem in 2019 when he proposed multi-query attention ("Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need"), writing explicitly that incremental decoding is limited by memory bandwidth rather than by arithmetic. That observation motivates many of the KV-cache compression schemes in this book. A prefix cache cuts the prefill term without changing the model.

chunks.h: Time to first token and prefix reuse
chunks.t: The cache stores the KV state for previously seen token prefixes. On a new request, the scheduler walks the prompt from the start and finds the longest matching prefix. It reuses the stored KV for that prefix and prefills only the remaining tokens. The saving in time to first token is the matched token count divided by the prefill rate. When many requests share a long system prompt or a retrieved document, most of their prompt tokens match, and the saving is most of the prefill. An aggregate hit rate is not the same as the per-request saving: requests arrive with different prefix lengths and different match lengths, so one number hides a wide spread.

chunks.h: Batching gains and admission limits
chunks.t: Batching behaves differently in the two regimes. Decode gains from more streams because a bandwidth-bound kernel has spare arithmetic capacity. Run four streams together and each weight read serves four tokens instead of one, so intensity rises from one operation per byte to four. If the kernel were perfectly bandwidth-bound and KV traffic did not grow, aggregate throughput would scale by 4×. It does not, because each stream adds its own cache read to the step. Write f for the KV share of per-token traffic at concurrency one; the speedup ceiling is 4/(1+3f). At f = 0.4 the ceiling is 1.8×, and the shortfall is cache traffic rather than wasted arithmetic.

chunks.h: Batching gains and admission limits
chunks.t: The real figure also carries kernel-layout costs: a decode kernel that packs rows wide amortizes each weight fetch across the batch, but its row slots go idle when the batch is smaller than the slot count. Prefill gains less from batching than decode does, because it is already compute-bound. Adding a second prompt to a prefill batch raises intensity further, but the ALUs are the constraint, so the two prompts split the same finite compute instead of filling idle capacity. This asymmetry is why mixing prefill work into decode steps is expensive. A long prefill inserted between decode steps stalls every stream in the batch.

chunks.h: Batching gains and admission limits
chunks.t: Continuous batching, taken up in its own chapter, is the scheduler's answer to that tension. The scheduler admits new requests at decode step boundaries and chunks long prefills into pieces that fit between decode steps. Concurrency also runs into a memory ceiling with nothing to do with arithmetic. The KV pool holds 262,144 positions shared across four streams, so an equal split gives 65,536 positions each. Admission reserves the default 32,768-token reply budget, plus 16 round rows, plus two positions of overhead. The reply budget is the maximum number of tokens the request may generate, reserved up front so the KV cache never needs to evict mid-generation.

chunks.h: Batching gains and admission limits
chunks.t: The 16 round rows are the batch width of the decode kernel, which needs KV slots for each row. The two positions are alignment padding required by the attention kernel. The admission check compares prompt_tokens + 32,768 + 16 + 2 against 65,536. What remains is 32,750 tokens of context per stream. A prompt longer than that cannot be admitted at concurrency four no matter how much compute is free. If the pool is full, the scheduler evicts the least recently used prefix cache entries to free KV space, but it cannot evict active streams.

chunks.h: Batching gains and admission limits
chunks.t: Raising the pool to the model's native 1,048,576 positions would lift the per-stream ceiling to 229,358 tokens, and the cache would grow in proportion to the positions it stores.

chunks.h: Why one tokens-per-second number misleads
chunks.t: The habit of quoting one tokens-per-second figure for a model is a genuine mistake, and it survives because benchmarks rarely state their concurrency. A number measured at concurrency one describes decode bandwidth. A number measured on a long prompt describes prefill compute. They are not comparable and they do not trade off linearly. The honest report is a curve, with time to first token and inter-token latency plotted separately against concurrency and prompt length.

chunks.h: Why one tokens-per-second number misleads
chunks.t: Some systems push the logic further and put prefill and decode on different machines altogether, the argument Splitwise (2024) and DistServe (2024) both made, on the grounds that a compute-bound job and a bandwidth-bound job should not share a scheduler. The gain is independent scaling of each phase on hardware suited to its regime. The cost is the KV transfer between machines: at a 100,000-token context the cache is tens of gigabytes per stream, and moving that costs bandwidth and latency that must be weighed against the prefill time it saves.

chunks.h: Why one tokens-per-second number misleads
chunks.t: As a rule of thumb, disaggregation struggles when the KV transfer cost exceeds the prefill time saved, or when prompts are short and concurrency is low. But that is not the whole criterion: the decision should be made on end-to-end latency and throughput and on pool use, and SLO isolation or decode-interference avoidance can still justify disaggregation in those regimes. That case has real force and real costs, and the chapter on splitting a model across devices takes it up.

chunks.h: 27. Continuous Batching and the Scheduler
chunks.t: Four requests arrive within a few milliseconds of one another. The naive move packs their prompts into one tensor, pads the short prompts up to the longest, and decodes until every sequence has emitted its last token. Call that static batching. It wastes the machine twice. Padding wastes prefill. A batch whose longest prompt runs to 100,000 tokens forces every shorter prompt out to that length, and the attention and feed-forward layers chew through the padding as if it were text. Decode wastes more. Sequences finish at different times.

chunks.h: 27. Continuous Batching and the Scheduler
chunks.t: When one request stops after 200 tokens and its neighbour keeps going, the finished sequence still holds a row, still has its KV cache read on every step, and emits nothing. The batch runs at the speed of its slowest member.

chunks.h: What a decode step costs
chunks.t: A word on what a decode step costs, since everything below depends on it. A transformer layer projects each token into queries, keys, and values, attends over the keys and values of all previous tokens, and writes the new key and value into a cache. Generating token n+1 reuses the cache from tokens 1 through n, so the step reads the whole cache plus the weights and does one token's worth of arithmetic. That ratio of bytes read to FLOPs separates decode from prefill. On an H100 the balance point is 295 FLOPs per byte; a decode step at batch one sits near one FLOP per byte, so the memory bus is the constraint and the arithmetic units wait.

chunks.h: What a decode step costs
chunks.t: A 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB of weights per token, which at 3,350 GB/s sets a floor of 10.4 ms per token. The cache read is on top of that. Llama 2 70B has 80 layers with 8 KV heads at 128 dimensions, so each layer holds 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per position, and keys and values across all layers come to 2 × 80 × 1,024 = 163,840 values per position. At two bytes each that is 327,680 bytes per position.

chunks.h: Iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
chunks.t: Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues at Seoul National University named the fix at OSDI in 2022. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling, which rebuilds the batch at every decode step. At step t the scheduler holds a set of active sequences, picks a subset that fits the memory budget, runs one forward pass, samples one token per sequence, appends it, and retires anything that emitted an end-of-sequence token or hit its length budget. New requests fill the slots the retirements freed. The batch dimension changes every step. A request can join at step 40 and leave at step 41; another can hold a slot from step 41 to step 900. That requires attention to stop being one dense matrix multiply.

chunks.h: Iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
chunks.t: Sequences in a batch sit at different positions and carry different masks. Orca's answer, selective batching, splits the work by operator. The linear projections are position-independent, so every row in the batch goes through one batched matmul. Attention needs per-sequence work. Each query must see only the keys and values of its own sequence, so the kernel segments the batch. It packs the token rows into one buffer, carries a per-token position id so rotary embeddings land at the right offset, and builds a block-diagonal mask that zeroes out cross-sequence attention.

chunks.h: Iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
chunks.t: In practice the kernel either launches one attention call per sequence and concatenates the outputs, or runs a single fused kernel that reads a per-sequence block table and a per-sequence query range. Either way the projections batch and the attention does not.

chunks.h: Chunked prefill and the roofline
chunks.t: Orca left the second problem alone. A new request arrives with a long prompt, and prefill for that prompt is one lump of compute. A fully uncached 100,000-token prompt occupies the machine for as long as its prefill takes, and every decode in flight waits behind it. Sarathi-Serve, published by Amey Agrawal and colleagues in 2024, split prompts into chunks and interleaved those chunks with decode steps. The justification is a 29-roofline|roofline argument, and the arithmetic is short. For a decode step at batch size B, the machine reads roughly the weight bytes and performs about 2NB FLOPs, where N is the parameter count. Arithmetic intensity is 16B/p FLOPs per byte for p-bit weights.

chunks.h: Chunked prefill and the roofline
chunks.t: For 16-bit and 8-bit weights that is B to 2B; 4-bit weights give 4B and fp32 gives 0.5B. At B = 4, the 16- and 8-bit range is 4 to 8 FLOPs per byte. For a prefill chunk of L tokens, intensity is about 2L/w, where w is bytes per weight; with fp16 weights a 2,048-token chunk is about 2,048 FLOPs per byte, and 4,096 only for one-byte weights. The machine's ridge point, where compute and bandwidth take the same time, falls between those figures: 295 FLOPs per byte on an H100. Decode at batch 4 is two orders of magnitude below the ridge; a 2,048-token prefill chunk is above it. That gap is what chunked prefill exploits.

chunks.h: Chunked prefill and the roofline
chunks.t: The chunk's FLOPs ride on arithmetic units that decode leaves idle, and the weights are already resident. The memory hierarchy matters here. The SMs have small SRAM caches, the HBM stack is the next level down and holds the weights and KV, and every byte that misses SRAM costs a trip to that larger pool. When does the trick fail? When the chunk grows large enough that its compute time stops hiding under the decode step. Decode at batch 4 reads four caches instead of one, so its step is longer than the single-stream floor of 10.4 ms but nowhere near four times that, because the weight read is shared.

chunks.h: Chunked prefill and the roofline
chunks.t: Write f for the KV share of per-token traffic at batch one; the speedup ceiling is 4/(1+3f), and at f = 0.4 that is 1.8×. A chunk of 512 tokens at the ridge is a serious fraction of such a step, so it lengthens the step by a visible margin. A chunk of 128 tokens is a tenth of that. The scheduler's per-step prefill cap is the knob. With a cap of C tokens, a prompt of length L takes ceil(L / C) iterations to prefill, and any decode sharing those iterations waits at most C tokens of extra compute per step. For the 100,000-token prompt, C = 128 means 782 iterations and C = 512 means 196 iterations. Small chunks buy smoothness and pay in iteration count.

chunks.h: The scheduler's phases and admission arithmetic
chunks.t: Every iteration runs the same five phases. First, retirement. Sequences that emitted an end-of-sequence token or hit their budget release their KV blocks and their stream slot. Second, admission. The scheduler walks the queue in arrival order, tests each candidate against the memory budget, and admits the ones that fit. Third, preemption. If a high-priority arrival cannot fit, the scheduler picks a resident sequence, usually the newest or the one with the largest KV footprint, and either swaps its blocks out or drops them for recompute. Fourth, the prefill cap. The scheduler takes at most C uncached prompt tokens from the admitted requests. Fifth, the forward pass.

chunks.h: The scheduler's phases and admission arithmetic
chunks.t: Decode rows and the prefill chunk go through one batched call. The memory test is where the arithmetic lives. A KV pool of 262,144 positions shared across four concurrent streams gives each stream 65,536 positions. Admission then reserves the default reply budget of 32,768 tokens, rounds the batch width up to the decode kernel's 16-row granularity, and adds two boundary tokens. The arithmetic is 65,536 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 32,750 positions per stream. That is the context ceiling a request sees. The model's native window is 1,048,576 positions, so the pool is a deliberate slice of the memory that also holds weights and live streams.

chunks.h: The scheduler's phases and admission arithmetic
chunks.t: Raising the pool to the full window multiplies the cache cost by four, since the pool covers a quarter of the window at 262,144 positions. The ceiling arithmetic would then run 1,048,576 / 4 = 262,144, minus 32,768 = 229,376, minus 16 = 229,360, minus 2 = 229,358 positions per stream. The scheduler divides the pool equally and reserves the full default reply budget for every stream, whether or not the stream will use it.

chunks.h: Eviction and fairness
chunks.t: When the pool fills, the scheduler has three options. It can refuse the arrival and leave it queued. It can swap a resident sequence's blocks to another region of memory and read them back later. Or it can drop the blocks and recompute the prefill when the sequence returns. The costs differ by orders of magnitude. Take a 32,750-position sequence on Llama 2 70B, whose cache is 327,680 bytes per position: the sequence holds 32,750 × 327,680 = 10,731,520,000 bytes of KV. Copying that out and back moves twice those bytes, which at 3,350 GB/s is well under a second.

chunks.h: Eviction and fairness
chunks.t: Recomputing the same sequence means running every weight matrix over 32,750 rows, which is orders of magnitude more work than moving the bytes. Swap wins, which is why the allocator matters as much as the policy. vLLM's PagedAttention, published by Woosuk Kwon and colleagues in 2023, gave the allocator page-sized blocks, 16 tokens by default, so a sequence's cache can be non-contiguous and reclaimed incrementally. The fragmentation cost is bounded. A sequence wastes at most one partial block, so the waste is bounded by 16 positions × 327,680 bytes = 5,242,880 bytes per sequence, and the average is half that.

chunks.h: Eviction and fairness
chunks.t: A contiguous allocator that reserves the maximum length up front wastes the difference between reservation and use instead, and for a request that declares 32,768 tokens and generates 200, that difference is most of the per-stream slice. Fairness is the second decision. First-come-first-served is simple and predictable, but a long generation can occupy a batch slot for a long time and, once the batch is full, delay every arrival behind it. Shortest-remaining-first lowers mean latency, and it can starve. Work an example. Suppose a long request has 200 tokens left and each decode step costs 10.4 ms of memory time, so the long request needs about 2.1 seconds of service.

chunks.h: Eviction and fairness
chunks.t: Now a stream of 10-token requests arrives every 50 ms. Each short request needs 10 × 10.4 ms = 104 ms of stream time, so the arrival rate exceeds the service rate and the queue never drains. The long request waits forever. A per-step prefill cap bounds the damage in the other direction, because no single admission can add more than C tokens of prefill compute to a step, and a scheduler that also ages queued requests eventually runs the long one.

chunks.h: Prefix caching, throughput, and the reservation tradeoff
chunks.t: Prefix caching changes the scheduler's workload before the scheduler sees it. The engine matches a new prompt against blocks already resident in the pool. A hit means the KV for that prefix is already computed, so the prefill job shrinks from L tokens to L minus the matched length. The projections and attention for those matched tokens are skipped, their KV blocks are reused in place, and the kernel starts at the matched length to compute only the suffix. Attention for the suffix reads the cached prefix blocks alongside the new ones. A 100,000-token prompt that matches 65,536 cached tokens prefills 100,000 − 65,536 = 34,464 tokens.

chunks.h: Prefix caching, throughput, and the reservation tradeoff
chunks.t: The saving counts as wall-clock time only when the machine would otherwise have been busy with that work. The throughput payoff is real and bounded. Aggregate decode sums the tokens per second across all active streams. Four streams in one step emit four tokens and read four caches, while the weight read is shared, so aggregate throughput rises and the per-stream rate falls. The ceiling is 4/(1+3f) with f the KV share at batch one; at f = 0.4 it is 1.8×. The mechanism shows up per step. At batch one a step emits one token for one weight read and one cache read.

chunks.h: Prefix caching, throughput, and the reservation tradeoff
chunks.t: At batch four the step emits four tokens for the same weight read plus four cache reads, so the weight read is amortized and the cache traffic is not. Admitting one more stream costs almost nothing until the 16-row width fills. The kernel launches in the same shape whether it holds 4 rows or 16, and the 12 padding rows at concurrency four consume registers and issue slots but no KV bytes, so the step time does not grow in proportion to the row count. Past 16 rows the kernel runs a second wave, and each wave re-reads the weights, so the step time roughly doubles.

chunks.h: Prefix caching, throughput, and the reservation tradeoff
chunks.t: What grows before that point is KV traffic, because every step reads the cache of every resident sequence, and those reads all come out of the same memory bus. Continuous batching recovers the waste static batching creates. It does not manufacture bandwidth. Any throughput figure needs its definitions beside it. Time to first token runs from request arrival to the first sampled token and is dominated by prefill on long prompts. Decode duration runs from the first token to the last and scales with the reply length. Aggregate tokens per second is the sum over active streams, so it rises with concurrency while per-stream latency falls.

chunks.h: Prefix caching, throughput, and the reservation tradeoff
chunks.t: A number quoted without its concurrency and its prompt length describes a workload, not a model. My view is that continuous batching is the most consequential serving idea of the last several years, and it lives in the scheduler. Orca's contribution was noticing that the batch is a queue. The part I would argue with is the equal-split reservation. Reserving 32,768 tokens of reply budget for every stream at admission is simple, and it throws away capacity when requests are short, since a typical request generates 200 tokens. A scheduler that sized each reservation to the request's declared budget and rebalanced as sequences retired would fit more streams into the same 262,144 positions.

chunks.h: Prefix caching, throughput, and the reservation tradeoff
chunks.t: This engine chose predictability, and the cost of that choice is measurable in the gap between 32,768 reserved positions and the 200 tokens a typical request actually uses.

chunks.h: 28. Splitting a model across devices
chunks.t: A model that does not fit on one device has to be cut somewhere. Where you cut decides where the communication goes. Cut through the layers and you get pipeline parallelism, which sends activations between stages and leaves devices idle during fill and drain. Cut through the matrices and you get tensor parallelism, which keeps every device busy and pays for it with collectives inside every block. Megatron-LM’s 2019 paper named the two halves of the tensor-parallel pattern f and g. GPipe, from Huang and colleagues in 2019, introduced the micro-batch schedule that made pipeline parallelism usable.

chunks.h: Column-parallel f and row-parallel g
chunks.t: Tensor parallelism starts with a linear layer computing y = xW. Let x have shape B×H, where B is the batch of tokens and H is the hidden width. Let W have shape H×K. Split W by columns into N slices W_i of shape H×(K/N). Rank i computes y_i = xW_i, which has shape B×(K/N). The full output is the concatenation of the y_i along the feature dimension. No rank needs another rank’s y_i to form its own slice, so the forward pass has no collective. Megatron-LM calls this f. The next layer projects back down. Let its weight V have shape K×M. Split V by rows into N slices V_i of shape (K/N)×M. Rank i computes z_i = y_i V_i, which has shape B×M. The true output is z = sum_i z_i.

chunks.h: Column-parallel f and row-parallel g
chunks.t: Each rank holds a partial sum over its slice of the input features, so the forward pass needs an all-reduce sum across ranks. Megatron-LM calls this g.

chunks.h: Two all-reduces per block and their volume
chunks.t: An f layer followed by a g layer has one all-reduce at the end of the pair. A transformer block contains two such pairs. The QKV projection is column-parallel f, and the attention output projection is row-parallel g. The MLP up-projection is column-parallel f, and the down-projection is row-parallel g. That gives two all-reduces per block in the forward pass; during training, backward through each f layer adds another all-reduce, for four per block per training step. The count of collectives per block is fixed at two, so the total count grows linearly with the number of blocks L. The volume per collective depends on B, H, and the number of tensor-parallel ranks N.

chunks.h: Two all-reduces per block and their volume
chunks.t: For a ring all-reduce over N ranks, each rank sends 2(N−1)/N times the B×H partial-sum matrix per collective. At N=2 that is B×H elements sent per rank per collective. At N=8 it is 1.75 B×H. A tree all-reduce trades that volume for log N latency. The per-layer cost is fixed in count but not in volume as N grows.

chunks.h: The per-collective latency budget
chunks.t: That cost has two parts. The first is latency. Every device must wait for every other device before the next block can begin, and a round trip does not shrink when you add more compute at either end. The second is volume. At decode batch sizes of a few tokens the all-reduce volume is small. At prefill batch sizes of thousands it is not, which is why prefill and decode stress tensor parallelism differently. Put the latency part against a concrete decode rate. A 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB of weights per token, and on an H100 at 3,350 GB/s that sets a floor of 10.4 ms per decode step. Take a 32-block model. Two collectives per block gives 64 collectives per forward pass.

chunks.h: The per-collective latency budget
chunks.t: The budget per collective is 10.4/64 = 0.1625 milliseconds. If the link’s round trip is above that, the schedule cannot reach the memory-bound floor: the forward pass would spend its whole budget waiting. A slower interconnect does not just add latency, it changes which phase is the constraint.

chunks.h: Pipeline stages and the micro-batch bubble
chunks.t: Pipeline parallelism avoids the per-block barrier by putting whole layers on each rank. Rank 0 holds layers 0 through k−1, rank 1 holds the rest, and the only communication is rank 0 handing rank 1 the activations for the tokens it has just processed. That is a point-to-point send rather than a barrier. The volume per send is B_micro×S×H values, where B_micro is the micro-batch size, S is the sequence length, and H is the hidden width. For M micro-batches and P stages, the step has M(P−1) sends. That volume is small compared with tensor parallelism’s per-block collectives, but it is not zero.

chunks.h: Pipeline stages and the micro-batch bubble
chunks.t: The naive pipeline is miserable, because rank 1 sits idle while rank 0 works and rank 0 sits idle while rank 1 works. GPipe mitigates it by splitting the batch into micro-batches. Rank 0 can start micro-batch 2 while rank 1 is still chewing on micro-batch 1, and in steady state every rank has something to do only when M is large enough relative to P, roughly M ≥ P. At decode batch sizes of a few tokens M is small, so the bubble stays large. What remains is the fill and drain at the two ends of the step, which everyone calls the bubble. With P stages and M micro-batches the pipeline takes M + P − 1 slots, of which P − 1 are bubble. The idle fraction is (P−1)/(M+P−1).

chunks.h: Pipeline stages and the micro-batch bubble
chunks.t: Four stages and eight micro-batches leave 3 of every 11 slots idle. Sixteen micro-batches leave 3 of every 19. The second bubble is a little over half the first, so doubling M cuts idle time by well under half. The formula shows the diminishing return. Memory is where PipeDream, from Narayanan and colleagues later in 2019, made its contribution. GPipe’s schedule keeps every in-flight micro-batch’s activations alive, so raising M raises memory. PipeDream’s 1F1B schedule alternates one forward pass and one backward pass per rank. The steady state holds only a bounded number of micro-batches, so activation memory does not grow with M.

chunks.h: Pipeline stages and the micro-batch bubble
chunks.t: That made deep pipelines practical rather than a scheduling curiosity. The trade is coarse. Each rank holds whole layers, so with two devices each holds half the model. A layer count that does not divide evenly forces you to imbalance the stages. Tensor parallelism is finer, because it splits inside each matrix, but it demands that head counts and hidden widths divide by the device count too. Neither is free of arithmetic constraints.

chunks.h: Message counts, sequence parallelism, and expert parallelism
chunks.t: Message counts make the difference concrete. Pipeline parallelism sends M(P−1) messages per direction per step, so 2M(P−1) total. Tensor parallelism issues 4L collectives per micro-batch, so 4LM collective operations per step. With P=2 and L=32, tensor parallelism issues 64 collective operations for every pipeline send, before counting the extra rounds a ring all-reduce uses when N is larger than two. That is tens of times more collective operations, not orders of magnitude in every case. The cutoff for tensor parallelism is a per-collective budget set by the link and the workload, not a fixed number. It moves with the model, the batch, the concurrency, and the collective size.

chunks.h: Message counts, sequence parallelism, and expert parallelism
chunks.t: Pipeline parallelism tolerates latency because it has one send per micro-batch per boundary and overlaps micro-batches. The choice comes down to the per-collective budget against the link’s round trip. The hybrid that large training runs settled on puts tensor parallelism inside a node, where the link is NVLink, and pipeline parallelism across nodes. Narayanan and colleagues laid out the combination in 2021. The rule of thumb that tensor parallelism stays inside the fast domain has held. Sequence parallelism, from Korthikanti and colleagues in 2022, splits the sequence dimension for the operations that are replicated across tensor-parallel ranks.

chunks.h: Message counts, sequence parallelism, and expert parallelism
chunks.t: LayerNorm, dropout, and the residual add act on the full hidden vector, so every tensor-parallel rank holds a copy. Let the hidden state have shape B×S×H. In the sequence-parallel region each rank holds B×(S/N)×H. At the entry to the tensor-parallel region, an all-gather along S restores B×S×H on every rank. Then f produces B×S×(H/N) per rank, attention works per head, and g produces B×S×H partial sums. The all-reduce over tensor-parallel ranks gives the full B×S×H. At the exit, a reduce-scatter along S returns B×(S/N)×H per rank for the next sequence-parallel region. The ordering is all-gather before f and reduce-scatter after g.

chunks.h: Message counts, sequence parallelism, and expert parallelism
chunks.t: The win is activation memory, which raises M, which shrinks the bubble. Expert parallelism changes the model rather than the schedule. Shazeer and colleagues introduced sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layers in 2017. GShard in 2020 and the Switch Transformer in 2021 scaled them. Each token is routed to a few experts. Experts live on different devices, so the dispatch is an all-to-all. Each device sends its tokens to the devices holding the selected experts and receives tokens routed to its local experts. The traffic matrix is not symmetric because routing counts vary by expert and by batch.

chunks.h: Message counts, sequence parallelism, and expert parallelism
chunks.t: If one expert receives more tokens than its capacity, the device holding it becomes the bottleneck while other devices idle. A capacity factor c sets per-expert capacity to c times the average tokens per expert. Tokens beyond capacity are dropped, or capacity is padded; under top-2 gating, a token may still be processed by its other selected expert. That bounds the imbalance but wastes computation and can change model quality.

chunks.h: The bandwidth and stall budget of a split
chunks.t: Splitting a bandwidth-bound job across devices buys nothing unless each device brings its own memory pipe. Decode is bandwidth-bound: a 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB per token and needs 10.4 ms on one H100, and the arithmetic units sit idle for most of that time. Two devices each holding half the weights, each with its own 3,350 GB/s of HBM3, halve the read per device and therefore halve the step time. That is the case tensor parallelism is built for, and it is why the split is worth its collectives when the link is fast. Two devices sharing one memory pool get the opposite result.

chunks.h: The bandwidth and stall budget of a split
chunks.t: Each rank still draws from the same 3,350 GB/s pipe, so the step time does not fall, and the collectives add latency on top. Splitting across ranks that share a memory bus is a capacity move, not a speed move: it lets a model that does not fit become loadable, and it costs throughput rather than buying it. The stall side of the ledger needs both terms. Let C be compute time and S stall time per step. A split that halves C but doubles S gives C/2 + 2S. It beats the unsplit C + S only when S < C/2. So a split pays while the communication stall stays below half the compute it removes.

chunks.h: The bandwidth and stall budget of a split
chunks.t: The two quantities are measurable before deployment: the per-collective budget from the model's layer count and the step's floor, and the link's round trip from a ping. A split that fails that test is not worth the collectives. Raising the KV pool from 262,144 positions to 1,048,576 multiplies the cache cost by four, because the pool covers a quarter of the model's native window. With four streams, each gets 65,536 positions before overhead. After the 32,768-token reply budget, the 16-row decode round batch, and two rows of slack, 32,750 tokens remain per stream.

chunks.h: The bandwidth and stall budget of a split
chunks.t: If the pool were raised to 1,048,576, the per-stream ceiling would be 229,358 tokens, and the cache would grow in proportion to the positions it stores. My view is that pipeline parallelism is under-chosen for inference and tensor parallelism is over-chosen, largely because tensor parallelism was the first thing Megatron-LM made easy and because the NVLink topology of a training node rewarded it. On a pair of machines joined by anything slower than NVLink, pipeline is the safer default, and the bubble is a number you can compute before you deploy rather than discover afterwards.

chunks.h: What the hardware actually allows
chunks.t: Ask someone who runs inference for a living how many tokens per second a given box will produce and they will usually answer before they run anything. The arithmetic is short. It needs two numbers, the bytes the machine can move per second and the bytes the model must move to emit one token.

chunks.h: The roofline model and decode's intensity
chunks.t: The formal version is the roofline model, published by Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson in 2009 in Communications of the ACM. Attainable performance is the minimum of peak floating-point throughput and memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs performed per byte moved. Plot performance against intensity on log axes and you get a rising line that meets a flat ceiling. The flat part is the compute roof, the rising part the bandwidth roof. Where a workload lands tells you what to tune. Decode lands far to the left. To emit one token, the model runs the new token's hidden state through every layer in sequence.

chunks.h: The roofline model and decode's intensity
chunks.t: At each layer the engine streams that layer's weight matrix out of memory, through L2, into the SMs, multiplies, and discards the tile before moving to the next layer. Nothing survives from one token to the next, because the matrices are far larger than any cache on the device. A 70-billion-parameter model in FP16 occupies 140 GB, and no single accelerator caches 140 GB. Bytes read per token are therefore approximately the active parameter count times bytes per parameter, and the arithmetic is about one multiply-add per parameter, or 2 FLOPs per 2 bytes at FP16. Intensity near 1. Put that against the hardware.

chunks.h: The roofline model and decode's intensity
chunks.t: An H100 SXM has 989 TFLOPS of dense FP16 tensor throughput and 3,350 GB/s of HBM3 bandwidth, a ratio of 295 FLOPs per byte. That ratio is the ridge point. A workload at intensity 1 sits three hundred times below it, so decode is bandwidth-bound by a wide margin, and the compute units spend most of the step waiting on memory.

chunks.h: What batching amortizes
chunks.t: Batching changes the read without changing the arithmetic. When b requests decode together, the engine still streams each weight tile once, but it multiplies that tile by b rows before discarding it. The read is amortized b ways; the FLOPs are not. The bytes moved per decode step, for the whole batch, has four terms B_step = P_active × bytes_per_param + b × KV_bytes(L) + b × workspace(L) + TP_exchange(b) where P_active is the parameter count the batch actually touches, L is context length, and TP_exchange is tensor-parallel all-reduce traffic. For a dense model P_active is the whole parameter count.

chunks.h: What batching amortizes
chunks.t: For a mixture-of-experts model it is the shared layers plus whichever experts the router selects, and with a batch of b tokens the union of selected experts grows, so the weight term rises with b even though each token touches only a fraction of the weights. The KV term needs its own derivation. Every layer stores the key and value vectors for every position already generated, so attention does not recompute them. The layout is per layer, per KV head, per position, per head dimension. Bytes per token of context is KV_bytes = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × d_head × dtype_bytes where the 2 covers K and V, and a sequence of L positions at batch b multiplies the result by L × b.

chunks.h: What batching amortizes
chunks.t: Work it for Llama 2 70B, which has 80 layers, 8 KV heads and a head dimension of 128, stored at two bytes. Each layer holds 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per position. Keys and values across all layers come to 2 × 80 × 1,024 = 163,840 values per position, which at two bytes each is 163,840 × 2 = 327,680 bytes. At a 100,000-token context that one stream's cache is 100,000 × 327,680 = 32,768,000,000 bytes, which is nearly the size of the model's four-bit weight footprint.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind a bandwidth number
chunks.t: Now a worked budget on a single H100. The card lists 192 GB of HBM3 and 3,350 GB/s. A 70B model at FP16 stores 140 GB of weights, approximately the bytes read per decoded token, and its bandwidth-bound ceiling is 3,350 ÷ 140 = 23.9 tokens per second. At four bits the same model needs 35 GB, and the ceiling is 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7 tokens per second. A 7B model at FP16 needs 14 GB; the ceiling is 3,350 ÷ 14 = 239 tokens per second. At four bits that model needs 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5 GB. The ceiling is then 3,350 ÷ 3.5 = 957 tokens per second. GPT-3, described by Brown and colleagues in 2020 at 175 billion parameters, would need 350 GB per token at FP16.

chunks.h: The arithmetic behind a bandwidth number
chunks.t: Its ceiling would be 3,350 ÷ 350 = 9.57 tokens per second, and it would not fit on the card at that precision. Those ceilings are upper bounds, not predictions. They assume the kernel reaches peak bandwidth, which it does not; real decode on a large model typically lands at half to two thirds of the roof. They assume nothing else is moving bytes, and the KV cache, the workspace and the collectives all share the same bus. They also assume batch one, where the weight read dominates. Raise the batch and the roof itself moves.

chunks.h: Quantization as a bandwidth multiplier
chunks.t: 21-quantization|Quantization is usually sold on the wrong grounds. It is pitched as a way to fit a model into memory; its larger effect on serving is proportional speed. Halving bytes per parameter doubles the bandwidth-bound ceiling, provided the kernel still reaches the same fraction of peak bandwidth and the arithmetic does not become the new constraint. It is not exact, because dequantization costs instructions, group scales cost bytes, and kernel efficiency at 4 bits is rarely the same as at 16. Group-wise quantization, as in GPTQ (Frantar and colleagues, 2022) and AWQ (Lin and colleagues, 2023), stores a scale per group of weights rather than per tensor.

chunks.h: Quantization as a bandwidth multiplier
chunks.t: Both papers motivate this with outlier channels that dominate a per-tensor scale and leave the rest of the matrix with a coarse step size; smaller groups confine the damage. A group size of 128 with FP16 scales adds 2 bytes per 128 weights. Against a half-byte four-bit weight that is a few percent of the stream, so the 70B ceiling drops slightly from 95.7 tokens per second rather than falling off a cliff. The same reasoning explains why 8-bit weights buy less than the label suggests. Going from FP16 to 8 bits halves the read and doubles the ceiling, and going to 4 bits halves it again.

chunks.h: Quantization as a bandwidth multiplier
chunks.t: But the arithmetic intensity doubles with each step too, so a workload that was comfortably bandwidth-bound at 16 bits can approach the ridge at 4 bits if the batch is large. At some batch size the compute roof takes over, and further quantization stops helping.

chunks.h: What real decode reveals about the step budget
chunks.t: The roof inverts into a diagnostic. If a model emits X tokens per second at batch one, then bytes per token is at most bandwidth ÷ X, because time is at least bytes divided by bandwidth. The bound holds without knowing which model or precision is loaded, which is why it is worth stating when the model card is not in front of you. Run the inversion at the roof. A 70B model at four bits tops out at 95.7 tokens per second on an H100, and at that rate the implied read is 3,350 ÷ 95.7 = 35 GB per token, exactly the weight footprint. Any measured rate below the roof implies a larger read, which is the KV cache and the workspace showing up on the same bus.

chunks.h: What real decode reveals about the step budget
chunks.t: The same rate on a card with 1,000 GB/s would imply a read of at most 1,000 ÷ 95.7 = 10.4 GB, less than the weights themselves, so the roof there is lower and the same rate is not achievable. The gap opens when you batch. If decode were purely weight-bandwidth-bound, four streams should give close to four times the aggregate, because one pass over the matrices serves all four rows. Nothing like that happens once the cache dominates. Take the same 70B model at four bits and a 100,000-token context on four streams. The weight term stays at 35 GB per step, because one read serves all rows, but the KV term quadruples: 4 × 32,768,000,000 = 131,072,000,000 bytes.

chunks.h: What real decode reveals about the step budget
chunks.t: The KV term quadruples: 3 × 32,768,000,000 = 98,304,000,000 extra bytes per step, on top of the 35 GB weight read. Per-stream throughput falls even as aggregate throughput rises, and long context changes which term sets the step. That is the asymmetry worth carrying away. Batching amortizes the weight term, which is fixed per step, and multiplies the KV term, which scales with batch and context. Attention arithmetic grows the same way: per token per layer, the score and value products cost 4 × n_heads × d_head × L FLOPs, linear in context length and not shared across streams.
