The weight read does not grow with L at all.

chunks.h: What real decode reveals about the step budget
chunks.t: So the crossover from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound arrives sooner at long context and large batch, and the roofline point slides right.

chunks.h: Why prefill, speculation, and capacity set different limits
chunks.t: Prefill behaves completely differently, and the contrast is the clearest illustration of what the roofline is for. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once, so the weight read is shared across all T prompt tokens. The linear-layer term gives roughly T FLOPs per byte, since each weight is used T times and costs two bytes at FP16, but attention adds about 4 × n_layers × h × T FLOPs per token, so the true intensity carries a term quadratic in T. At a 100,000-token prompt the linear term alone is 100,000 FLOPs per byte, more than three hundred times the H100's ridge point of 295 FLOPs per byte.

chunks.h: Why prefill, speculation, and capacity set different limits
chunks.t: Prefill is compute-bound on that part while a decode step at intensity 1 is bandwidth-bound, and the two phases want different optimizations for that reason. Speculative decoding bends the decode budget in the other direction. A small draft model proposes k tokens, the main model verifies them in one pass, and the accepted prefix plus one bonus token is emitted. If each draft is accepted with probability a, the expected yield from a step that drafts k tokens is 1 + a + a² + … + a^k, which converges to 1/(1 − a). At a = 0.8 the limit is five tokens per weight read; at a = 0.5 it is two.

chunks.h: Why prefill, speculation, and capacity set different limits
chunks.t: No draft length pushes the yield past the limit, so effective bytes per token is at least the weight footprint divided by that yield. The draft model's own reads and the verification overhead eat into the gain, which is why the realized speedup falls short of the bound. Capacity then constrains context directly, and the arithmetic is the same admission rule the serving chapters use. A KV pool of 262,144 positions shared across four streams gives each stream 65,536 positions. Admission subtracts the 32,768-token default reply budget, 16 rows for the decode round batch, and 2 positions for boundary overhead, which gives 65,536 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 32,750 tokens per stream.

chunks.h: Why prefill, speculation, and capacity set different limits
chunks.t: Raising the pool to the model's native 1,048,576 positions lifts the ceiling to 1,048,576 ÷ 4 = 262,144, minus 32,768, minus 16, minus 2, for 229,358 tokens per stream, at four times the cache cost. On a 192 GB card that fits beside a 70B model at four bits; on an 80 GB card it does not fit beside the same model at eight bits. What follows is a view about hardware. For single-stream decode the number that matters is bandwidth, and the capacity number decides whether the model fits at all. A card with 3,350 GB/s and 192 GB can hold a 70B model at four bits with room for a large KV pool, and its decode roof is 95.7 tokens per second.

chunks.h: Why prefill, speculation, and capacity set different limits
chunks.t: A card with 80 GB can hold the same model at eight bits and little else, and its roof is half as high. The two limits bind at different points, and quoting one without the other describes a benchmark rather than a deployment.

chunks.h: Chapter 30: How to know any of this is true
chunks.t: You are reading a table. Model names down the left side, hardware names across the top, tokens per second in the cells. It looks authoritative. Almost none of the numbers in it are comparable to each other, because each was produced by a different method, and the method is rarely printed. Take a single card serving a 70B model at four bits. One report lands near the memory-bound ceiling for batch one. Another reports two thirds of that, from a mixed workload. Both are honest. The first divides the tokens the model generated by the seconds the decode loop ran, on a batch of one, with the KV cache already warm.

chunks.h: Chapter 30: How to know any of this is true
chunks.t: The second divides every token the client received by the wall-clock seconds the client waited, across a mixed workload with prompts arriving during the run. Change the completion budget, the prompt length, the concurrency, or the cache state and the same card gives you a different number. Each measurement is real. On its own it is a rumour.

chunks.h: Three instruments, three different answers
chunks.t: Three instruments produce these numbers, and each answers a different question. Counters are the engine's own bookkeeping, exported for scraping. They are monotonic sums since the process started, things like prompt tokens submitted, seconds spent in prefill, and requests completed. Dividing a sum by its count gives a mean. Counters are cheap, they are always on, and they do not care what the client's network did. What they cannot give you is the shape of the distribution. A summary type that publishes only a sum and a count is a mean with extra steps.

chunks.h: Three instruments, three different answers
chunks.t: If the exporter publishes a histogram you get buckets, but the boundaries were chosen by whoever wrote the exporter, and anything finer than the narrowest bucket is gone. Counters also reset when the process restarts, so a rate computed across a restart is nonsense unless you detect the reset. Logs are per-request records. They can give you the distribution, provided each line carries a start and an end timestamp, or an explicit duration, alongside its token counts; a single completion timestamp plus token counts gives you throughput and inter-arrival times, not per-request latency. They fail in three ways.

chunks.h: Three instruments, three different answers
chunks.t: The timestamp is taken somewhere inside the server, not at the client, so the latency it records excludes network transit and client-side queueing, and the number is lower than what the user experienced. Logs are sampled or rotated under load, so the requests you most want to see are the ones most likely to be missing. And logging costs time, synchronously in the request path or asynchronously in CPU, memory and I/O contention, so a heavily logged run can be slower than the run you were trying to measure. Wall-clock timing is what the user experiences.

chunks.h: Three instruments, three different answers
chunks.t: It includes tokenization, queueing for an admission slot, the scheduler's decision, prefill, decode, detokenization, and the client's own overhead. It is the only instrument that answers how long I waited, and it is the only one that cannot tell you why. When a request takes eleven seconds, the wall clock says eleven seconds. The counters say eight seconds of prefill and two of decode, and the gap between the sum and the wall clock is where queueing and overhead live.

chunks.h: Units, averages, and what the mean hides
chunks.t: The first trap is a units problem that looks like an arithmetic problem. Decode throughput and end-to-end throughput share a unit and measure different things. A 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB of weights per step, so on a card with 3,350 GB/s the memory-bound step floor is 10.4 ms, which is 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7 tokens per second at batch one. Divide generated tokens by decode seconds and you can approach that ceiling. Divide every token in the request, prompt included, by the total request seconds and you are averaging the prefill in, so the same run reports less. Neither is wrong. Quoting one without saying which is. The second trap is the average itself.

chunks.h: Units, averages, and what the mean hides
chunks.t: A mean of a bimodal distribution describes a request that never happened. Serving traffic is routinely bimodal, because a request that hits the prefix cache skips the prefill matrix multiplies for its whole prefix and pays almost nothing, while a request that misses pays for every token. Average the two populations and you get a prefill duration that describes neither. To compute a percentile you sort the durations and use the nearest-rank method. For p99 with 100 requests the rank is ceil(0.99 × 100) = 100, so p99 is the maximum. For p50 the rank is ceil(0.50 × 100) = 50. Report percentiles, and report the sample size next to them.

chunks.h: Units, averages, and what the mean hides
chunks.t: A mean without a percentile is a claim about a population that may not exist.

chunks.h: How the prefix cache contaminates prefill rates
chunks.t: The prefix cache is the confound that contaminates most published prefill numbers. The mechanism is worth stating plainly. The serving stack splits the prompt into fixed-size token blocks. For each block, the engine computes a hash over the token IDs in that block and the hash of the preceding block. The chained hash means a match at block k implies that every earlier block matches. A lookup walks the chain until a block hash is absent. The matched blocks are reused, and the first missing block and everything after it are recomputed.

chunks.h: How the prefix cache contaminates prefill rates
chunks.t: Collisions are handled by storing the full token block beside the hash and comparing token IDs before reuse, so a collision produces a miss rather than wrong key and value tensors. Eviction is by least-recently-used block under a reference count; a block shared by several sequences is not freed until the last sequence releases it. Partial trailing blocks are not cached, so a prompt whose length is not a multiple of the block size pays for the remainder. The reused tokens still count as submitted tokens, because the counter counts tokens accepted, not tokens computed. Divide submitted tokens by prefill seconds and you are counting work that was skipped.

chunks.h: How the prefix cache contaminates prefill rates
chunks.t: Suppose a 65,536-token prompt arrives against a warm cache holding the first 32,750 tokens. Only 65,536 − 32,750 = 32,786 tokens are computed. The apparent rate, submitted tokens over prefill time, is therefore 65,536 ÷ 32,786 ≈ 2 times the computed rate, because the same seconds bought half the work. The apparent rate is a legitimate measurement of a warm-cache workload, and it says nothing about raw prefill speed. Publishing it without the hit ratio invites every reader to draw the wrong conclusion. Report both: tokens submitted, tokens computed, and the seconds they took.

chunks.h: How the prefix cache contaminates prefill rates
chunks.t: Prefix caching changes the prefill budget rather than the decode budget, and its economics are simple once the ratio is explicit. A block that hits costs a hash lookup and a reference-count bump. A block that misses costs a full pass through every layer for every token in the block. A miss at any block invalidates the rest of the chain, so the hit rate depends on how much prompt structure the workload shares. System prompts, tool schemas and few-shot prefixes are the usual source of sharing; independent user questions are not.

chunks.h: Warm-up costs that steady state never pays
chunks.t: Warm-up is the third trap. The first request after a process starts pays costs no later request pays. Four distinct costs can be separated with timestamps. CUDA graph capture records the decode loop's kernel launches into a graph; capture happens once per captured shape and batch size and costs a few iterations of the loop, and new shapes or concurrency levels can trigger additional captures. The memory allocator grows from its initial reservation to steady state as KV blocks and activation buffers are first touched. Kernel autotuning benchmarks candidate implementations for the shapes the first request presents. Weight paging covers any loader work deferred until first use.

chunks.h: Warm-up costs that steady state never pays
chunks.t: The engine can log a timestamp at process start, after graph capture, after allocator steady state, after autotune, and at first token. If each phase is independently instrumented and prefill is timestamped separately, the differences can attribute the penalty; otherwise overlapping phases and prefill inside the first-token interval make the deltas ambiguous. Without those timestamps you cannot say which share dominates. Do not average the first request into steady state. Report it separately, because a user who sends one request and waits experiences exactly that penalty and does not care about your steady state.

chunks.h: Concurrency, rooflines, and the remaining confounds
chunks.t: Concurrency changes the answer by a factor no single number can express, and the roofline is the tool for reasoning about it. Let W be the bytes of model weights touched per decode step, K the KV bytes read for all active sequences in that step, B the bandwidth, and N the number of active sequences. One pass over the weights serves every row, so the step moves W once and produces N tokens, and the aggregate ceiling is N × B ÷ (W + K). Work it on the same card. A 70B model at four bits gives W = 35 GB. For the cache term, take Llama 2 70B with 80 layers, 8 KV heads and a head dimension of 128 at two bytes per value.

chunks.h: Concurrency, rooflines, and the remaining confounds
chunks.t: Each layer holds 8 × 128 = 1,024 values per position; keys and values across all layers come to 2 × 80 × 1,024 = 163,840 values per position, and at two bytes each that is 163,840 × 2 = 327,680 bytes. At a 100,000-token context one stream's cache is 100,000 × 327,680 = 32,768,000,000 bytes, comparable to the weight read. Four streams still read the weights once but re-read the cache per stream, so the cache term is 4 × 32,768,000,000 = 131,072,000,000 bytes and dominates the step. Per-stream throughput falls even as aggregate throughput rises, and the crossover from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound arrives sooner at long context.

chunks.h: Concurrency, rooflines, and the remaining confounds
chunks.t: That is why quoting a single rate is misleading in both directions. Quote the batch-one rate and you have understated what the card can do for a batch job. Quote the aggregate at concurrency four and you have promised a user a rate they will not see, because each stream gets a quarter of it. Quote both, with the concurrency and the context length stated, and the reader can pick the one that matches their workload. Four more confounds deserve a line each. Clock throttling: an SM clock observed under load is not the silicon maximum, and the gap is consistent with a power limit, a current limit, or a thermal limit, and the clock alone does not identify which.

chunks.h: Concurrency, rooflines, and the remaining confounds
chunks.t: Report the observed clock with the run conditions and the power and temperature telemetry if you want to claim a cause. Cumulative counters: a stall or error counter that accumulates since process start must be read at the start and end of a run and subtracted, and publishing the cumulative value without the delta is not evidence that a particular run was affected. Health events: a run in which a process was killed and restarted halfway through is not a run, so state the watchdog, the memory floor, and whether any restart occurred. Feature attribution: an acceptance rate, a cache hit rate or a kernel occupancy is a covariate, not an explanation.

chunks.h: Concurrency, rooflines, and the remaining confounds
chunks.t: To attribute a throughput number to a feature, run an ablation with the same prompts, the same concurrency, the same cache state and the same completion budget, and toggle only that feature.

chunks.h: What a reproducible benchmark must state
chunks.t: A benchmark someone else can reproduce needs to state the model and its quantization, the hardware including memory type and bandwidth, the concurrency and the number of streams, the prompt length distribution and the completion budget, whether the prefix cache was cold, warm, or shared between runs, whether warm-up requests were discarded and how many, the clock observed under load, and the percentile table with its sample size. It should publish the raw counters alongside the derived rates, because the derived rates are where the errors live.

chunks.h: What a reproducible benchmark must state
chunks.t: It should say which instrument produced each number, because a wall-clock throughput and a counter-based throughput are different quantities that happen to share a unit. Capacity belongs in that note too, because it decides whether a long prompt is admitted at all. A pool of 262,144 positions split across four streams gives 65,536 positions per stream. Admission subtracts a 32,768-token reply budget, 16 rows for the decode round batch, and 2 positions for boundary slack: 65,536 − 32,768 − 16 − 2 = 32,750 tokens per stream. Raise the pool to 1,048,576 positions and the same arithmetic gives 1,048,576 ÷ 4 = 262,144, minus 32,768, minus 16, minus 2, for 229,358 tokens.

chunks.h: What a reproducible benchmark must state
chunks.t: A benchmark run at a context length above the first figure is measuring a different admission regime, and the report should say so. MLPerf, the benchmark suite launched in 2018 by an industry and academic consortium and now maintained by MLCommons, exists to enforce this. Its inference rules, maintained in the MLCommons inference_policies repository, specify warm-up, cache state and allowable substitutions. The rules are long because the alternative is a table of numbers that cannot be compared, which is what most of the field publishes anyway. When you read a tokens-per-second claim, ask what the cache hit rate was. Ask whether the figure is wall clock or counter-derived.

chunks.h: What a reproducible benchmark must state
chunks.t: Ask what concurrency it was measured at and what the per-stream rate was. Ask whether the first request was included. If the answer to any of those is not stated, you are reading a rumour with a decimal point.

chunks.h: Chapter 31: Two small machines, by arithmetic
chunks.t: This chapter is a case study, not a benchmark. Two GB10 boxes sit on a desk with a cable between them, and nothing below was measured on that pair. Every number comes from a published specification or from arithmetic printed in the sentence that uses it. The question is how far the previous thirty chapters carry you before you plug anything in.

chunks.h: Why a pair of small machines is interesting
chunks.t: NVIDIA's DGX Spark hardware guide describes one memory system for the GB10: LPDDR5X shared between the CPU and the GPU, moving at 273 GB/s, in a coherent pool of 128 GB per box. There is no separate VRAM on a faster path and no host memory to spill into. Weights, KV cache and live activations compete for the same bus. That single number decides what the pair is good for. An H100 moves 3,350 GB/s, so one H100 sustains 3,350 ÷ 273 = 12.3 times the bandwidth of one GB10. A decode step is a bandwidth problem, so for single-stream work that ratio is close to the whole story. The pair's advantage is 256 GB of pool and a second memory bus at a price and power draw a single H100 does not reach.

chunks.h: Why a pair of small machines is interesting
chunks.t: Capacity is generous and bandwidth is the constraint. Keeping those two facts apart is most of what follows.

chunks.h: The weight budget on one box
chunks.t: Start with what has to fit. A 70B model at four bits is 35 GB of weights. One box holds that inside its 128 GB pool with room left for cache and activations. The same model at FP16 is 140 GB, which does not fit in one box, so a single box cannot serve it at full precision no matter how the kernel is written. Two boxes change the arithmetic twice. The pool doubles to 256 GB, so 140 GB fits. The model then has to be split, and the split is what costs you: every layer boundary that crosses the cable becomes a collective. Capacity is solved by adding a box, and the bill for adding it arrives in the next section.

chunks.h: The weight budget on one box
chunks.t: The 4-bit case is the one worth carrying forward, because it is the configuration the rest of the book has been computing with. At 35 GB the weights fit on one box, so the pair is needed for context rather than for parameters.

chunks.h: Splitting the model across the pair
chunks.t: Tensor parallelism splits each weight matrix by row or by column, so each rank holds half of every matrix rather than half of the layers. For a 70B model at four bits the shard is 35 GB ÷ 2 = 17.5 GB per rank. Each rank reads its own 17.5 GB per decode step and neither reads the other's half. The split needs agreement at two points per transformer layer, after the attention output projection and after the MLP down-projection. A model with 32 layers therefore runs 2 × 32 = 64 all-reduces per forward pass. Each one moves the activation matrix in bf16 across the cable and blocks both ranks until it lands.

chunks.h: Splitting the model across the pair
chunks.t: At decode the batch is small, so the payload is small and the cost is latency rather than bandwidth. At prefill the matrix has one row per prompt token, so the payload grows with the prompt and the collective becomes a bandwidth problem of its own. This is the structural difference between one box and two. On one box the decode step is one read of the weights and nothing else. On two boxes the same step is one read of half the weights plus 64 waits, and no roofline contains those waits.

chunks.h: What the pair's roof looks like
chunks.t: The roofline for one rank follows from the two numbers already printed. One rank reads 17.5 GB per step and can read it at 273 GB/s, so its ceiling is 273 ÷ 17.5 = 15.6 tokens per second. Two ranks each produce tokens, so the aggregate ceiling is 2 × 15.6 = 31.2 tokens per second, provided the collectives are free. They are not free, so 31.2 is an upper bound the pair cannot reach. Set the single card beside it. An H100 reads the whole 35 GB at 3,350 GB/s, so its batch-one ceiling is 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7 tokens per second. The ratio is 95.7 ÷ 31.2 = 3.07.

chunks.h: What the pair's roof looks like
chunks.t: One H100 is about three times the aggregate ceiling of the pair at batch one, and that comparison is generous to the pair because it ignores the collectives, which push the real figure lower. The ratio does not make the pair useless. At batch one the pair is a bandwidth-limited box with a cable attached; at larger batches the shared weight read is amortised across rows and the picture changes. What the ratio does say is that the pair is not a substitute for a single fast card on latency-sensitive single-stream work.

chunks.h: Where the arithmetic stops being enough
chunks.t: Three things the arithmetic leaves out, and each matters more than the last digit of 31.2. The collectives come first. Every all-reduce has a fixed latency plus a transfer term, and 64 of them per forward pass serialise with the matmuls unless the implementation overlaps them with the next layer's compute. A pair on a fast link hides most of that. A pair on a slower link does not, and the published bandwidth says nothing about which link you have. The KV cache comes second. The roofline above assumes the step reads only weights. At long context the cache is re-read for every active stream, so the bytes per step become the weights plus the cache, and the ceiling falls.

chunks.h: Where the arithmetic stops being enough
chunks.t: The chapter on the step budget ran that arithmetic for a single card; the same arithmetic applies here with 17.5 GB in place of 35 GB, which makes the cache term relatively larger rather than smaller. The third is the fraction of the roof a real kernel reaches. A published bandwidth is a peak. A decode kernel that reads 17.5 GB in small tiles reaches some fraction of 273 GB/s, and that fraction is the one number in this chapter that cannot be derived. It has to be measured on the pair, with the context length and the batch stated next to it. That is the job the methodology chapter describes.

chunks.h: What this setup can and cannot answer
chunks.t: This chapter gives the shape of the answer. A 70B model at four bits fits on one box with room to spare. The pair doubles the pool and halves the per-rank weight read. The per-rank roof is 15.6 tokens per second and the aggregate roof is 31.2. A single H100's roof is 95.7, about three times higher. Every one of those figures follows from 273 GB/s, 35 GB and arithmetic printed beside it. It cannot tell you what the pair will actually do. One configuration, one model size, one precision, and a roofline that is an upper bound rather than a result. The link between the boxes is unspecified. The achieved kernel bandwidth is unspecified. The context length is unspecified.

chunks.h: What this setup can and cannot answer
chunks.t: Any of those can move the real number by a factor of two, and none can be filled in from a specification sheet. What it can do is make a prediction checkable. Run the pair and see something far below 31.2 tokens per second at batch one, and the gap is collectives, kernel efficiency or cache traffic, in that order of likelihood. See something far above it, and one of the inputs is wrong, because a bandwidth roof is a roof. That is the use of a derived case study: it tells you which direction to be surprised in.
